speakerposition: topic
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. C. C. BALLANTYNE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved that the House go into Committee of Supply.
He said: Before this motion carries, I desire to place before hon. members the particulars concerning the operations of the Canadian Government merchant ships during the fiscal year ended December 31, 1920. I thought it well to do so at this time in order that hon. members may be in possession of the facts. Hon. members

will be in a better position, after a perusal of the Hansard report of my remarks, to ask whatever questions they may deem proper when the House is again in Committee of Supply. If it is agreeable to hon. members, I would suggest at the outset that they be good enough to allow me to finish without interruption whatever I have to say. When we are in Committee of Supply I will, to the very best of my ability, and with the greatest pleasure, give the fullest information to hon. members regarding the operations of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine.
Mr. Speaker, when, on April 4, 1918, I had the honour of announcing to Parliament the Government's shipbuilding programme, I gave the reasons which impelled us to enter upon such an undertaking. Although it may be a repetition of what I then said, I shall now briefly restate the reasons which caused the Government to create a Canadian Government merchant marine. During the spring of 1918 the war was at its most critical period, and losses in shipping tonnage throughout the world were very grave. Indeed, so serious was the situation at that particular time that it amounted to a race between the enemy submarines and the shipbuilding yards of the British Empire-in the one case to destroy allied tonnage as rapidly as possible, and in the other case to make good, as far as possible, that loss of tonnage. In the first place, therefore, this Government thought it wise to enter upon shipbuilding as a war measure. Before that decision was reached the British Government was utilizing our steel shipbuilding yards throughout the Dominion for the construction of steel ships for its own purposes, which ships were under British registry, the Canadian Government providing the necessary funds. However, as these vessels were being built for the Mother Land, and under British registry, the moment they were ready to be put into commission they would necessarily pass into the possession of the British Government to be utilized by it in the way it might deem best. The Dominion Government, therefore, came to the conclusion, and its decision received the unanimous approval of the House at that time, that it would be better for Canada in the national interests, seeing that she was financing the construction of these ships that were being built for the British Government, that we should build ships under Canadian registry and for the benefit of the Canadian people. Accordingly our first reason for entering upon the shipbuilding

programme at that time was the imperative need of providing shipping to make up the immense losses that were occurring almost hourly during the most critical period of the war. The second reason for embarking upon this policy was that the Government owned a large system of railways amounting to about 18,000 miles, and which will be increased to something like 23,000 miles if the acquisition of the Grand Trunk goes into effect. Having this vast system of national railways, the Government deemed it necessary to complete the chain of transportation by providing ships to carry the cargoes that would be transported over this immense railway system to our seaports for exportation. The third, but by no means the least important, reason for the construction of these ships was to enable Canada to expand- her export trade; and as I proceed with my remarks hon. members will see that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine has performed a very great national work in opening up' new trade routes and in helping to develop and expand the export trade of the Dominion. At this stage permit me to say, Mr. Speaker, that no new contracts for ships have been let since the year 1919. I have noticed from time to time that the press of Canada, and occasionally some gentlemen engaged in banking-the presidents of our large financial institutions

have called upon the Government not to construct any more ships, expressing the opinion that the time had arrived when shipbuilding by the Government in this country ought to cease. I find no fault with these financial gentlemen except to say that when they made such appeals they seemingly were not aware that the Government had not placed any new contracts for the construction of ships since the year 1919, but was simply carrying to completion its original shipbuilding programme. Some of those who made this demand were of the opinion that when the armistice was signed the Canadian Government should not have given any more contracts for ships. Now, I explained to the House last year, and I repeat the statement, that the Government's reason for continuing the shipbuilding programme was the serious labour conditions that existed throughout Canada at the time of the signing of the armistice, and which conditions prevailed through the year 1919. Thousands of skilled and unskilled workmen were out of employment in the Dominion; and as, at that time, hundreds of thousands of our brave men were returning from the front, the Government 81
felt that it was its plain duty, to carry on shipbuilding and to give employment not only to the men then needed in the industry, but to others who were likely to require work, and especially the returned soldiers-that from the point of view of making provision for unemployment it would be a wise policy for the Government to continue its shipbuilding programme. I hope the House will pardon me if, from this point, I adhere somewhat more closely to my notes in order to afford hon. gentlemen that detailed statistical information which is so imperatively necessary in connection with this important matter.
The year 1920, as was generally anticipated, proved unsatisfactory to shipping interests the world over, more especially from the point of view of net earnings. The loss of tonnage that had been sustained during the war was more than overtaken, with the result that there had been throughout the year a surplus of available tonnage. The world tonnage at the commencement of the war was about 49,000,000 tons. The available world tonnage at present is about 65,000,000 tons.
The costs of operation that had reached abnormally high proportions during the war and to which reference will be made later, continued throughout the year. That taken in conjunction with the substantial decline in freight rates from those of the previous year, added very materially to the difficulties with which shipowners had to cope. During the year there was a very severe decline in freight rates from United Kingdom ports over well defined routes, such as those to India and South America. While the decline in trans-Atlantic rates to United Kingdom ports was not so acute, it was nevertheless very substantial, and had a marked effect on the earnings of vessels. For instance there has been a decline of 65 per cent in the rate on flour; on grain 61 per cent; on deals 55 per cent; on cereals 48 per cent; and on apples 41 per cent. On cargoes from Canadian ports to South American ports decreases have averaged from 17 per cent to 50 per cent. On cargoes to India there has been a decline of 20 per cent in the comparatively short time since the route was established. From British Columbia ports to Australia there has been a steady decline averaging between 15 per cent and 35 per cent. On the one article of lumber the decline over the rate for 1919 was, during 1920, at least 25 per cent.
Over all the principal trade routes, both transatlantic and transpacific, there has been a corresponding decline in freight

Now I come to the comparative cost of construction. The average cost of constructing all the vessels under the Government shipbuilding programme figures out at $191.95 per deadweight ton. The average cost of the vessels constructed by the United States Shipbuilding Board has been stated in a recent official communication to be about $215.00 per deadweight ton. So that on a much smaller programme our cost compares very favourably indeed with the cost of construction of similar steel vessels by our,friends to the south, being nearly $24 per ton less than theirs.

In accordance with the trade agreement concluded during the year with the British West Indies it was decided to equip two of the 5,100-ton vessels then under construction with passenger accommodation, in consequence of which a regular service every three weeks has been established between Canada and the Bahamas, Jamaica and British Honduras. The delegates at the very important conference held in this city in June of last year-I refer to the conference in Ottawa held with a view to negotiating a preferential trade agreement between Canada and the West Indies- particularly the delegates from the Bahamas, Jamaica and British Honduras, claimed that they were very short indeed

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
of passenger services. I informed them, as your Minister of Marine, that the Government did not own or intend to build any passenger ships, but the delegates were very much interested in the matter and continued their pressure upon me and the other representatives of the Government, requesting us to equip, if possible, some of our freight ships with a limited passenger accommodation. I pointed out to them that I did not think it would pay to equip freight ships with a limited passenger accommodation and to operate them on such a long route as that of Halifax to the Bahamas, Jamaica and British Honduras and back over the same route in the winter, and from Montreal in the summer. The representatives from the West Indies then said that if it did not pay, the countries they represented would each contribute a certain amount. I am sorry I have not before me the amount that each of the Islands stipulated in the agreement that it would be willing to pay, but if my memory serves me correctly the amount in all would be about £13,000. We cannot tell at the present time whether or not this new route will pay, but judging from one or two voyages that the ships have made, it looks as if it might break even. I would not, however, he prepared to make that as a positive statement; we shall have to wait until the end of the fiscal year. While the accommodation provided is but for twenty-six cabin, passengers on each vessel, it is of such an excellent character that it attracts a full passenger list for each sailing. Full cargoes also have been carried, and it is confidently expected that the regularity and character of the service generally will build up a profitable business in the interchange of the products of these British possessions and Canada. The first vessel on this route sailed from Halifax on January 25 last, with a full complement of passengers and a general cargo of flour, potatoes, oats, cement and general merchandise.
The House and the country generally, and the exporters of Canada in particular, will he interested to know what these ships are capable of doing in the way of expanding Canada's export trade. In this connection, Sir, I regret to have to express my dissappointment with the efforts so far made by the Canadian manufacturer and exporter. These ships have been equipped with one or two extra passenger cabins in order that Canadian business men might either go themselves to these British possessions and foreign countries, or send

their commercial agents. While the showing of exports is not a bad one so far, I would like again to make an urgent appeal to the manufacturers and business men of Canada to reach out more aggressively for export trade. I said last year, and I say it again, that if Canada is to wipe out her immense war debt within a reasonable time, Canadians must not only look after the home trade but reach out aggressively for foreign markets. We have provided this magnificent fleet of freight ships and these new routes have been opened up. No, old-established steamship company would take the chance that the Government ships have taken in opening up one new route after another; these old companies would naturally hesitate and first try to ascertain whether or not it would be profitable to put ships on the various new routes to which I have referred. But these ships are Canadian ships, built in the national interest. The Government has never attempted, and, I hope never will attempt, to interfere in the management of these ships; all I have said to the management as the responsible minister was, that they should make all the money they could, at the same time keeping the national interest in mind and assisting the Canadian people in every possible way to export the products of fishery, forest, farm, mine, and factory. Canadians, therefore, have reason to be proud that they possess this immense fleet of new ships going to all corners of the world, and making a very creditable showing, to which I shall refer in a moment. But the great feature of a Canadian merchant marine is the fact that this country can say:	We want
this ship, or so many ships, run on whichever route we think there is a possibility of Canada obtaining trade and thus expanding her export business.
The principal exports of Canadian products by the vessels of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine have been:
From Atlantic ports to Malta, Barcelona, India, Ceylon and Java.
From Atlantic ports to Liverpool, London, Glasgow, Cardiff and Swansea.
From Atlantic ports to the British West Indies, Cuba and South America.
To Australia from Vancouver.
To Newfoundland from Montreal and Halifax.
The exports to Malta, Barcelona, India, Ceylon and Java consisted of iron and steel products, glass, furniture, agricultural implements, rubber goods, automobiles, grain, flour, etc.

To United Kingdom ports the exports have been grain, flour, cereals, canned goods, bacon, cheese, apples, pulp, paper, lumber, iron and steel, machinery, implements, etc.
To the British West Indies the products exported have been cement, flour, trunks, iron and steel products, paper, machinery, furniture, etc.
To South America the exports have been pulp and paper, malt, agricultural implements, dried fish, steel products, lumber, etc.
To Cuba exports have consisted mainly of pulp and paper, malt, flour, hay, lumber, fish, potatoes, whiskey, oats and cement.
To Australia there have been exported from British Columbia ports, lumber, paper, cement, fish, machinery, rubber goods, etc.
From Montreal and Halifax to Newfoundland, there have been exported flour, hay, oats, paper, cheese, cement, etc.
The importance of the merchant marine to Canadian trade cannot be too strongly emphasized. Canadian goods to the value of over $50,000,000 have been transported during the year in Canadian-built ships, each named vessel with its prefix "Canadian" being the best advertisement for Canada in the principal markets of the world.
I have now arrived at what, I presume, will be the most interesting part of my statement this afternoon, and that is: What results have been obtained from the operation of these ships during the past calendar year? I will, therefore, proceed at once to give this information to the House.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I am sure we have listened with a great deal of interest to the exhaustive statement of the Minister of Marine. It is difficult for the ordinary man not fully trained in business, to grasp the details so as to be able to say whether or not we are in a solvent condition in connection with the business of shipping. One thing that strikes a person at once is the fact that we have built ships, according to the statement of the minister, costing something like $191 per deadweight ton. These ships are not to-day worth half the money paid for them, but in making out his statement the hon. gentleman puts upon his balance sheet the value of the ships as if it were really what the ships cost in the first instance. They are probably worth less than half of what they cost, and the minister will find that possibly he could not sell any one of his ships to-day at one-third of the price he paid for its construction. Indeed, it is doubtful whether he could sell them at all; it is exceedingly doubtful whether he could give them away. It is therefore a grave question for the Canadian people whether or not the expenditure of seventy-five million dollars in ships, which certainly will not pay for their operation, and which we could not get off of our hands if we wanted to sell them, is a wise venture. That, of course, will be brought out more fully when we are studying the details of the minister's estimates, when we shall have an opportunity of going carefully into these matters. Perhaps it is interesting to know that it is just twelve years ago to-day when the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) moved his famous resolution involving the building of ships in this country. That resolution was moved on the 29th March, 1909, and the final action of the House, so far as the resolution itself was concerned, took place on the following day, the 30th March, 1909. The policy that was agreed to by both sides of the House at that time involved the building of a Canadian navy, and, incidentally, the building of merchant marine ships as they might be required for the general purposes of the country. It is unnecessary to say to-day that, if that policy had been adopted, when the war broke out we should have had warships at normal prices, costing about a fourth of what we

are paying for ordinary tramp ships today; and the prices of other ships would have been proportionate. But a change of government took place; new men came to the helm, and new policies followed, a policy of delay, a policy of do nothing, a policy in regard to shipbuilding which stood in abeyance for some years, from 1909 until the 4th day of April, 1918, as the minister has just announced. I would say to my hon. friend at once that when he came to parliament on the date referred to with a shipbuilding policy for the construction of tramp ships, of freight ships, that if it had not been for the war he could not have had a "look in" for this policy at all. But we were then suffering under the stress of war, and anything that would have a tendency to relieve the existing situation was likely to receive and did receive the support of both sides of the House. But I say to the minister, and I address my remarks also to the Government, that when that distressing situation ceased, when the armistice was signed-which I believe was on the 11th of November, 1918, a few months after the Government's policy was inaugurated-when the necessity for building ships for war purposes had disappeared, and he should have halted, he should have finished the construction of the ships then in hand and not have ventured any further into the business of shipbuilding. I am sure that if I had been in the House at that time, and I suppose I was, I would have given my assistance-at all events by a vote if that were necessary-to the establishment of the policy of building ships for purposes rendered necessary by the war; but I am not so clear that it was necessary, even according to the statement of the hon. gentleman, to step in and build these ships. He says that all the Canadian shipyards at that time were fully engaged in the building of ships for the Home Government for the purposes of the war; that we were supplying the money and the ships were being built as rapidly as they could be built. If that was the case I do not at all see the necessity why we stepped in. If there was a possibility of adding to the quantity of tonnage that was imperatively required, owing to war reasons, I would put up both hands for making a start; but when the armistice was signed there was no further necessity for the building of ships by this Government

not a vessel was then being torpedoed and we
had plenty of shipping in this country for all practical purposes. Such being the case, I do say that from that moment forward the Minister of Marine and the Government have been following a policy which is absolutely wrong and absurd, as far as business principles are concerned, and have followed a policy that will be as bad for 'Canada as it has been in the case of the national ownership of railways. When we come to put a proper value on these ships, when another year comes and we get an honest statement from the Department of Marine, we will find that in proportion to the amount of money invested we are just as badly off as we are in connection with the government-owned railways. Therefore it is only a further evidence that governments should, as far as possible, keep their hands off private enterprises and allow private individuals, who are trained in these enterprises, to look after them-the Government should confine itself to looking after the administration of the affairs of the country generally. That is the position which I have always taken in connection with the railroads. Of course if, during the war, it was necessary for railroads to be built by the nation for war purposes I would have voted for such a policy and said that was the proper thing to do; but when the war ended I would certainly be opposed to any further building of railways for war purposes. In the same way I am opposed to the building of ships on any such ground.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if these ships are for the development of Canadian trade we should undertake that development where it is most necessary, and where it will be of direct advantage to the people of Canada. What is the matter, if the ships of the Canadian Merchant Marine are lying idle, with using these ships to develop the coal trade of this country? Last week the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) moved a [DOT] resolution for an investigation into the coal situation, and in speaking in its support he declared that conditions in Ontario, particularly in the western part, were such that the inhabitants dreaded the approach of winter because they had no supplies of coal available. Well, there is an abundance of coal in the province of Nova Scotia and in the Maritime Provinces generally. Evidently, according to the minister, we have lots of shipping. In that case, seeing that navigation in open up to a point beyond Montreal, what is the matter with

using the ships of the Canadian Merchant Marine for the transportation of coal from the Maritime Provinces and having it stored at places inland where it would be available for our own people-in other words having Canadian coal carried by our own ships and by our own railways, if that is necessary, for the safety, protection and well being of our own people? Is it not much better to have our ships engaged in that way than for them to be swinging idly at anchor in the different harbours along our coasts, while in the meantime the overhead expense goes on just the same, the officers, the sailors, the engineers, and the firemen being paid just the same although they are doing nothing? Would it not be better if we had a statement from the minister that such a service as I have indicated was about to be put into operation? Would it not be better that, possessing shipping and facilities for transportation, we should get the benefit of them in our own country? But what, sir, are the facts? The minister made the remarkable statement that the Government is competing with itself in the matter of the carriage of freight. We have two ports on our Atlantic coast from which we send goods to Newfoundland. The terminus of the Intercolonial Railway, and of the National Railway system, is at North Sydney. From that port large quantities of goods-and we would like the amount to be very much larger-are sent to Newfoundland. Halifax is the only other Atlantic port from which we export goods from Canada to Newfoundland, so far as I know. Well, the minister has told us that he is competing at Halifax with the Government railway at North Sydney. That railway, to make money, must carry goods from North Sydney whence they go to Newfoundland. If these goods are taken off at Halifax and the Canadian Government 'steamships are employed in their carriage, thus operating in competition with the government railway system, we have the most .aubsurd spectacle of a government competing against itself in the carriage of freight and cutting down its own profits. That is the situation as it is to-day.
I repeat, the minister should have called a halt when we reached the stage that there was no further necessity for building ships on account of war conditions. But he made the mistake of continuing in his policy, and now he finds that he has a white elephant on his hands in the shape of these ships. He cannot sell them to advantage and cannot operate them at a profit under present conditions. Of course

the same cry will be raised by his department that was raised by the Department of Railways in regard to the railway situation: This is not of our choosing, these vessels are on our hands, what are we to do with them? That was the cry with the Department of Railways uttered with respect to the railways-these railways have been put on our hands, what will we do with them?-we will have to do something with them. And so it goes on and the people pay the piper every time. In conclusion, I wish to point out that if we are going to have these ships they should be used to the advantage of our own people and in improving trade conditions in Canada. The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer) pointed out, and ha was backed up by hon. gentlemen opposite, that the only way to fully develop trade from the east to the west in this country, is by the opening up of the St. Lawrence route-at least it is one of the routes available and the most feasible one. Let me say to the minister that if he is going to have these ships on his' hands he should make every possible effort to open up a proper channel, as far inland as possible in Canada, so that he will find a use for at least a few of these vessels. At present he has too many, far too many. Any person who has any sense of proportion, or any business capacity will invest his money in a trade in proportion to its development. The minister has gone far too fast in the building of ships in Canada and he will find that there is no work for these ships to do, that he has to compete with the world in the carriage of freight. He will not be in a position to get any business that will amount to a paying proposition. I hope that when we come down to details in regard to this matter the minister will be able to present us with fuller and better information.
I congratulate the minister upon his apparent willingness to throw the full flood of daylight upon the operations of his department. I am pleased to know that he is not following the Nieodemus-like practice of the Department of Railways and Canals; he is not moving in the night. He proposes by his open way of doing business to dispense with the secret manoeuvres of the "dark-lantern brigade" operating our railways and which has to report to us a deficit of something like $70,000,000 or $100,000,000. So not only in business but in all other matters, we, on this side of the House at all events, will commend and encourage the most open methods, and we trust that before we are

through with the minister's Estimates and our discussion of his general policy he will find that we are quite capable of appreciating the situation. And he had better come here equipped with the fullest information that he can give the House in regard to this enterprise.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should wish as far as possible to accede to any request so courteously made as the request of the hon. Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne) that discussion upon the statement which he has presented to the House this afternoon should be postponed until we have had time to read it and are seized of the details of the very large question involved. But in that connection it occurs to me that the Government have not been well advised in bringing this matter before the House this afternoon. We had better look at this thing squarely without any camouflage,- to use the word which is so common on our lips and in our newspapers to-day. There is a great deal of talk about this shipping scheme in the press, there is a great deal of talk about it in the business circles of Montreal and other shipping points of the country, and there is a great deal of talk about it amongst serious citizens who are to any extent apprized of the grave financial position of this country. And while, I repeat, I should have desired to wait for details, I think the postponement might very well have been on the part of the ministry until we had a full House to discuss a question which is bulking so large in the public thought and is of such vital importance to this country. Not having any knowledge that this statement would be submitted this afternoon, and not having had time to peruse the speech of my hon. friend, I am a little at a loss to go into this whole question, but I should not have been doing justice to my own conscience as a citizen of Canada and as a member of this House, and I should not have been doing justice to a great public question, if I allowed it to pass without at least a word or two of comment.
My hon. friend from Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) does not seem quite content to have any part or lot in this shipping business at the present moment. Well, he betrays considerable agility in that respect in being able to turn a pretty sharp corner, Mr. Speaker, unless my memory fails me. I am not fortified with any more than my recollection of Hansard, but if my recollection is correct, my hon. friend the Minister of
Marine might very well have thanked the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria, as well as the hon. members for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) and Shelburne and Queen's (Mr, Fielding) for the initial support, at any rate, which was rendered to his scheme. As for me, Sir, my garments are clean. Any member of this House can read the debates in regard to the shipping programme that have taken place from the first day that my hon. friend brought his scheme before Parliament and he will find me on record as having warned the minister that he was embarking upon a scheme which was going to lead to financial disaster for the country -and I do not mind telling him very frankly that there are a good many of his own friends who know that that financial disaster, if not actually here, is very close at hand. My recollection about my hon. friend from North Cape Breton and Victoria is that this shipping business bulked very largely in his political career. I am not at all sure that it was not in a debate on shipping that he made his famous avowal of being a protectionist. If I am wrong he will correct me. I am nearly sure that it was in that debate. He was leader of the Opposition at the time, and naturally on a question of this size and importance being introduced he, as leader of the Opposition, had to stand up and tell the people what he thought, and he did not hesitate much about it. He said: I am a protectionist. I am all for selling steel plates as long as they are made in Nova Scotia; I am for building ships, if it furnishes a market for steel plates in Nova Scotia. I hope I am not misrepresenting my hon. friend. I am nearly sure that that is the substance which a reasonably good memory furnishes me with of what he said on that occasion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: This is a case, Mr. Speaker, in which silence does not give consent.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I did not
catch what my hon. friend said. It was addressed in so low a tone and so exclusively to the Speaker that it could not possibly reach me at this end of the chamber.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I said
that this is a case in which silence does not give consent.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, there*are times when it is necessary to keep silence even from good words. But I do not know that my hon. friend

has any very good defence to make in any very good words, for I know his pugnacity is so great that that defence would be forthcoming at the point of the usual dagger which he carries so handy. I think that his silence certainly does give consent, and that he practically agrees that I am not misrepresenting what his attitude was on that occasion.
Now, we are not in any doubt about what the attitude of other hon. members was, because the minister, who doubtless has refreshed his memory for the occasion, has offered his thanks to the hon. members for Shelburne and Queen's and for Maison-neuve for their kind support to his scheme at the time, I think he said, of its initiation. Well, I have not misunderstood that point. That may account in some measure for what, I repeat, is a somewhat extraordinary line of procedure. I do not know why a statement of this importance should have been brought on the first day after the holidays when notoriously it is the general expectation that we have a small House, unless it was thought that it could be crowded through and no discussion take place upon it. I seriously hope there was no understanding of that kind in the House. I should be very sorry for parliamentary traditions and parliamentary practice if we had got to that point. But, I repeat, I should not have done my duty to myself and to the country if I had not stated where I stand in the matter and repeated the warnings that I have given before. I do not know how far my hon. friend the minister intends to go with this scheme. He now has not the leader of the Opposition to deal with apparently, but the ex-leader of the Opposition, in a very much chastened frame of mind compared with that in which he spoke about shipping in the early stages of this scheme.
Now, I just want to say this about this shipping measure as far as we have it before us this afternoon. I did not hear the minister's whole statement, so I do not know what he intends to do further in the matter. But I want to endorse what my hon. friend the member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) pointed out-that this is a scheme which in its magnitude is now almost as serious as the railroad problem which is exercising the mind of every thoughtful Canadian. I say that without fear of successful contradiction. The minister went into it with his eyes open, with warnings in frojjt of him. He has gone into it by stages from year to year. At the time of the armistice-I rely

upon public prints for my information, but if I am correctly informed, at that time an expenditure of only sixteen and one-half millions of money had been embarked upon in the carrying out of this scheme. Now, that was a considerable sum of money, but as my hon. friend from North Cape Breton says, these contracts were given in war time, for a specific purpose, when the whole country was behind any step that was necessary for the winning of the war. Our losses could have been cut to a very small proportion indeed if we had stopped this business at the time of the armistice-even if my hon. friend had stopped at the time I warned him he should stop; at the time I warned him that he was backing a "wrong 'un" for the people of this country.
Now, what is the condition of affairs? The same public prints tell me that including the contracts that were entered into with the Imperial Munitions Board, this country has embarked upon an expenditure up to date of no less a sum than $140,000,000 in connection with this shipbuilding scheme. These are very serious statements; they are statements which require an alert Opposition. One hundred and forty millions embarked upon; these statements are made in public. And what is the condition of the property? I have a recollection of recent statements, made, I think, last year; I have a recollection of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine saying that he could sell these ships for more than they had cost to build.. Would he repeat that statement to-day? If he did he would correct the best business columns of the best newspapers in this country, because we are told what is in accordance with the shipping knowledge of everybody who has studied shipping at all, that the value of the ships has been cut in half. I question whether for any ship he has built the minister could get half of what it cost him to build it. That is a very serious matter, Mr. Speaker, for the people of this country. It is a very serious position for any minister of the Crown to be in in regard to a scheme with which he persevered in spite of warnings that he was going in the wrong direction.
What about freights to-day? Why, before coming east I read a statement issuing from the port of St. John from the man who is responsible for getting cargoes for the government ships, that cargoes were not to be had. I warned my hon. friend that it would be so. I told him from my own personal experience what shipping in Britain had paid during the Boer war and what it was paying within a year and a half after-

wards; percentages of twenty had shrunk to one and one and one-half, and the people holding the shares were glad to get it. He had these warnings before him. Despite his attempt to make a rosy story this afternoon, that is the position the Government of Canada is in with regard to these ships: The value of the ships is cut through the middle; freights cannot be had. Why, only the other day I read in the columns of the Montreal Star-a publication coming from a very good town, one which has a reputation for political leanings that would lead one to think it would be favourable, if it could be, to the Government in power and to the Minister of Marine-that some of the merchant ships of Canada were coasting along the shores of Scandinavia seeking cargoes, and that some of them have even been looking furtively to Germany for cargoes, until Canadian exports revive; a very interesting statement to me, and it ought to be a very interesting statement to my hon. friend the Prime Minister, because it contains the admission that Canadian exports at the present moment are in need of being revived. Last summer the right hon. gentleman was rather jaunty about the condition of Canadian exports, but now it seems that Canadian ships have to coast along the shores of Scandinavia seeking cargoes, "until Canadian exports revive." Yet one of the objects of the building of these ships, according to my hon. friend's statement this afternoon, was to promote the export trade of Canada.
Now, that is the position of my hon. friend's enterprise up to date, according to statements that are printed in almost every newspaper in the country. For some of this information I depend on what my memory recalls to me of what appeared not later than Saturday in the parliamentary correspondence of the government organ, the press supporting the Government in this city.
We had this scheme entered lightly upon -and I dwell upon this for a moment without wishing to extend my remarks- we had this scheme entered upon according to old, bad political conditions Jin this country. Such schemes are as common under a protective tariff as withered leaves in autumn. My hon. friend to whom I have referred took occasion to avow himself a protectionist, thereby, with very great courage, probably losing the leadership of his party. The scheme is very simple; it was very simple at the time; it was simple to carry it on. We traded upon the patriotism of the people-the Government did, anyhow.
It looked so fine. "We have to help out the winning of the war"-we all agreed about that end of it. "It will be a splendid thing to build ships in Montreal and in Three Rivers"-I do not see my hon. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) here, but Three Rivers, I think, was included. Then, of course, there was Vancouver, and where else were they built? I do not remember all the places, but the minister is an adept at that sort of thing, and he got fine support for his scheme from both sides of the House. He introduced it, the steel plates were sold, and the orders were issued. Why shouldn't they be? We were getting subscriptions to Victory bonds at the time by the hundred million. I have, in private and in public, expressed the opinion that the last victory bond issue in this country, subscribed to the tune of seven hundred millions, was a positive curse both to the Government and to the country. It indicated vast patriotism on the part of our people, but it put money by the hundred million into the hands of a government that did not know how to handle it. So you had your ship schemes and your housing schemes-thank God, in regard to that the provinces have used only half the money that was voted-and a hundred other channels were opened for the frittering away of the wealth of the people, until the finances of this country are in the condition they are in to-day and that every man from one end of the country to another who follows public affairs knows they are in. That, shortly, is the history of what happened after the war was over in regard to this shipping business.
Now, as I said in beginning, Mr. Speaker, I merely wanted to put myself upon record for, I think, the fourth time-at any rate, I have gone on record whenever my hon. friend has had the question before the House in one sense-that this was a financial escapade that was going to end in disaster for the country. On each occasion I warner my hon. friend that that was so, and while it is never any great line of conduct to say "I told you so," I would still confine myself to a warning and I would say to the hon. minister, for goodness sake, stop this thing now. You have had your eyes opened to the real nature of it; let us have the thing cease now; let us cut our loss as the stockbrokers advise us to do.
The project was carried out, I am sorry to say, with large support from the other side of the House-support derived from the old, bad system of looking at the needs

of the constituency rather than the needs of the country. If ever there was a scheme which should have been supported as a great national scheme, it was this, if there was anything in it at all; but, as I have said in this House again and again, it was looked at, as politics teaches us always to look at these measures, for its local value at certain points. So that the plates were sold at one place and something else was sold somewhere else; the ships were placed in various localities whether they were represented by Tories or by Liberals, and the result is that to-day, to the tune, according to some newspapers, of $140,000,000, we have "a painted ship upon a painted ocean." That is the scheme of my hon. friend up to date and I hope we have heard the last of any extension of it. The further one goes with it, the worse off this country will be. How we shall get out of our difficulties, the Lord only knows. We will get good help towards getting out of them when we get, to handle the finances of this country, people who have more sense of financial responsibility than, I am sorry to say, has been displayed in this shipping scheme that is-I endorse what the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) says-a white elephant only second to that of our railways themselves.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
(Maison-neuve) : Mr. Speaker, as we have not before us the figures which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) gave to the House this afternoon, I will defer to a later date, when he brings down his Estimates, the general discussion and the specific discussion of some features of this venture. But in order that the House may understand at once my position in the matter, I wish to state that it is quite true that in 1918, during the war, before the armistice, I supported the shipbuilding programme of my hon. friend. Is that a crime, or is that an indication, as is suggested by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), of a dark association between both sides of this House in favour of some big interests? During the war, and because of the war, the Liberal party in the House of Commons stood for any sane and big national measure. From my seat in this House, I supported this shipping programme because we were officially informed that it was absolutely urgent that Canada should build ships in order to relieve the shipping situation of the Allies. I am not sorry in a way

that the experiment should have been made. We were told not so very long ago that it was absolutely impossible to build ships in Canada; that we could hardly find riveters; that we could not manufacture plates; that we could not have men to man our navy. I, as a Canadian, had enough pride that, even although told by Mr. Winston Churchill, that we were not able to build ships, we were, indeed, able to do it.
If I was in favour of the shipping programme of the Government during the war, before the armistice, one must not infer from that that I stand in favour of this huge expenditure now that the war is over. I can only re-echo what all business men in the country have been stating during the last two years, namely, that a halt should be. called to that carnival of expenditure. It is a well known fact that, since the armistice, and especially during the last fifteen or sixteen months, ships have been like a drug on the market in Great Britain, the United States and France. I have seen the figures; I have read the articles, and I have never understood why the Canadian Government and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) should have gone with such pig-headedness into this wild expenditure when they were warned from all sides, from all sources, that they were riding to a certain fall-because, from what I have learned this afternoon from the very attitude of the hon. gentleman, it is pretty certain that he is very gloomy as to the future of the Canadian Mercantile Marine Company.
I am glad, however, that he was able to state that Parliament could have access to all books, documents, even telegrams, which passed between the contractors and his department. His announcement is a justification of the attitude taken the other day by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and this side of the House, when we pleaded in vain with the Government for access, not to confidential documents which might injure the Canadian National Railway system, but to documents to which Parliament is naturally entitled. I suppose my hon. friend has been warned by responsible people, by friends of the Government, that the attitude of the leader of the Government (Mr. Meighen) and of his party, as well as the attitude of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) the other day, was not in conformity with British traditions and institutions. Why should we have

freer access to documents concerning the building and managing of a Government-owned navy than to documents referring to the building and managing of a Government-owned railway system? the two cases are parallel. But the other day the Government thought, perhaps, that the motion made by the leader of the Opposition was inopportune and that they should, therefore, vote against it. They have found out since however, from their own friends. I have in mind two articles published by a leading paper in this country, the Montreal Gazette, strongly condemning the Government and their friends for the vote they gave in the House the other day on the question of the production of documents. Is it not, Mr. Speaker, one of the elementary rights of hon. members of this House, elected by the people, that they are entitled to have access to the books and documents concerning the administration of the affairs of the country? Our railway system, our merchant marine, are both parts of the administration, perhaps in an indirect way, if you please, of the affairs of the country, and why should we have been refused by the Government the right to have access to these documents and books? I am glad my hon. friend has learned better and has taken heed of the advice from his friends in Montreal who complained bitterly of the refusal given by the Government.
As to the Canadian Merchant Marine, the Government will learn on that question also, they have lost the support of their best friends. My hon.' friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries said this afternoon that the bankers were not well informed when they dared criticise the administration of that branch of his department. Mr. Speaker, there are no two men in this country better informed than the President of the Bank of Montreal and the President of the Royal Bank, and they both condemn the Canadian Government Merchant Marine as an unwise enterprise which in the long run would bring disaster to the country and to the Government. I have not here the words of the President of the Bank of Montreal or those of the President of the Royal Bank, but I have read them. These gentlemen were only too well informed.
I speak to-day with some sense of pride, because I remember that just a year before the election, during a discussion on some of the branch lines of the Canadian Northern system, when I ventured to express the opinion that government ownership of railways would bring disaster to this country, what a howl of protest there was from the ranks opposite, and I remember well the lecture given me by the then Minister of Finance. Well, Mr. Speaker, who was right, and who was wrong? Government ownership not only as regards the railways but as regards the merchant marine is simply a mistake, if not a crime, and Canada to-day is facing the issue squarely. The country realize that for a passing whim the Government has sacrificed its best interests. I am not afraid, Mr. Speaker, to take the same stand to-day that I took two years ago, and especially after the admissions made this afternoon and the disappointment expressed by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. If he could give us his honest opinion, if he could tell us his own intimate sentiments on the GoV' ernment railway policy, I am sure he would be at one with me and would condemn the Government and his colleagues for the crime they have committed against Canada.
The time will come when we shall discuss in detail the pragramme of the Government with respect to the merchant marine. This afternoon I just wish to state that if in 1918 I supported the programme of my hon. friend, it was because Canada was then at war, and because the Mother Country, on account of the destruction of so much tonnage in the North Sea and elsewhere by enemy submarine raids was most insistent on receiving aid from Canada. I did not commit myself to any policy of a Government-owned Merchant Marine. On the contrary, I say that my hon. friend should have halted his programme immediately after the armistice, because, being a business man, he should have known that from that moment ships would be available at half price in the United States, in France, and even in the Mother Country.
My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries says that the merchant marine has not been appreciated as it should have been by the business community, by the manufacturers of Canada. Sir, the merchant marine was not built simply for the manufacturers. It was built for the whole Canadian people-fot^ the farmer, the miner, the fisherman, just as much as for the manufacturer. My hon. friend has said that he thought to expand the export business of Canada by means of the merchant marine. He will certainly have to revise his views on the tariff if he thinks

that by raising it " as high as Haman's gallows " he can develop any export business. My hon. friend may be able to develop an export business with the merchant marine if he invites the world at large to trade with Canada, but if when inviting the world, he a't the same time raises a barrier to prevent any trading with this country, I am afraid his hopes are doomed to disappointment.
Mr. Speaker, once more I say I am glad that the ships were built in Canada, although as I said a moment ago, my hon. friend should have stopped building immediately after ' the armistice. We have taught John Bull that Jack Canuck is able to take care of himself. Some years ago, as my hon. friend will remember, in 1913, we were solemnly told by the right hon. gentleman who was then Prime Minister, that he had received a communication from the Right Hon. Winston Churchill that Canada, forsooth, could not build ships, and that we should be satisfied to rely on the Mother Country in that regard. Well, though it has cost several million dollars, Mr. Speaker, we have at least this, satisfaction that we were able to demonstrate to the Right Hon. Winston Churchill that Canada can build ships.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
The subject under discussion is one to which I have given some attention. I have listened with a great deal of care to the observations of hon. members and the criticisms which have been levelled at the policy of the Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne). The objections seem to be two-fold: first, that the merchant marine should never have been built-which, I understand, is really the view of my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark)-and second, the view of my distinguished friends of the official Opposition, that all shipbuilding should suddenly have been stopped when the armistice was declared. Now, it is only reasonable to view the situation in the light of the conditions that existed when the shipbuilding policy was adopted. What was the world-wide situation then? What was the world-wide cry? It was that every country associated with the Allies should build ships. Not only was that cry insistent, but the condition in the Mother Country showed the imperative necessity for ships. She was not only building all the ships which her own shipyards could contain, but she was straining every nerve on the continent of Europe, and was spending millions of dollars in

this country building ships for which, as I understand, the people of Canada were lending her money, since they were anxious to have the shipbuilding programme carried on in view of the submarine menace. The minister, backed up by practically all the people of this country, except my hon. friend from Red Deer, thought that it was only fair, instead of allowing Great Britain to borrow money from Canada and build ships in this country, that Canada should assume that burden and put her own money into ships. What was the position in the United States? They took possession of every private shipyard. They took over, I suppose, at least a dozen large shipyards, and they have invested billions of dollars in ships which were constructed at the same time Canada was making her small effort in this direction. The fact of the matter is that there was not a country in the world that did not believe that shipping was going to be the best property any one could build, and they were all tumbling over one another to build ships. The belief of the people in every country at that time was that the building of ships was not only a good policy from the point of view of the war, but that it would prove good business. There was not a nation that was not anxious to build ships, and certainly no nation was more anxious than the United States. The American Government took over the orders of the Cunard and White Star lines in American shipyards because they said that the United States needed ships. Why, the paltry effort of Canada alongside of what the United States has done is a mere bagatelle; and, as I have observed, the position taken by every civilized people in the world at that time, was that it was the best thing to build ships. This was the conviction of everybody except my hon. friend from Red Deer, who, because of his belief that shipbuilding could be carried on in Canada only under a protective policy, is opposed to the building of ships in Canada.
Mr. MICHAEL CLARK .(Red Deer) : My hon. friend will allow me to say that I never said a word in public or private that could be construed as being in favour of a protective policy.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
My hon. friend misunderstands me. I suggested that his opposition to the construction of ships in Canada was because the work could be done only by virtue of a protective tariff, and his position was that it could not be done so cheaply here as in the Old Country. We

are all aware of that fact, and that was one of the reasons why last year the Government passed a shipbuilding Act to lend money for the building of ships in this country. But the point is that the world was shipbuilding crazy, and we had only the small end of the craze in Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: "Craze" is the word.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
There was no one who did not believe that it was a good policy and one that was ncessary in the exigencies of the time.
Now, to come to the armistice. What was the position then? The Government of this country had shipyards working overtime constructing ships. There were yards that came into existence that would never have been established but for our national shipbuilding policy that had been instituted during the war. There was some $250,000,000 invested in this industry in Canada, and practically 250,000 men, directly or indirectly dependent on it, besides some 50,000 who directly derived their subsistence from the building of ships. What was the Government to do? Were they suddenly to cancel contracts and turn every one of these men loose, with the resultant unemployment throughout the country? Such an action, in my humble judgment, would have been suicidal; it would have been adverse to the best interests of the country. It is strange that only to-day, for the first time, we hear this wonderful criticism of the whole subject, and suggestions as to what should have been done at that time. I fancy it is a case of foresight and hindsight; it is wonderful how wise one can be after the event.
My hon. friends say that these ships are worth only half of what they cost. Well, 1 venture to say that if our ships are worth only half of what they originally cost, the ships in the United States are probably worth two-thirds less than what it cost to construct them. Our ships were constructed very much cheaper than the ships in the United States, where the average price was something like $300 against our price of $185 per ton dead weight. Not only did we construct better ships than those built in the United States, but ours were vastly cheaper. Our neighbours to the south were building ships under conditions similar to ours, but conditions in Canada were worse because we had to import plates from the United States for a long time, until the Govern-82
ment adopted a policy of establishing a plate mill in this country, which made it possible for Canada to build every part of a ship and not be dependent on the United States. Before that policy had been adopted, we had to wait until the United States were good and ready to give us plates.
My hon. friends' complaint is that some of the ships are not earning money to-day; they say that the ships are tied up. Well, there are other ships than Canadian that are tied up; the ships of England and every other country are largely in this condition. To hear hon. gentlemen talking about ships being tied up in Canada, one would imagine that there was not such a thing as a worldwide cessation of trade since last November; one would think that conditions in France and Germany were perfectly settled, and that peace reigned throughout Russia. To hear the criticisms that are levelled at the minister on the ground of Canadian ships being tied up, one would suppose that conditions were normal in every country except Canada. That suggestion is ridiculous, because every one knows that there has been practically a worldwide cessation of trade, and the ships of England, good as they are

although they are no better than the boats built here-are equally as idle as Canadian vessels. Until our railways and the railways of the United States are on a stable basis; until there has been a worldwide readjustment of the rates of exchange; until trade is again normal; and until the situation in Germany and Russia, and elsewhere, is settled, no man can reasonably expect the business of shipping to resume its pre-war status. And my hon. friends would be helping the country much more if, instead of the destructive criticism which they level at the Government for a state of things, which is only similar to that existing in other countries, they would offer some patriotic suggestion of a constructive character in regard to the railway and shipping situation in Canada at the present time. The construction of ships is one thing, and their management in the future is another; and that is a fair field for discussion. But to go back and discuss now the question as to the date at which the Government's shipbuilding policy should have ceased to operate, and to criticize the Government because some of their ships are idle, when there is a similar situation throughout the world, is futile and is a waste of time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
The intention of the Government in having this statement placed on Hansard to-day was to enable hon. members to acquaint themselves with the details of the operation of the vessels, in order that they might approach the discussion of the general policy later on, or of the Estimates having to do with that policy, intelligently in the light of the figures there presented. The occasion of going into Committee of Supply was taken in order that, if it was desired, there should be comment on the part of hon. members, particularly by the leader of the Opposition, as is sometimes the case when such statements as these are presented. I do not think the presence or the absence of a portion of the House to-day has any real bearing on the question. The intention was to give hon. members an opportunity to read the statement in print, because only by doing so could acquaintance with the actual situation be at all thorough or detailed. Consequently the day chosen was most appropriate for that purpose. I am sorry that, as things have turned out, hon. members opposite were found prepared for a very dismal presentation, whereas, as a matter of fact, the statement made by the Minister of Marine reflects anything but a disastrous situation-possibly it is not as rosy as many of us expected when the programme was launched, certainly not as rosy as there were just reasons for expecting at that time, but on the whole fair and satisfactory; and particularly so when compared with the experience of any other country not excepting Great Britain herself. In fact there is no country that today can show as creditable a record in the matter of shipbuilding, and in the results of shipbuilding and operation in the period of time which we have been in them as can this Dominion of Canada. It is important, and I think it is due to the House, that an opportunity should be given for the study of the details of operation by a perusal of the printed statement in Hansard; otherwise errors are very easily fallen into, errors such as we have had many examples of this afternoon. It is a good thing to study Hansard. It is a practice that I would commend to hon. gentlemen opposite, and, if I might specialize this afternoon, I would commend that practice to the hon. member for Maison-neuve. I believe if he will spend a night or two reading some of the good portions of Hansard-his own speeches above all, delivered on occasions when the Estimates for shipbuilding were under weigh

he 'Mr. Bristol.]
would come to this House better prepared for the discussion of these matters, and would never fall into the mistake of making a speech such as he did this afternoon. I have some recollection of the eloquence with which my hon. friend applauded, not only the launching of the shipbuilding programme but every step taken in that programme from the date of its launching, and-so far as I am aware, and I venture to say with great positiveness-up to a year ago. Now the fact is that not one single ship has been laid down-that is to say not one contract has been entered into, no commitment has been made in regard to shipbuilding construction-for just the time he says we should have known it would be better not to build any more ships, just sixteen months. Would the hon. member say that as the armistice was signed on November 11, we should have thrown a ship into the ocean upside down that was perhaps two-thirds constructed at that time, or one-third constructed, or even twenty per cent constructed? Did the hon. member support this programme in the first place, or did any hon. member opposite support it, merely as a war programme? If that is the case my recollection is not very accurate. We supported this programme because we needed ships for the purposes of Canadian commerce. It is true that we needed ships to carry Canadian commerce during the war; but the vessels that carried Canadian commerce, and world commerce, were destroyed by the submarine and we needed them not only during the war but after the war period. It was known that when the war was over there would be a very serious shortage of ships, and each country vied with the other in an endeavour to catch up with that shortage and to give its own people the benefit of the industry that would be entailed in the process of catching up. In that etfort Canada bore a creditable part-not a part as great relatively as the efforts of larger nations but a creditable part. The vessels constructed were creditable to this country, and the contracts for that construction reflected honour, not dishonour, upon the Department of Marine. We have the ships to-day and there has been nothing in the way of substantial complaint with respect to their construction; and in that particular regard, above all others, our experience compares most favourably with that of other nations.
The hon. member made, or at all events set out to make, a point on the reference

by the Minister of Marine to the availability to Parliament of all documents, letters, correspondence and papers relating to the construction of these vessels-

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: And telegrams also.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Certainly, telegrams
form part of correspondence. The hon. member affected to see in that a recantation of the position the Government took the other day in relation to documents and papers respectng the operation of the Canadian National Railways, as well as the operation of the national shipping. The hon. member affected to see in it an inconsistency with the position the Government took at that time. His imagination led him on until he leaped to the conclusion that that inconsistency was due to the dictation of the Montreal Gazette and the financiers of Montreal, who had told the Government that it was all wrong on this question of correspondence on the subject of operation, and that it should right about face at once. I want to compliment my hon. friend on his imagination, but I cannot compliment him on his hearing. Actually what the Minister of Marine said what this-it happens to have been committed to writing and the minister read it directly from notes:
There is the further consideration from which, as the minister primarily responsible for the programme I derive some comfort, and that is that every contract made, every voucher paid, every letter and telegram exchanged between the department and contractors, is open for the fullest inspection of any member of the House who desires any further information.
Every word of this is in line with what I uttered myself in stating the position of the Government in relation to the national railways-every single word. All correspondence with any department of the Government in relation to any subject at all is available to this House. That has always been the case, it is the case to-day. Were we, under a department of government, to construct railway cars, were we to make rails, were we to build anything at all, everything relating to the activities of that department and passing between that department and the contractor, or passing between the department and anybody else, necessarily is available and must be produced on an order of this House. That is true in regard to the construction of ships. But what has that to do with the operation of the vessels or of railways under a corporation?-That is a different thing altogether.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Are not the Canadian
people the shareholders in the enterprise?
82i	'	.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
We know all that, but the difference is the same difference which I pointed out the other day, and I know I have convinced the hon. member that the position taken by the Minister of Marine is the position which I take myself. My hon. friend contends that there is no difference when the ships or railways are operated under a corporation. Well, the judgment of this House is that there is a great deal of difference. The judgment of the House, and it was pronounced very emphatically, is that we had to go very carefully in determining what in the nature of correspondence and details of operation should be producible in Parliament from day to day if we were going to make a business success either of the operation of our shipping or of our railways.
If we are going to get any man who is big enough and able enough to take in hand the tremendous responsibility of operating them, Parliament must proceed very carefully in deciding what part of his operations is to be exposed to his competitor and to the public from day to day. That is the principle I sought to enunciate then; by that principle I stand to-day; and from that principle the statement of the Minister of Marine makes no deviation whatever. The hon. member says it is too bad. It is too bad, because the whole basis of half his speech falls down.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve made some other statement to which I was anxious to reply. Before I do so, let me refer to the rather doleful lamentation of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark).
I readily accord to the hon. member full credit for consistency as regards the whole shipbuilding programme of this Dominion. On that score there is no fault to be found with ^ him. But when he says that this Dominion is to-day in a state of appalling financial calamity, and that second only to our railway trouble is the great difficulty we are in with respect to our mercantile marine, I am afraid he rather exaggerates a dread that he has been harbouring for some years. Our ships, he says, are worth very little. Well, they are at least earning a good sum over operating expenses,-and you cannot make any trains do that over the Transcontinental railway, nor over the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. Those ships are at least earning some million odd dollars over operating expenses, and after allowance for depreciation and every other just allowance that need be made they are still able to pay a small percentage upon their actual cost, although they were built at a time-and it was essential to build

them then-when that cost was necessarily abnormal. Surely that is not a position wholly disastrous. It they were able to pay a larger percentage of interest it would be better, but having in mind the fact that their construction was essential, and that it was commenced at a time when the cost was necessarily high-keeping in mind those two factors, which are the very bases of the whole case upon which we are now proceeding,-surely the result shown by the statement of the Minister of Marine is not a cause for tearful lamentations. We can face the situation as to our mercantile marine; we can face the situation, too, precipitated by premature and expensive railway building, not at a time when it was needed, but at a time when it was not needed at all-we can face both those situations because we are a strong and virile country. But in facing them do not treat them as comparable. We can look upon one with nothing except pleasure at having undertaken a great enterprise, and at least with satisfaction that it has gone through without any great cause for discontent; but the other is something which we cannot contemplate without, a very wholesome and unalloyed regret.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not attempt to follow my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) in his remarks concerning the Canadian Mercantile Marine, because I agree with him when he says that for an intelligent discussion of the statement which has been presented to the House this afternoon by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) it is obviously desirable that we should have before us for careful examination the various facts and figures contained in that statement. The whole subject is too large to be dealt with off hand; it is second only to that of the railway problem which we had brought before us the other day, and it is absolutely essential that we be fully seized of all the details before the public can be properly acquainted with their significance, I might say with their direful significance.
But, Mr. Speaker, there is one remark of my right hon. friend's which I would not like to pass unnoticed, and that is the reference to the statement made by the Minister of Marine as to the information which he was prepared to give to Parliament on matters pertaining to the Canadian Mercantile Marine. I do not think that my right hon. friend has strengthened either his own position or the position of
[Mr. Meighen.l
the Government in what he has just told us as to the real significance of the utterance of the Minister of Marine. If I understand him aright, the right hon. gentleman makes a distinction between giving to this Parliament information concerning the administration of a great public enterprise where it is in the nature of correspondence with the department, and giving information where the administration is carried on by a corporation, so-called, although created for the purpose by the Government itself. For example, so far as our railways are concerned, the Government has formed, for the purpose of control and operation, what I might call a phantom corporation. When it suits the purpose of the Government to withhold information from the public, we are told that that information is part of the information of which this phantom corporation alone has knowledge and control. The only information that Parliament is to be acquainted with is the routine correspondence exchanged with the deputy head or possibly with the minister of the department himself.
Now we are told that the Government proposes to adopt exactly the same course in regard to the Canadian Merchant Marine. This is another colossal enterprise involving an expenditure of millions of dollars of the people's money, and yet, when it comes to accounting to the public for this expenditure, the public is to be told that they are to get no information whatever as the enterprise is being carried on by a corporation and this notwithstanding that the corporation is the creation of the Government itself. Let me say to my right hon. friend and to his Government that the people of Canada will hold him and his Government accountable for every cent of public money, whether it is expended directly by the minister in charge of a department, or by any corporation or other creature which the ministry itself may create for the purpose of carrying on its business. The public have to meet the bills in the shape of the heavy taxation which is being imposed upon them, taxation as regards the railways alone amounting to $169,000,000, according to the Estimates brought down for the present year, and taxation amounting to many millions of dollars for this merchant marine, according to the statement which the minister has just given to the House. It is impossible to imagine that the people of Canada will consent to pay the enormous sums which they are being called upon to pro-

vide by way of taxation for the conducting of these enterprises and will sit silent under the Government's refusal to give them any information as to how their money has been spent.

In other words, where it suited the political and partisan ends of the Government, they were alert and ready to see that the representation was quickly made complete so far as this House of Commons was concerned; but where it was not their own political ends which were concerned, but rather the rights of the people to representation in this House, they were ready to ignore completely the fundamental right of the electors to representation.	.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it would seem that the Government purposes, in the case of the six constituencies I have just mentioned, to adopt a course very similar to that which they adopted in the case of the constituency of East Elgin; in other words, unless this House of Commons is prepared to express its opinion in no uncertain terms that every constituency in Canada should be represented in this Parliament just as quickly as possible, the Government in all probability will act in such a manner as to deprive the electors of these six constituencies of any representation during the present session of Parliament.
My right hon. friend may say that according to a statute which was passed by this Parliament on the 10th of November, 1919, the Government has a period of six months after a vacancy occurs within which to issue a writ for the filling of any vacancy. I would direct the attention of my right hon. friend to the wording of that statute.
