He will see that it was not drafted with a view primarily of affording the Government the latitude of running six months; it was framed rather with a view of putting a time limit on the period within which it would be possible for the Government to deny to the electors any representation. The Act will be found in the statutes of 1919, second session, being chapter 18, 10 George V, section 1, 11A. I quote:
In me event of a vacancy occurring a writ shall be issued within six months after the receipt by the clerk of the Crown in Chancery of the warrant for the issue of a new writ for the election of a member of the House of Commons.
Note these words, Mr. Speaker: shall be issued "within" six months. That is the time limit imposed on the Government, hut, as has been made apparent in so many debates in this House, the really important consideration in matters of public policy is not the letter of the law but the spirit of it, and the spirit of this enactment is that

there shall be some restraint upon the Government with a view to preventing it from denying to constituencies the right of representation to which they are justly entitled. I contend, Sir, that the Government's attitude towards vacancies should be one of endeavouring to see that so far as can conveniently be arranged every constituency in Canada shall have its due representation in Parliament.
Let me say just a further word, Mr. Speaker, in regard to the attitude assumed by the Prime Minister in this matter. Hon. members of this House as well as the public have a right to expect from any hon. gentleman holding the high and dignified position of Prime Minister of this country something more than ordinary courtesy and consideration when matters of great public concern are brought to his attention. I think it would be impossible for anyone to read the replies which have been made by my right hon. friend to questions put to him in this House concerning its representation without feeling that he has been, to say the least, very cavalier in the nature of his replies. Let me quote, for example, the reply of my right hon. friend to a question which was put to him on March 3. I addressed the right hon. gentleman in what I thought was a courteous and proper way when I asked if in the opinion of the Government the hon. member for Leeds had not forfeited his right to a seat in this House by virtue of having accepted a position as one of the arbitrators on the board which is to value the stock of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. When I asked that question I was not asking it in order to obtain personal information. I was asking it as a representative of the people, to obtain from the Government a statement which the people might have as the expression of the Government's view on that all-important matter. I think that my right hon. friend, as Prime Minister, should have given to that question an answer befitting its importance and significance. What was the reply made by my right hon. friend? It is to be found in Hansard of March 3, page 505, and is as follows:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I do not know that the Government gives legal opinions, especially on the floor of Parliament. If the hon. gentleman will submit hiS question in the usual way on the Order Paper, he will receive an answer.
I might say to my right hon. friend that I did move in this House for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General:
For a copy of the Order in Council of July 9, 1920, appointing the Honourable Sir Thomas

White as an arbitrator to value the stock of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, any subsequent Orders in Council having reference to this matter, and for all correspondence between the Government and the Honourable Sir Thomas White respecting such appointment.
On March 10 of this year the House voted that address; but up to the present time- and to-day is the 29th of the month-it has been impossible for any one on this side of the House to secure the papers on this particular subject. That is not treating Parliament with the courtesy which hon. members have a right to expect from the Government on matters of this kind. I regret to say this, but I feel called upon to do so.
Not only has my right hon. friend been very cavalier in the nature of the replies he has made, but he has lacked candour in some of the replies which he has given. If there is one thing above another which the people of the country have a right to expect from its first citizen, I think it is the utmost frankness and candour on any question of great public concern. Let me, in this connection, read to the House the replies of my right hon. friend in regard to the resignation of the hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames). On March 3,1 addressed the following questions to the Prime Minister:
Is the Prime Minister aware of the hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) having made any public declaration to the effect that he had tendered his resignation as a member of this Parliament? Has the Prime Minister or any other member of the Government received an intimation from that hon. gentleman of his desire or intention to tender his resignation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: the ministry; the Speaker made the reply, possibly in the ordinary way, but this is the circumstance to which I wish to draw the attention of my right hon. friend. He was sitting in his seat, the chief whip, the hon. member for Grey North, and the other witness to this document, the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Whidden), were both in their seats when the Speaker of this House made that statement respecting the resignation of the hon. member for St. Antoine. On March 4, you, Mr. Speaker, were permitted, in the presence of those gentlemen, to say that the hon. member for St. Antoine had not resigned his seat, and all the time there was in the possession of the chief whip the declaration of that hon. gentleman to which the chief whip had himself been a witness on February 14.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: My hon. friend has made a misstatement. That resignation which was handed to the Speaker, I suppose, later on, was not in my hands more than two minutes. The hon. member for St. Antoine one day came to my seat in this House and presented me with that resignation, saying: "I am going overseas; I want to have my resignation witnessed; I am going to send it in later on." I know nothing more about it than it was sent later on. It was signed in blank; the date was blank, and he was to use it as he saw fit.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: What was the date when the resignation was handed to my hon. friend?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I do not know the date. He just came to me when I was in my seat in the House during last session. He came over to me and the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Whidden) with it all drawn out; the date was left in blank; it was witnessed in blank, and he took it away.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
That only
makes the case worse than ever. The statement we now have is that during last session of Parliament the chief whip received from the hon. member for St. Antoine his resignation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Nonsense.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: It was not left with me. He simply came to me and said: "I am going to. resign."-he did not say when- "Will you and Dr. Whidden kindly sign this?" We sat down in a seat here and we signed it. It was in blank. I gave it back to him. It was the property of the hon. member to do what he pleased with it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member will now explain to the House how the document came to be dated February 14-witnessed February 14 of the present year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I suppose the hon. member for St. Antoine has a perfect right to date that document whenever he pleases.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: And you to assert yourself as witnessing his signature on February 14.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
My hon. friend
knows better than that. He knows the date was blank.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: But it is stated in the document.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Order. I
would remind hon. members that the leader of the Opposition has the floor.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Let me direct the attention of the House to what is stated in the declaration of the hon. member for St. Antoine:
Given under my hand and seal at Ottawa, this fourteenth day of February, A.D. 1921.
Witness, W. S. Middlebro.
Witness, Howard P. Whidden.
Now there is something false in that statement according to what my hon. friend has just told us. Either he did not witness that document on February 14, or he did. He tells us now that he did not witness it on February 14, but that he witnessed it last session. Now the question I wish to ask my right hon. friend the Prime Minister is this:	Where
was that document from that time until the day on which this Parliament opened? I say that my right hon. friend owes it to this House, when he gets up to speak in reply to what I am now saying, to clear away this mystery completely. He owes it to his own reputation, and to the honour of members of this House, and the honour of the hon. member for St. Antoine. This document is dated February 14. Now that date is significant. That is the day on which this Parliament opened, and when Parliament opened on February 14, how does it come that this document signed that day never reached the Speaker's hands until March 17? Will my right hon. friend tell the House in frankness and candour, when he rises to speak, where that document was in the meantime? Some one must know. The chief whip waives responsibility in the matter, but the Prime Min-

ister cannot waive it. He owes it to his position to tell the House where that document was in the meantime.
May I add this further. I am informed, and I believe credibly, that on the night of the division on the Address my hon. friend the chief whip on the Government side sought to have the member for St. Antoine paired with an hon. member on this side of the House, notwithstanding that he knew that that resignation was already signed by Sir Herbert Ames. I asked my right hon. friend the Prime Minister when I brought this matter up in the House, tvho was responsible for having withheld this important document from you, Mr. Speaker, for over a month, from February 14 until March 17?
The Prime Minister made no reply to that question whatever. He evaded it altogether, and confined his remarks to generalities respecting what in his view might have happened to the resignation in the meantime.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at Eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock we had been discussing the several vacancies existing in this chamber, and the lack of popular representation ensuing as a consequence. We were referring more particularly to the vacancy in the electoral district of St. Antoine, in the City of Montreal. I think I express the feeling of the House when I say that we had had the somewhat painful disclosure that on March 3, the Prime Minister had conveyed to this House the impression that the member for St. Antoine had not tendered his resignation as a member of the Canadian Parliament and further permitted that impression to be confirmed by you, Mr. Speaker, on March 4, by allowing you to state from the Chair as 'a positive fact, that the resignation of Sir Herbert Ames as the member for St. Ahtoine had not been tendered. There was the further circumstance that all of the time there was in existence, and in the possession of someone, a signed declaration by the hon. member, dated at Ottawa on February 14, in which the hon. member formally tendered his resignation as a member of this House. More remarkable still, Mr. Speaker,
was the disclosure made, in the course of discussion, by the chief whip of the Government party to the effect that he, himself, together with one of his colleagues, witnessed the resignation of the member for St. Antoine as long ago as the last session of Parliament. That would bring the resignation, as made out by Sir Herbert Ames, to a date prior to July 1, 1920, when Parliament prorogued. Now what the Government whip has stated in that connection is borne out by the statement of Sir Herbert Ames himself which was read in this House during an earlier debate. Speaking in London, England, on July 21, 1920, before the Empire Parliamentary Association during an address on "The Dominion and the League of Nations," Sir Herbert Ames made this statement:
Now, I have just returned from a hurried visit to Canada. Mr. Balfour has alluded to the double capacity which I occupied at that time, and for the moment still occupy. For sixteen years I have been the representative of Western Montreal in the Canadian House of Commons. My resignation is in the hands of the Speaker because I have found that my new work is quite enough to occupy all the time and attention that I am capable of giving to it.
In other words, Sir Herbert Ames made the statement, in London, on July 21, 1920, that his resignation was in your hands, Mr. Speaker. My hon. friend, (Mr. Middlebro) tells us that when Sir Herbert Ames visited this House during a preceding session-that is prior to July 1, of last year-he made out his resignation and it was witnessed by two hon. members of this House. Under these circumstances, we have a right to assert, notwithstanding any language that may be used by hon. gentlemen opposite in the way of evasion or trying to circumvent the real issue, that a vacancy has existed in the electoral district of St. Antoine ever since July of last year. Sir, the important point is not whether hon. gentlemen opposite did this or did that with a particular resignation which was placed in their hands, not whether the Government for its own reasons inserted a date which served its particular purpose- but the real question at issue in this matter is, the right of the people of the electoral district oi St. Antoine to be represented in Parliament. They have been defrauded of that right by virtue of the action of hon. gentlemen opposite.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman say that resignation was placed in the hands of any member of the Government?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I must leave it to my right hon. friend to explain the circumstances.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman
does not say that, why does he assert that the electors were defrauded of representation by the action of any member of the Government?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
My reason is that the hon. member who had been representing that riding made the public statement in London that he had tendered.his resignation. Sir Herbert Ames himself was the one person who knew what his motives were and what he intended to do; and if Sir Herbert Ames-a man of the highest [DOT]honour and integrity, I believe-said on July 21st, 1920, that he had tendered his resignation to the Speaker I, for one, believe that he intended his resignation to be in effect at that time or he would never have uttered the statement. I must leave it to my right hon. friend to extricate himself and his colleagues from the somewhat embarrassing, if not painful, position in which they have placed themselves.
Now what, among other' results, is the effect, Mr. Speaker, of the action of the Government in this matter? The law, which I quoted a few moments ago, requires that elections must be held within six months after the resignation of a member is in the hands of the Speaker and His Honour has issued his warrant for the issue of a new writ of election. Had the resignation been tendered, as Sir Herbert Ames said he believed it had been tendered in July, 1920, an election would have had to be held in the St. Antoine division of Montreal before the end of 1920, and we would have had in Parliament, at the beginning of this session and at the present time, some one representing that constituency instead of the electors of the riding being unrepresented as they now are.
But there is another consequence, Mr. Speaker, which I think, in some ways, is even more serious and unfortunate than the one I have just mentioned. In view of the attitude which the Government has taken and of the evasions of my right hon. friend, what are we to believe in regard to any other vacancies that may be existing at the present time? There is now, we believe, a vacancy in Leeds. We have every reason to believe that the right hon. member for Leeds (Sir Thomas White), having accepted an office of emolument under the Crown and being an honourable man, has, in his own estimation, no longer the right to a seat in this House. Indeed, we know

that ever since Parliament assembled the right hon. gentleman who formerly represented Leeds has not taken his seat here. I am right, I think, when I say that the former member for Leeds has been in Ottawa repeatedly during the time that Parliament has been in session-may I say that I believe he was in Ottawa to-day- but he has not entered this House or taken his seat here.
Under these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, we have a right to believe there exists in the mind of that hon. gentleman, just as there did in the mind of Sir Herbert Ames, the belief that his resignation should be given to this House, and that the electors of the constituency of Leeds as a consequence are entitled to other representation in Parliament. There may be in the pocket of some hon. gentleman opposite, handed to him by some other hon. gentleman to suit the partisan ends of the Government, the resignation of the hon. member for Leeds. We have a right to ask my right hon. friend when he speaks in reply to-night to state unequivocally whether in his opinion, as one holding the highest position of trust in the gift of this country, the constituency of Leeds is not entitled to have a representative in this Parliament at this particular session. In order that there may be no possible further evasion of the exact situation, let me quote the law on this subject. Section 15 of chapter 10 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, provides in part as follows:
If any member of the House of Commons accepts any office or commission....or performs any service for the Government of Canada or for any of the officers of the Government of Canada, for which any public money of Canada is paid or to be paid,... the seat of such member shall thereby be vacated, and his election shall thenceforth be null and void.
The preamble of the Act for the acquisition of the Grand Trunk railway, chapter 13 of the Statutes of 1920 provides that one of the parties to the agreement is called the Government; and clause 6 of this schedule, which forms part of the Act, provides:
That the value of. the stock of the Grand Trunk Railway company shall be determined by a board of three arbitrators, one to be appointed by the Government.
And the first sentence of clause 21 of the schedule reads as follows:
Each of the parties to this agreement shall pay its own costs of and in connection with the arbitration subsequent to the date of this agreement, including the remuneration of the arbitrator appointed by it.

I am informed that on July 9, 1920, the hon. member for Leeds, the right hon. Sir Thomas White, was by order in council appointed the Government arbitrator, to be remunerated by the Government for his services in that connection. As I mentioned to the House this afternoon, it has been impossible to secure from the Government any of the papers relating to this particular appointment, so that we on this side of the House are unable to tell the electors of Leeds whether they are legally represented in this Parliament or not. Under the circumstances, I say to my right hon. friend that he owes it to the electors of Leeds, he owes it to hon. members of this House, and he owes it to the people of this country to state unequivocally tonight whether the electors of Leeds are or are not at the present time unrepresented, and whether it is his intention, as the leader of the Government, to see that a by-election is brought on in that constituency as soon as possible, in order that their representation may be made good at the earliest possible moment.
That I may conclude with the several phases of this matter at this moment, let me say to my right hon. friend that we will not only expect him to make a statement in regard to the situation in the St. Antoino division in Montreal, and in regard to Leeds, which will be unequivocal in its terms, but that we will expect him also to state to this House whether or not he intends to allow the electors in the other constituencies where vacancies exist the right to have representation before the present session of Parliament is at an end. When, on March 3 of this year, I asked my right hon. friend about the vacancies in the several constituencies, I said:
May I ask my right hon. friend if he can inform Parliament when the writs will be issued for by-elections to fill the vacancies that exist in the constituencies of Yamaska, Quebec; York-Sunbury, New Brunswick; Medicine Hat, Alberta; and West York, Ontario?
Right Hon. Arthur Meighen: I am able fully to conform to precedent in that regard, and to tell my hon. friend that the writs will be issued in due course.	.
Mr. Mackenzie King: May I ask my right hon. friend if the writs will be issued simultaneously, or at different times?
Mr. Meighen: That will appear when the writs are issued.
As Prime Minister of this country my right hon. friend has a great responsibility and a solemn trust imposed upon him, and as part of that responsibility and of that trust it is his duty to take this House and
the people of Canada into his confidence in very considerable measure, on matters of great public concern, and in this connection to state at the present time in a frank, open and straightforward manner what he intends to do in order to give these constituencies their rights to representation. I need not draw the attention of the House to the circumstance that virtually every answer that my right hon. friend has made this session in regard to this matter has been in the nature of an evasion. We expect from now on that he will take a little more care as to the manner in which he makes his replies to hon. members on this side of the House and that he will give the country through Parliament the information to which it is justly entitled.
I presume that when my right hon. friend does reply he will take refuge as regards the answers which he has made in a retort to the effect that having fooked up previous records he finds that other administrations were not over hasty in filling vacancies from time to time. Any comparison made with the conduct of previous administrations has not a true parallel in the present instance. So far as I am aware there never has been a condition quite the same as that which now exists in this Parliament. I do not recall any government that has ever held on to office so tenaciously in violation of the pledges by which it had obtained power. Moreover, I think my right hon. friend will find on looking up the records, at least during the period of the Liberal administration, that there never was a time when the fate of the administration hung on the thread of the possible outcome of a series of by-elections, as I think is the case with his administration to-day. Nor, indeed, has there ever been a time in the history of the country when the problems demanding solution at the hands of Parliament were as vast as the problems which confront us at the present time. We have a series of problems arising out of the war as a result of which colossal sums of money are being asked for by the Government in appropriations amounting to almost $600,000,000. No previous administration, I think, prior to the time that hon. gentlemen opposite took office ever asked much beyond, if indeed, it came to a total of, $100,000,000 by way of annual appropriations. With these serious matters confronting Parliament it is of the utmost importance that every constituency should be represented in this House and that the best intelligence possible should be brought to bear on their solution.

In conclusion, let me say, Mr. Speaker, that the one fact above every other which is causing concern to the people of this country is how they are going to meet the vast expenditures which hon. gentlemen opposite are subjecting the country to. It is true that the Government has given us very little in the way of a legislative programme for the present session. Indeed, that programme is as sparse as it can possibly be, save in one particular, and there it is prolific enough. The particular to which I refer is the colossal amount of money which the Government expects this House to vote, and which the people will be obliged to bear in taxation during next year. When the Government is asking appropriations of $576,000,000, which will probably run into $600,000,000 or $700,000,000 before this session is over, if the Government bring down Supplementary Estimates such as they did last session-and that vast sum does not include a single cent set aside for paying off the war debt, amounting to a couple of billion dollars-when there is an appropriation for our railroads alone amounting to $167,000,000; when the Government proposes, as we are led to understand, further indirect taxation through the revisions that they are about to make in the tariff-there are, I think, Mr. Speaker, the strongest reasons why the electors in -every riding should have the right to have their voice heard in this Parliament at this particular session, and for that reason I beg to move, seconded by my hon. friend for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding):
That as respects the motion before the House all the words after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor: "The House is of the opinion that representation in Parliament being a fundamental right of the people, writs should be issued at once to fill the existing vacancies in- the House of Commons, and that polls should be held at the earliest possible time so as to ensure representation of all constituencies during the present session of Parliament."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure if any improvement of character or conduct on my part could be looked for as a result of the scolding from the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), I rise very much chastened and purified by it. I recognize the privilege of being given lessons in candour and honesty and frankness at the hands of my hon. friend.
I would indeed profoundly regret if any default on my part were responsible for the rather unseemly bickering to which the House has been treated this afternoon.

I have read again the various reference to which my hon. friend has alluded. I have read the questions asked me, and the replies, and I say first of all that I am conscious of no error whatever, however slight, however negligible, as affecting the accuracy of a single reply, nor am I conscious of having withheld from him or from Parliament anything that it was my obligation, or even my right, to give as a member of the Government and of this House. The hon. member has chosen this occasion-it is very rarely if ever that the House is moved into Committee of Supply without some attempt being made to delay almost indefinitely the deliberations of Parliament in Supply-he has chosen this occasion, to move a resolution demanding that all vacancies be immediately filled by by-elections, but he has used it mainly to revamp some difficulties he finds in connection with the resignation of a private member of this House and to try to give rise throughout the country to the idea that the Government of Canada is responsible for the time or the method in which a private member of this House chooses to put in his resignation. The Government of Canada is responsible for the advice it gives the Crown in relation to public affairs; the time and the method of a resignation is the responsibility of the member concerned. Sir Herbert Ames was quite capable of discharging that responsibility, and he discharged it. He was capable of getting advice from any source he chose, and those giving it are responsible to him for that advice.
Now, the hon. gentleman complains that information misleading Parliament has been given. I have often been sorry that my hon. friend seemed utterly incapable of reasoning carefully on any set of facts. I do not presume he intends to throw out intimations to the House and to the country that are inconsistent with the facts. If he would reason carefully on the facts we would not come to these rather disagreeable incidents in this House,-there is no necessity for it. Much less would we ever reach the time when the accusation of falsehood would be lightly thrown across the floor of Parliament. I do not know whether it was his intention to create the impression that something I had given this House was false, but in the plainest language and apparently without even a moment of reflection he hurls at my hon. friend from North Grey an accusation of falsehood. I do not think that any hon.

member of this House on either side would even in his heart conceive the hon. member for North Grey capable of misleading Parliament or of uttering a falsehood to this House.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I made no reference of any kind reflecting upon the hon. member for North Grey-none whatever.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Well, the facts are
these: the hon. member quoted from the resignation and quoted from what he said was the assertion of the hon. member for North Grey as a witness to that resignation; he then referred to his statement in Parliament and said that one or the other was false. I do not know whether he conceives that that reflects on the member for North Grey. If he does not, it is only another illustration of what I referred to a moment ago,-my hon. friend's utter incapacity for reasoning on any set of facts.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: What is bothering hon. gentlemen opposite? On what ground did the leader of the Opposition hurl that accusation across the floor of this House? He quoted from a resignation signed by Sir Herbert Ames dated February 14 of this year, a resignation witnessed by the hon. member for North Grey and the hon. member for Brandon, and, reading the attestation clause-"Given under my hand and seal at Ottawa this Fourteenth day of February, A.D. 1921," signed as witnesses to the signature of Sir Herbert Ames by Mr. Middlebro and Mr. Whidden-he asserted that it was false to affirm that that was signed on February 14. Now, the hon. leader of the Opposition has, whenever it has suited him, when he thought it would pander to the prejudices of an audience, been in the habit of complaining about too many lawyers elected to this House.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Shame.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
One cannot help noting that surrounded as the hon. gentleman is in Parliament he very carefully refrains from making that complaint in this House. I have often regretted that the hon. member had not at least some little acquaintance with law; it would save him a lot of trouble. It would not require more than two days of the five years of the study of
law required in most provinces for the hon. gentleman to acquaint himself with the fact that the signature of witnesses is a signature attesting the authenticity of the signature to the document. The witnesses by signing say that that is an authentic signature; they saw him sign. They do not attest the fact that it was signed on the day on which the instrument is dated.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Hon. members say "oh, oh"; and I heard a lawyer like the member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), when the. leader of the Opposition was on his feet, applaud him with a huzzah the utterance of that sentiment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Yes, and I am sorry the Prime Minister of Canada is of another opinion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Take, by way of illustration, the case of a legal document signed by two, three, or four parties, some of them living in different cities. Is there not one date to the document? Yet is it not essential that one sign on one day and another on another? Do the witnesses assert when they sign as of a certain date that the document was signed by all on the same day? Why, the merest tyro knows that is not the case.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: What is the hon. member talking about? Does the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) wish to dispute that? Does he mean to assert that a witness affirms, when there is a date to a document, that it was signed on the date of the document?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Suppose a man signed as witness to a will dated as of a certain day. Does my right hon. friend mean to say that it is not important to have the date on it? It is a sort of dying request.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
This will illustrate what the hon. gentleman's ingenuity amounts to. He knows that a will has a special attestation clause in which it is specifically asserted that the witnesses saw the person sign on the date of the will. Indeed, the law in our province calls for that, and I am pretty sure the law of Ontario does. But for hon. members to state in this House that a witness to a document is a witness to anything more than the authenticity of the signature is

to talk nonsense. Does the hon member say that it was the duty of the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Middlebro), or the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Whid-den), to see that the date was filled in at the time they signed the document? The law does not call for any date at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: They had a right to do so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
That is the business
of Sir Herbert Ames. It is the business of Sir Herbert Ames to decide when his resignation shall come to Mr. Speaker, and the time he chooses and the method he chooses for doing so are matters within his own concern. It is for him to choose them, and in the choosing of them the Government of this country has no responsibility whatever. Sir Herbert Ames did not leave his resignation with any member of this Government. I told the House that he left it with a friend of his, and he did; but the resignation becomes a resignation when it reaches you, Mr. Speaker, as every hon. member knows. The hon. member for Prince, P.E.I. (Mr. Mackenzie King) would seem to think that Sir Herbert Ames was bound, the moment he wrote out his resignation, to tender it at once to you, Sir. He can choose the time he tenders it; he did choose the time; he chose the method; and whether or not the person to whom he confided it carried out his instructions is a matter between that person and Sir Herbert Ames. The hon. member asks me, as leader of the Government, to tell him what method Sir Herbert Ames adopted, to tell him what the custodian of Sir Herbert Ames' resignation did. That is a matter concerning Sir Herbert Ames, and 1 will so continue to tell my hon. friend as long as he asks the question. I am responsible for what I do as leader of the Government. The Government is responsible for the advice it gives to the Crown and for the conduct of public affairs. Sir Herbert Ames is responsible for the time he resigns and the method he takes for resigning, and if anybody, no matter who he is, were he a member of the Government or anybody else, advises him in that regard, for that advice no one is responsible and no one is answerable to the leader of the Opposition or to this House; the man is answerable to the person to whom he gives the advice. Sir Herbert Ames chose the channel by which his resignation should reach the Speaker, and he had a right to do so. My hon. friend reads a report-I do not know what 
it is from; I presume it is a newspaper report of a speech made by Sir Herbert Ames, supposed to have been made in London on July 21, 1920, in which he asserted that his resignation was in the Speaker's hands. I never saw the report; I do no know whether he made the speech or not.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Hon. members may think it clever to laugh. I do not know what is laughable about the matter. If the hon. member (Mr. Lapointe) has anything clever to say to this House, he will have an opportunity of standing on his feet and doing so when I am through. I know, if Sir Herbert Ames made that statement-I can scarcely think he made it, because I know he was aware of the fact- he made it before the date on which he handed his resignation to the custodian. I venture to give that information to the House. It was after that date that his resignation was handed to the custodian and limitations placed upon the time at which it would be handed to Mr. Speaker. I do not know what mystery there is about this matter. Has Sir Herbert Ames not the rights of an ordinary member? Can he not choose his agent, his time, his method? That right he had; that right he exercised, and for the exercise of it he is responsible.
Now let me come to the subject matter of this resolution. The hon. member says that six seats, are vacant, and he demands that before we go into Supply, the Government be instructed that all those writs must be issued, and right away, because very great harm is going to be done to the constituencies and to the country if those writs are not issued immediately.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: May I ask whether in the six seats he includes one of the two held by the hon. member for Gaspe and Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is very silent on that. I may refer to that subject later. No, he referred to the seat held by the hon. member for Leeds. Although he reviled lawyers, he was not at all the first to stand in the House and argue, as a matter of law, that that seat was vacant. I do not know how far his legal opinion will be accepted by hon. members; but at all events, he gave it for what it is worth. Not only that, but he abuses me because I refuse to give my legal opinion. The hon. member has moved in this

House for the papers relating to Sir Thomas White's appointment as arbitrator in the Grand Trunk arbitration. That motion passed this House; those papers the hon. member has a right to; those papers he shall have. Necessarily,, in the preparation of that file-because this is only one of a great number of resolutions that pass Parliament-some time must be taken. Only a little over two weeks have passed since the resolution was passed by this House; it will not be very long until the papers are brought down; and I may tell the hon. member now that, when that correspondence is brought down, it will contain the opinion of the Department of Justice as to the tenure of the seat by Sir Thomas White. It is the opinion of the Department of Justice by which this Government is governed, and that will he known to Parliament in the usual way by bringing down the papers. That will be of more value to the House than any opinion of any individual member, however eminent in law he may be.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Will it be more valuable than the opinion of the Minister of Justice himself, who is a member of this House?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
The Minister of Justice is head of the Justice Department; but the law officers under the Minister of Justice are the officers that are followed in public business, and it is their opinion, not necessarily that of the Minister of Justice, to which the House in answer to that motion is entitled.
The resolution states that a writ must be issued immediately for each of the vacancies that now exist, applicable only to the five that undoubtedly do exist, the constituencies of Yamaska, Quebec; York-Sunbury, N.B.; Medicine Hat, Alberta; West York, Ontario, and St. Antoine, Montreal. The first observation I wish to make is this: Two sessions ago this Parliament altered the law with regard to the issue of writs for by-elections. Prior to that time, under the law of the land, it had been left entirely to the Government of the day to determine when it was in the public interest that by-elections should be brought on and writs issued, and no limitation at all was placed upon the discretion of the Government in that regard. In the session of 1919, Parliament altered that by special statute, by which Parliament declared that writs should be issued within six months after the receipt by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery of a warrant for the issue of a new writ for the
election of a member of the House of Commons. That is to say, the discretion that Parliament had theretofore granted the Government, an unlimited discretion, was specifically limited to six months after the receipt by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery of the notification of a vacancy. Why Parliament so acted, the debate at the time pretty clearly shows. It appears that the subject matter of the Bill had been referred to the Committee on Privileges and Elections. The committee reported the Bill in this form: it limited the discretion of the Government to six months in the case of all vacancies occurring otherwise than by resignation, but they took the view that it would not be well to limit the discretion of the Government at all in relation to vacancies arising out of resignation, because to do so would put it in the power of an individual member by the exercise of a mere idiosyncrasy or whim, to declare a seat vacant and bring on a by-election at any time he chose. Whether that recommendation of the committee was valid or not may be doubted, but at all events Parliament in considering it afterwards, came to the conclusion that there should be no exceptions, and enacted that the time within which the writ should be issued should be six months from the receipt by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery of the warrant to issue a writ for the vacancy. That is the discretion now given to this Government and to all governments in this country. Does anybody know why the exercise of that discretion should be specially limited as regards this Government?
Has anybody heard any. reason why, after Parliament had so decided, this same Parliament should alter an Act, which has passed all its stages, upon the mere resolution of the leader of the Opposition? That is the orbit of discretion given the Government of the country. By what process of reasoning is this Government to be denied the exercise of that discretion while other governments are to be accorded it? Oh, the hon. member says, there are special circumstances; you are hanging on, he says, by a thread. He has been imagining that thread for quite a long while now; he has been giving interviews about it, making statements about it, making speeches in this House about it, but the "thread" still hangs, and it seems a pretty substantial thread; there are at least 25 strands strongly holding it together. How does

that affect the case anyway? Even were it so, how is that relevant to the argument? Did Parliament make an exception and say that discretion should only be exercised when the Government had a large slavish and reliable majority? If that had been the intention of Parliament, they would have said so. But Parliament placed no restriction; Parliament intended no restriction. Now, the hon. gentleman is fearfully outraged about the poor electors of St. Antoine, and of Yamaska and of York-Sunbury being denied representation in the House this session, and hp is seconded in this by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). He too is becoming very impatient, and is very anxious indeed that this process of non-representation, which in the longest case has continued for only three months, and in the shortest case for about three weeks be immediately stopped, or the fundamental rights of the electors are being ignored. Well, if the electors have fundamental rights to-day in this regard, they have had the same fundamental rights for fifty years or more in this country. They had the same fundamental rights when the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's was a member of the Government, and when the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) was its enthusiastic supporter. The fundamental rights of the electors have not changed between then and now. Let me ask the hon. member: how is it that he is scandalized to think that three months should have elapsed in the longest case that now constitutes a vacancy in this House, when he was quite content to support a Government that allowed a whole year and nearly two years to elapse?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Will my right hon. friend wait a few moments for an answer, or does he want it now?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I await it now-I took up his challenge, but he does not answer. Let me give the hon. member just a few cases. Starting back in 1897, shortly after hon. gentlemen opposite came into power, I find in the contituency of Champlain, Quebec-he will know about that-

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: The Government ought to know too.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Certainly they know about it. In that case three months elapsed. Next, three months elapsed in Colchester, Nova Scotia; four and a half

months in the case of Temiscouata, at the time the present hon. member for that constituency was elected.
Mr. CASGRAINi'It was worth waiting for.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
In that case the constituency waited from June 25, 1897, when the former member died, until the 6th day of November, 1897. Such was the outrage perpetrated on the people of Temiscouata, an outrage which hon. gentlemen opposite quite cheerfully assert was abundantly vindicated by the election of the present hon. member himself. I agree that my hon. friend is a creditable representative in this Parliament, and I know he will agree with me that the outburst of cheers of hon. gentlemen opposite at the assertion that it was all right to wait until he was elected is only another of a thousand proofs of the assertion that all their interest in this matter is politics, and party politics. It is not the electors of these constituencies they are concerned about at all: all they are concerned about is to gain some party advantage if they can, and it will only be a moment till I show you how they hope to gain it, if they are able to bring the House to their point of view at this time.
We go on to the case of Bagot, Quebec. Mr. Dupont died on March 12, 1898. There was no election in that county at all until December 14, 1898, or nine months and two days afterwards. What an outrage was perpetrated on the people of Bagot, an outrage to which the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's the seconder to this resolution, was a party:	Next is the case
of North Simcoe, where the late D'Alton McCarthy died on May 11, 1898, and where the election was deferred until December 14, 1898, or for seven months and three days. We pass unto Montmagny, Quebec. There the election was deferred for five months and seven days. We pass from that to West Huron, Ontario, where Mr. M. C. Cameron was appointed Lt. Governor of the North West Territories on May 30, 1898. The election in that case was deferred until February 21, 1899, nine months and twenty-five days after the vacancy occurred.
The next case is Chambly and Vercheres -'and this outrage was not at all redeemed by the election of the present hon. member. There the Hon. C. A. Geoffrion died on July 18, 1899. The election did not take place until January 18, 1900; six months elapsed in that case. That is only half

as long as one I read a moment ago, but twice as long as the worst case which noW outrages hon. gentlemen opposite at the present time.
Then I refer to the city of Winnipeg, which at that time was possibly the largest single member constituency in this Dominion, had the largest number of electors, and perhaps the greatest individual arid property interests. There Mr. Jamieson died on February 31, 1899, but the election did not take place until January 25, 1900, or practically one year after the death of the hon. member for Winnipeg. The next case is Lotbiniere, Quebec, Where five months elapsed. Then there is the case of	Sherbrooke, Quebec, where
six	and	one-third months elapsed.
Passing on to subsequent years, there is the case of Antigonish, Nova Scotia, when four months elapsed. There is the case of West Lambton, Ontario, in the same year, when five months elapsed; the case of Wentworth, Ontario, in the same year, when nine months elapsed; the case of the resignation of Mr. Walter Scott in 1906 for the constituency of West Assiniboia, when five months and six days elapsed; the case of Saskatchewan, North West Territory, in 1906, when five months elapsed; and later on, the case of East Elgin in 1906, when ten months elapsed, the resignation of Mr. Ingram taking place on December 8, 1905, the election being held on October 4, 1906. Then there is the case of the Hon. Peter White, who died on May 3, 1906, having represented the constituency of North Renfrew, and for whom no successor was elected until October 9, of the same year. There is the case of Quebec county, Quebec, when there was a lapse of four and a half months. In the case of St. Mary, Montreal, in 1906, four months elapsed; in the case of Victoria in New Brunswick, when the Hon. John Costigan was summoned to the Senate, four months elapsed. In the case of St. John city and county, in 1907, six months and three days elapsed; in. the case of London, Ontario, in 1907, six and a half months elapsed; in the case of East Northumberland in the same year, seven and two-thirds months elapsed; in the case of North Wellington, Ontario, in the same year, seven and a half months elapsed. And so on, down the list. I doubt whether there is one single year in the whole time that hon. gentlemen opposite were in power when there were not cases -or, numbers of cases-in which twice the time, or almost twice the time, elapsed that has elapsed in the most extreme case of which those gentlemen complain to-day.
The hon. member says: But this is a very important session; we must have a lot of money this session. Well, it is an important session. But it was not wrong at all in those days to deprive constituencies of representatives for a whole year; and I have a case here where they were deprived for a far longer time; indeed, where no election was held at all until the general elections came on. That was all right then, but for this Parliament it is a heinous political offence that any election should be deferred. But for this difference the hon. member gives the reason that this is an important session. Why, it is only a few weeks since the hon. gentleman was out on the stump, indeed since he spoke in this House, and said that we had no right to legislate at this session at all because this Parliament was defunct-

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: So it is.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
-and that it should not exist; so the reasoning of the hon. gentleman is that it is entirely right and proper to deny constituencies their representation in a good Parliament for a year or two, but that it is wholly wrong to deny them representation in a defunct Parliament for three months. Mr. Speaker, the fact is that this Parliament, except in the imagination of the leader of the Opposition, and perhaps in that of some other hon. gentlemen opposite, is in precisely the same position as all other parliaments. In this Parliament, precisely as in all other parliaments, constituencies have a right to be represented; the same right, no greater and no less. In this Parliament, the Government has the same discretion as to the issuance of writs as has always existed, save as restrained by legislation passed two years ago; and in this, as in every previous Parliament, the Government intends to exercise the discretion reposed in it by Parliament, subject only to the restraint Parliament has imposed, and not to the whim of any hon. gentleman, whether he be the leader of the Opposition or not. Now, there is another consideration that does especially weigh at this time. Parliament now in session has possibly two months more in which to sit, possibly longer. I believe it is the anticipation of hon. members on both sides that we may be able to get through towards the end of May, or early in June. Nothing will be done by the Government to hurry matters through, or in any way to constrain Parliament in the consideration of public questions. Nothing of that nature will be done



at all. But it is the common anticipation that Parliament will get through in the time I have suggested. An election called now could not be held until about the middle of May, under the law passed by this Parliament; and there would be but a very short time in which any candidate who might be returned could sit in this Parliament this session. But more than that, when by-elections are on it is the duty of hon. members on both sides to see that the case from their point of view is presented as fully as possible to the electors concerned Under present conditions what do we find? We find that hon. gentlemen opposite, within their legal right, have adopted the policy of refusing pairs. The courtesy of pairs is a tradition with Parliament, but it has been refused by hon. gentlemen directly opposite, not, I am glad to say, by hon. gentlemen of the Agrarian party. That is the course which hon. gentlemen opposite have pursued within the exercise of their right. Under the rules of this House hon. gentlemen may bring on a debate at any time on any subject of their choosing. They may precipitate a motion to adjourn; they may challenge the Government on motions that are not debatable, and which consequently may be brought on at any moment, in respect of which a decision cannot at all be delayed. Consequently they have the privilege of having their members present, by concert and agreement among themselves, choosing the time to suit their own convenience. Perhaps hon. gentlemen on this side might be away, necessarily engaged in the presentation of issues before the electors where a by-election was being held. But the courtesy of pairs has been refused, and while they refuse it hon. gentlemen opposite say to us: Go to the country with your by-elections; let your members go out there; and when they are away we will not give pairs, hut we shall have our members away or here just as we want them. We shall choose the time for a vote, and by that means shall get a snap verdict and thereby obtain some glory throughout the country. That, I think, is what is in the back of the head of the leader of the Opposition.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Bring on
your by-elections and we will give pairs.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Now, these resolutions come on with a minimum of notice. Of this one I received notice forty minutes before the meeting of the House this afternoon; and another I received this afternoon I got half an hour's notice of. It is

the privilege of hon. gentlemen opposite to take that course; but it is also the privilege of the Government to take a similar course. I have never pursued that course. Every evening before adjournment we have given the House a statement of what the Government intends shall be taken up the next day. We are not strictly bound to do that, we do it as a matter of courtesy, as advancing the interests of Parliament. I think hon. gentlemen opposite owe us the same courtesy, of giving us notice when these things are about to come on; and I do think that they should not pursue a course that is calculated to enable them to take the Government at a disadvantage when hon. members on this side might be away from the House. I do not think they should urge, under the rules of the House, the adoption of a resolution which is designed for the purpose I have stated.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
If my hon.
friend will permit me, I might say that it was not until one o'clock to-day that a few of us who happen to be sitting side by side decided that this amendment would be moved this afternoon. As soon as that decision was reached, I wrote a letter with my own hand to my right hon. friend and sent it over by special messenger to his office. As a matter of fact, he was informed long before hon. members on this side of the House knew anything about the matter. Besides, this is the only day this week we have of presenting these matters.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Not at all. What my
hon. friend says I do not dispute. He may have written me as soon as he knew of the decision to bring this matter up; but that does not help me in any way. Notice did not reach me until twenty minutes after two o'clock.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
It was sent
to my right hon friend's office.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Very well; but it is when the notice reaches me, just as it is when a resignation reaches the Speaker, that counts. It would not be a very good answer for the Government to say when the House was adjourning at night: "We have not decided what to take up to-morrow. We will likely decide that to-morrow at 2 o'clock, and then we will send a notification to the leader of the Opposition as to what it is." My hon. friend would not regard that as a very good answer on my part.
There was nothing to hinder this resolution from being taken up any day after my

hon. friend had placed it on the Order Paper.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: My right hon. friend will permit me to say that when we adjourned for Easter-*

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Order. The hon. gentleman has no right to the floor. He has already spoken, and I stretched the rule in his favour a moment ago.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: All I am seeking to impress upon the hon. member is that these amenities work both ways, and that when we on this side observe them-and we try to do so to the best of our ability-we expect the same consideration from hon. gentlemen opposite. If this amendment were to pass-and I have not the slightest apprehension that it will because it is not at all fair-it is not based on fairness, or the idea of fairness-it would not only deny to the Government the discretion that Parliament gave it by statute, but the discretion that this Parliament intends that other governments shall exercise in the future. It would not only do that but it would compel a course which, in the conduct of the business of the House and under its rules as they stand to-day, would put the Government at a disadvantage which it does not deserve. Therefore it seems to me that the amendment should not pass. Why should such a motion be moved as an amendment to the resolution to go into Committee of Supply? Why cannot the amendment be placed on the Order Paper as a resolution the same as any other motion? This is a matter of general public concern. This is a matter that seeks to get the opinion of Parliament on a subject which Parliament has already dealt with through the regular process of a statute. Surely that is something that should be brought to the attention of Parliament in the regular course, and not by way of an amendment to the motion to go into Committee of Supply.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: What is his reason for moving it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Well, that is for the hon. gentleman himself, or some one on his side, to state. I can only leave hon. gentlemen to divine the reason as best they can. We all know what amendments to the motion to go into Committee of Supply are; and I have heard it stated by the leader of the Government before 1911, that though an opposition might move the Ten Commandments in amendment to the motion to go into Committee of Supply they
83S
could not expect that those Ten Commandments would be affirmed by the Government when they were proposed in such a manner. It seems to me that my hon. friend has chosen this method in order to get the advantage that would result from an amendment to the motion to go into Committee of Supply, because no amendment can be made to it-it must be taken as it is or not at all. I therefore appeal to hon. members to vote down this amendment in fairness to themselves, in fairness to the Government of the day, in fairness to the Government in future years, and in fairness to Parliament for all time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) said in his opening remarks that after the castigation administered by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) he was'chastened and improved. I am afraid that his good resolutions were of short duration, and that he has quickly succumbed to his usual bad habits. Taking his last observation first, he complains that the notice of the intention of the leader of the Opposition to move his motion was only sent him at one o'clock this afternoon, or rather at two twenty o'clock. It is not the fault of the leader of the Opposition that the notice was not received by my right hon. friend until that hour, because the notice was sent at one o'clock. Although the right hon. gentleman complains about that proceeding, he himself at twelve o'clock sent to the leader of the Opposition a letter which reads as follows:
Ottawa, March 29, 1921.
Dear Mr. King,-Mr. Ballantyne proposes to make to-day his statement regarding the operations of the Canadian Mercantile Marine. He will make it on the motion to go into supply.
Tours faithfully,
Arthur Meighen.
Now what is sauce for the goose should be sauce for the gander. Is it any worse for the leader of the Opposition to notify the Prime Minister that he intends to mave an amendment on the motion to go into Committee of Supply this afternoon, than it is for the Prime Minister to notify the leader of the Opposition that the statement as to operations of the Canadian Mercantile Marine will be proceeded with the same afternoon?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Will the
hon. gentleman permit me a question? Does he not see the difference

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: The Prime Minister is distinctly in order in submitting his question, and if hon. gentlemen would permit the Chair to exercise its jurisdiction in maintaining order the results would be much more satisfactory.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I am quite willing to permit the right hon. gentleman to ask any question, but I am told he has just refused the leader of the Opposition the privilege of doing so.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
quite in error. The leader of the Opposition rose for the third time to make a statement which he had no right to do; he did not offer to ask a question.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I was going to ask my hon. friend if he does not see the distinction between a statement as to the Canadian Mercantile Marine shipbuilding, a statement placed on Hansard so that hon. members may study it-just as in the case of the statement regarding the operations of the national railways-and a challenge to the Government by way of an amendment to go into Committee of Supply. To the first no study is needed on the part of hon. members.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
The difference I see is that in the one case we are dealing with the Canadian Mercantile Marine involving the expenditure of many hundreds of millions of dollars, and in the other case with the holding of by-elections in this country. Now, I desire to read the amendment which has been offered by the leader of the Opposition. I wish to draw the attention of all hon. members to its language and to ask them if they can vote against the principle enunciated in it:
The House is of the opinion that representation in parliament being a fundamental right of the people, writs should be issued at once to fill existing vacancies in the House of Commons, and that polls should be held at the earliest possible time so as to ensure the representation of all constituencies during the present session of Parliament.
I believe that this resolution should be accepted and I cannot see that any government, nor any parliament, can successfully challenge the principle which it enunciates -that it is the undoubted right of the Canadian people to be represented here during the present session of Parliament, as well as during other sessions. I think the constitutional doctrine in that respect cannot be successfully challenged. Parliament must reflect the sense of the whole country.

Every citizen of Canada has the right to his share in the making of legislation-in the selection of his representative in Parliament and in the formulation of the laws of this country. This principle cannot be successfully challenged for it is the essence of responsible government, and when there are here and there throughout the country constituencies that are not represented in the House, the whole country is interested in having those vacancies filled, because otherwise Parliament is like a leaning tower-lacking foundation at important points. This, I repeat, is the constitutional doctrine. It is the doctrine of freedom, it is the doctrine of liberty, and for such a doctrine people have fought and shed their blood in days gone by.
This doctrine is recognized in all other countries. What is the law in Great Britain with regard to the holding of by-elections? There the Government has no say in the matter. When a vacancy is created a motion is made in the House of Commons by the chief whip of the party to which the late member belonged for the issuing of the writ. The writ is issued forthwith and sent to the returning officer, who fixes the date of the nomination and of the polling. In 1920 an amendment was enacted to the Representation of the People Act, chapter 35, of 10-11 George V, in which it is provided:
The day fixed for nomination in boroughs shall not be later than the seventh day after the returning officer receives the writ. . . . The poll shall take place on such day as the returning officer may appoint, not being less than six or more than eight clear days after the date fixed for nomination.
The Government there has no choice in the matter. Further, it is enacted that any person who causes delay in the holding of a by-election is guilty of a misdemeanour. I wonder what my right hon. friend would do if he were guiding the destinies of Great Britain to-day?
And that doctrine has always been recognized in this country, of course. My right hon. friend resorted to the tu quoque argument. I was not surprised, for it is a pet argument with him. With all deference, let me tell him that the tu quoque argument at its very best is a despicable argument. It lacks in logic, it lacks in conviction, it lacks in good faith, it lacks in force. In a word, it is a worn out argument.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: What is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I tell my right hon. friend that I am not using any tu quoque argument, nor do I intend to. I do not think that my hon. friend erred when he sent his notice this morning, no more than I think my hon. friend the leader of tl>e Opposition made a mistake when he sent his notice to the right hon. leader of the Government. So I am not using any tu quoque argument. But let me tell my right hon. friend that the men and women T>f this country to-day are not disposed to make permanent a wrong simply because it has been in existence. The majority of our people are not disposed to believe that a wrong becomes a right when it is done many times by succeeding governments or succeeding bodies. I wonder how progress could be achieved or reform accomplished in this or any other country if this doctrine, so dear to the heart of the right hon. Prime Minister, was the final doctrine accepted by our people. I will tell my right hon. friend that he is wrong when he uses the tu quoque argument. In the cases reported I think I am right in making the statement that the vacancies were filled in every instance before the opening of the succeeding session of Parliament. My right hon. friend shakes his head.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: There is no doubt about it.	|

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: There are no doubts about it in my mind; I am sure of my assertion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
There are cases of
vacancies not being filled for over a year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I have taken down the cases quoted by my right hon. friend, and in every instance the vacancies were filled prior to the succeeding session.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: You did not take them all down.	*

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Order, order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
My right hon. friend may discard that with a wave of the hand as he discarded the Ames matter the other day. He may shake his head in contradiction of what I say, but he cannot prevent the facts remaining facts. In the session of 1908-and this will serve to show that the doctrine I have just alluded to is the recognized doctrine in this country-the former Prime Minister of Canada, who was then leader of the Opposition, the present
member for King's, N.S., introduced a bill to amend the House of Commons Act. I refer my right hon. friend to page 5226 of Hansard of the session 1907-1908.
Mr. R. K Borden (Carleton, Ont.) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 66) to amend the House of Commons Act. He said: Mr. Speaker, the object of this Bill is to provide that writs to fill vacancies in the House of Commons shall be issued within a certain period, and in that way to avoid the prolonged disfranchisement of constituencies which has sometimes occurred. The Bill is framed on practically the same line as that which has been in force in Ontario since the year 1904.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier spoke as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) if he thinks, in view of the invariable practice that has been followed in this House since confederation, there is any necessity for such a Bill as this. If any vacancies have taken place during the recess these vacancies have always been filled before the ensuing session, and so far as I can remember no constituency has been left unrepresented, certainly not within the last ten or twelve years.
The member for King's, N.S., the then leader of the Opposition, did not deny that statement. He said:
