If Parliament were to expire in a month or a few weeks, the House could be given power to direct that the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery should not in a particular instance carry this provision into effect. My recollection as to what has taken place is a li-ttle different from that of the right hon. gentleman, because I think the constituency of St. James, Montreal, was unrepresented for a whole session.
That was one instance.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier: Do you say St. James?
Mr. R. L. Borden: I am speaking from recollection, hut I remember there was at least one constituency in which the writs should have been issued much earlier than they were.
So the leader of the Opposition of that day, without being sure about it, said that he could recollect only one instance in which the writs had not been issued before the ensuing session.
Now, as to the necessity of holding byelections and having the vacant constituencies represented during all the sessions of Parliament, I shall quote from the remarks of the same gentleman, the then leader of the Opposition, at the same fusion of Parliament, 1908, as reported on page 7,862 of Hansard. The then government had introduced a Bill to amend the Elections Act and on the second reading of the Bill the hon. member for King's complained as follows:
There is no provision in this Bill for the holding of by-elections within a reasonable time, nor is it provided-

I desire to direct my right hon. friend's attention to these words of his former leader:
-nor is it provided that, where several byelections are pending, they shall all be held upon the same day.
The member for King's was and is of an opinion quite different from that entertained by the present leader of the Government in that respect. Last year the House emphasized the necessity of having all constituencies represented in Parliament by enacting a measure compelling the Government to hold by-elections within six months of the opening of the seat. Public opinion forced that law upon Parliament. I remember that when the Bill was moved for second reading one of the hon. gentlemen on the other side, a whip-the member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) if I am not mistaken-moved the adjournment of the debate, which in the ordinary course would have had the effect of killing the Bill. But public opinion compelled the Government to afford another opportunity for the discussion of the Bill in the House. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) shakes his head, as if he had been the father of the Bill. He took great care last year to say on two or three different occasions that he was not responsible for the Bill; that the member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) was responsible for it and that he, the minister, was simply giving an opportunity to the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I gave to the hon member for George Etienne Cartier full credit for the Bill, but the hon. member for Quebec East will not deny that had it not been for the co-operation I gave, even when the member for George Etienne Cartier was not in the House, to the extent of taking the Bill up and putting it through, the Bill could not have been got through. The hon. member for Quebec East is too fair, if he knows these facts, to follow upon the lines he has just started to take:	I
appeal to the member for George Etienne Cartier if what I am saying is not the simple fact.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I am quite ready to
admit that the Bill could not have been adopted without the co-operation of my right hon. friend, and without his willingness to let the Bill proceed as he did.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: And in the absence of the sponsor of the Bill I took it up and put it through.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Yes, but what I want to state is that my right hon. friend at the 
same time took the trouble to say that he was not responsible for the Bill; that his part in putting the Bill though was simply to let the House have the opportunity of dealing with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman read what I said? I did not repudiate responsibility. As I say, I was giving due credit for the Bill to the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier; I did not want to steal his thunder.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Very well. Then my hon. friend will say with me that it was the intention of the House that the by-elections should be held within a reasonable time ' after the vacancy occurred, and that the intent of the law was not as stated tonight by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, who asserted that the provision in the Act for a delay of six months entitled the Government to delay the full extent of that period and to ignore the rights of a constituency to representation in Parliament, even though the by-election could have been held much sooner.
When that Bill was discussed in committee it was argued that the provision for a delay of sixty days which had been inserted originally in the Bill by the member for George Etienne Cartier was too short; that it had better be changed to six months in order that there might be sufficient time for the preparation of the lists. So the intention of Parliament was that the elections should be held immediately, or as soon as they could possibly be held, and the provision for a delay of not more than six months was inserted in order to obviate any possible objection in connection with the preparation of the lists.
There is another matter to which I wish to refer very briefly, the question of the resignation of the former member for St. Antoine. The Prime Minister said he was not aware that the member for St. Antoine had made a public statement in London in the month of July last to the effect that he had tendered his resignation. The right hon. gentleman said that this was probably a newspaper report, and expressed the belief that such words were not uttered by the former member for St. Antoine. Well, that "newspaper report" is the printed report of his speech; I hold it in my hand, and it is at the disposal of the right hon. Prime Minister. It is published by the Empire Parliamentary Association; 'surely the Prime Minister of Canada knows what the Empire Parliamentary Association is. The first stage of that pamphlet reads as follows:

Confidential. The Dominions and the League of Nations. An address by Sir Herbert Ames, M.P., (Canada), Financial Director in the Secretariat of the League of Nations, delivered at a Private meeting of Members of the Empire Parliamentary Association in the Home and Dominion Parliaments, in the Rooms of the Empire Parliamentary Association, Westminster Hall, on July 21, 1920. The Right Hon. Arthur J. Balfour, O.M., F.R.S., M.P., Lord President of the Council and Chairman of Executive Committee of the Empire Parliamentary Association (United Kingdom Branch), in the Chair. Issued under the Authority of the Empire Parliamentary Association (United Kingdom Branch), Westminster Hall, Houses of Parliament, London, S.W.I.
I suppose it is not necessary for me to read the names of the officers of the Empire Parliamentary Association as given in this pamphlet. Then, the reading matter preceding the report of the address is as follows:
A private meeting of the Empire Parliamentary Association was held in the rooms of the Association, Westminster Hall, on July 21, 1920, when Sir Herbert Ames, M.P. (Canada), Financial Director in the Secretariat of the League of Nations, delivered an address upon "The Dominion and the League of Nations." The Right Hon. Arthur J. Balfour, O.M., F.R.S., M.P., (Lord President of the Council and Chairman of Executive Committee of the Empire Parliamentary Association) occupied the chair, and there was a considerable attendance of members of the Association in the Lords and Commons and of visiting members of the Association from Dominion Parliaments.
The chairman, Mr. Balfour, introduced the speaker. I suppose it is not necessary for me to read his remarks; but I wish to read again this part of the speech of the former member for St. Antoine, and I shall now ask my right hon. friend whether he believes those words were uttered by Sir Herbert Ames or not.
My resignation is in the hands of the Speaker because I have found that my new work is quite enough to occupy all the time and attention that I am capable of giving to it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: What is the date?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: July 21, 1920. I shall be pleased to hand the book to my right hon. friend.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I have never seen it. I have no doubt my hon. friend is reading it aright. All I have to say is that if Sir Herbert Ames said that, he was manifestly mistaken.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Shame.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: My right hon. friend is modifying his position.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: My right hon. friend said a few minutes ago that he did not believe the hon. member for St. Antoine had made the statement. I took his words down at the time. Now he says that he has no doubt that those words were pronounced, but that Sir Herbert Ames was mistaken.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I did not say that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I intend to state a point of order, notwithstanding the noise. I state that the hon. member has no right to misquote what I said, especially a moment after I said it. I said that I did not know whether he made the statement or not; I could scarcely believe that he did. I know the authority is very good. I said that I did not doubt the hon. gentleman was reading correctly; but there is on record the Speaker's word, which I do not think hon. gentlemen intend to challenge, to the effect that if the statement was made, it was a manifest error. I do not know what hon. members are trying to make out. If they believe that there was any breach of honour on the part of any member of the Government in this respect, let an hon. member, on his responsibility as a member of this House, make that statement.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Everything I state in this House is on my responsibility, and my right hon. friend may be sure that I continue to have that responsibility for everything I shall say to-night. Can the right hon. gentleman say that a gentleman of the standing of Sir Herbert Ames, who has represented St. Antoine, Montreal, in this House for so many years, who has been appointed by this Government as a chief officer in the League of Nations, could have made such a statement without the statement being true? That gentleman stated that his resignaion was in the hands of the Speaker. I have no doubt that it was not in the hands of the Speaker; but there was certainly an error, or a mistake, or call it what you like, somewhere, and that is what we would like to find out-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: You had better ask Sir Herbert Ames.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
-especially under the circumstances which have surrounded the whole procedure. I do not want to dwell long on this question, although it is very interesting. I quite understand the right hon. gentleman cannot speak again, but I

should like to ask the hon. gentleman Who is going to follow me: who is the party who kept that resignation against the will of the hon. member for St. Antoine, because he expressed his formal will in that statement that his resignation should be in the hands of the Speaker. He said that it was in the hands of the Speaker. Who is the party who kept that resignation against the will of the hon. member for St. Antoine, while that hon. member was under .the impression that his resignation was in your hands, Sir? I will ask and call the attention of the House to this second point: how is it that the resignation should have been signed before the chief whip of the Government^ party and announced a few days later in the city of London by the hon. member who had written the resign-a^on? In all this, of course, I am quite willing to accept, and I do accept, the statement of the Prime Minister; but it seems a queer organization in the great Conservative party, that the chief whip should have witnessed the resignation of an important member; that this member should have announced his resignation^publicly in the city of London, and that the leaders of the party should know nothing about it. I will ask further: How is it that the gentlemen who signed that resignation as witnesses have certified that such resignation as witnesses have certified that such resignation was written on February 14? The	Prime Minister,	in his
very clever game of splitting hairs said that those gentlemen witnessed only the signature and nothing else, and everything was right.	He does not see anything
irregular in the matter. I will call the attention of the House to the language of the Statute. Section 5 of Chapter 11 of the Revised Statutes of Canada reads:
Any member of the House of Commons may resign his seat,-
(b>- By addressing- and causing to be delivered to the Speaker a declaration of his intention to resign his seat, made in writing under his hand and seal before two witnesses.
And so on. Not only must the signature be affixed before the' witnesses, but the resignation must be made in writing before the witnesses. Does my right hon. friend say that the date is not an important part of that writing?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Will my hon. friend sav, as a lawyer, that that section of the Act requires the date to be in the document at the time it was signed?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I certainly say that
as a lawyer.
lAIr. Lapointe.]

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I do not think so.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I am quite willing to
discuss this with my hon. friend, even before the courts of Toronto. It is so clear that it does not require discussion. I am surprised that the Prime Minister of Canada should say, on his responsibility as a public man, that there is nothing irregular in that proceeding. I am surprised that he should allow that statement to go broadcast in this country of ours. He may say that he is not responsible for the irregularity;. he may say that he did not know anything that occured concerning that resignation; but I am at a loss to understand how the leader of the Government and the chief citizen of this country can say that everything is regular with regard to that.
There is another point which I desire to bring to the attention of the House. My right hon. friend was quite indignant at the language of the leader of the Opposition with regard to the answers of my right hon. friend to questions put in this House by hon. members on this side. What my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition said was that there was a lack of candour. On March 2, I read in this House, in the presence of my right hon. friend, the words of the former member for St. Antoine as I have read them tonight. I stated then-I had the pamphlet in my hand, and it was at the disposal of my right hon. friend-that this statement had been made by Sir Herbert Ames before the Empire Parliamentary Association in the month of July last. On March 3, in reply to a question put to my right hon. friend as to whether he was aware of any public declaration having been made by the hon. member for St. Antoine, he said as reported at page 506 of the unrevised Hansard:
I have seen no public declaration made by or on behalf of the hon. member for St. Antoine, nor have I received any communication that I can give to the House.
Surely my right hon. friend knew on March 3, that there had been a public declaration made by the hon. member for St. Antoine. I had read it on the preceding day, and my right hon. friend was here when I read the very words that I have read again to-day. Surely my right hon. friend will not deny that he was here facing me all the time when I spoke on the Address. Does he deny that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Well, the hon. member may have read it, and I may have been pretty busy. I did not hear him read

it. If he thinks that is a matter of very great consequence, I think he is magnifying a trifle. If he read it, all right; but I did not hear about it until the leader of the Opposition spoke. But what in the world is the difference?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
May I refresh my
right hon. friend's memory? Does he remember that at the conclusion of my speech -the right hon. gentleman was then in his seat-Mr. Speaker rose and stated that in view of the statement I had read he felt it necessary to say that he had not received the resignation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I remember that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Now, Mr. Speaker
could not possibly have said that if I had not repeated the statement of the hon. member for St. Antoine. Another queer circumstance in this matter Is this:	How
is it that February 4 should be recognized as the binding date on that document? How is it that this document having been in the hands of somebody on the other side of the House was kept for three or four weeks after the alleged signature on February 14, and especially until after the division on the Address in this House?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
It was St. Valentine's
Day.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
These are all circumstances which have not yet been explained. Even the reasoning of my right hon. friend the leader of the Government has not cleared away any of what he himself has called the mystery. Now, Sir, by-elections, apart from giving representation to the people of this country, as is their constitutional right, have this other advantage, that they demonstrate whether the Government of the day still possess the confidence of the people of the country. They are very important in that respect, and as I showed the other day, governments in other countries have resigned because of the trend of public opinion against them as demonstrated in by-elections. Perhaps I should not use that argument here, because it is the very reason why my hon. friends opposite do not want to hold any by-elections. At the present time there are vacancies in various parts of Canada. There is a vacancy in the West of Medicine Hat, there is one in York, Ontario, there are two in the province of Quebec, and there is one in the Maritime Provinces, not to speak of the vacancy in Leeds. In most of these constituencies, the Government, and even the Conservative party, have always won by big majorities; they are considered
safe Tory constituencies. Why should the Government be afraid to take the plunge and give the electors of these ridings the chance to be represented in this Parliament? They have the right to be represented here. In the Speech from the Throne itself we are told that matters of supreme importance to the people of this country will be brought down to the House this session. It is announced that there will be a revision of the tariff. We are confronted with a railway situation which is most serious. Surely the people of Canada have the right to be heard in the solution of these problems. Take the case of the St. Antoine division in Montreal. Nobody will say that it is a Liberal constituency. I do not think it ever was represented by a Liberal member in this House. Now the electors of St. Antoine have strong views on certain questions which are now before the country. You may read letters in the Montreal Gazette every day discussing the railway situation in Canada at the present time, written by supporters of this Governemnt, electors of St. Antoine. When this matter is discussed in the House these electors of St. Antoine have the right to have their views expressed on the floor of this House. They have the right to demand that they should be represented when those questions are discussed. They have the right to demand representation when the tariff policy of this country is settled by this Parliament. The electors of these five or six constituencies that are not represented here to-day have the right to be heard on the Imperial problems which are going to be discussed at the Conference to which my right hon. friend desires to proceed in the month of June. All these questions will be discussed during the present session, and the electors of St. Antoine, West York, York-Sunbury, Yamaska and Medicine Hat have the right to have their representative in this House to speak for them when these matters come up.
There is the subject that was introduced this afternoon when the Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne), made his statement to the House. That is another big question. It is a most important question, and the electors of St. Antoine have pronounced views on the policy of the Government in regard thereto. They have the right to have those views expressed on the floor of the House, and what reason in the world can there be to prevent the Government from holding the by-elections in these various ridings? Why can they not trust the people? An evasion of that responsibility

implies that the Government do not trust the people of this country, and do not trust themselves. They are afraid that they have not the confidence of the people and consequently do not want an expression of this distrust at the polls. Let me say in conclusion that the more delay there is in this matter the worse will be the fate of the men who are responsible for that delay. The day will come when the people shall have the right and the opportunity to express their views and give their vote, and when that day comes we shall hear a different story from that told to-night.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I wish in a very few words to tell the House how I am going to vote, and why, on this question. My first reason for voting as I shall vote is in a measure explained when I express the hope that whenever it is desired to impugn the policy of the Government, or to carry a vote of censure upon them, we shall not have too large a rehash of the very prolific amount of campaign oratory which we had last fall. There is one thing which I think my hon. friend, the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), has by this time got thoroughly into the minds of the people of this country, and that is that he wants to have an election. There cannot be any doubt about that if one is to do what I do most fully and freely, that is, to give the utmost credit to him for sincerity in the various speeches which he has made upon that question. We had a resolution which was a vote of confidence or no confidence, and which I think the country looked for in connection with the speech from the ' Throne. It was proper that at the beginning of the session there should be a show-down in the circumstances which the country found itself in. In that resolution, to all intents and purposes, my hon. friend demanded an election. Well, the sense of Parliament was against his views at that time; and now he in effect says that if we cannot have a big election we will have several small ones. He is in favour of elections.	-
May I say to my hon. friend, in all sincerity, that an election is not a policy. It has no bearing one way or the other upon what my hon. friend and his supporters would do in regard to any one of the great problems before Canada if he came into power. It is the means of putting a policy into operation, if indeed a policy be the possession of those who might be put into power. Something has been said about evasion and I think my hon. friend himself used the word in another
connection. But this reiterated demand for an election, to my mind, almost amounts to an evasion on his part of his undoubted duty to tell the country what he is going to do if he becomes Prime Minister. In the debate on the Address my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Hon. Mr. Meighen), and his Government put the policy of protection right in the centre of the stage. He did that following a pointed question which he had put to my hon. friend all over the country: What is the position of the leader of the Opposition on the principle of protection? Did my hon. friend answer that question?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
He has never answered it, and I want to express the opinion-I do so in all humility, but it is my opinion, and so long as I am here I have the right to express my views-that at this moment from east to west the people of Canada are far more concerned to know what is the hon. gentleman's exact position in regard to that principle of protection than they are concerned about any resolution such as he has brought before the House. That is my honest opinion, and I should like him to see if there be anything in it, and clear it up, because otherwise he will inevitably come under the suspicion of a desire to get a blank cheque from the electorate without having avowed any policy upon this matter of protection. What the country would like is not an election cry raised again and again, but a policy that is to be carried out after an election. There is a long session in front of us, and I trust my hon. friend will lay to heart what I am saying in perfect good faith and friendliness.
That brings me to the second reason why I shall vote against the resolution of my hon. friend, the leader of the Opposition. This very day an excellent opportunity was offered my hon. friend and his supporters to bring in a resolution which would have been a vote of censure, and could not have been mistaken for anything else, upon a question on which the whole debate rests. What happened in the House this afternoon? Two of the leading supporters of my hon. friend, in effect, charged that the very Estimates that are before the House, of the Minister of Marine, had been inflated to the tune of millions upon millions of dollars of the people's money since the armistice, in a way which was contrary to the public good, contrary to public policy, contrary to the best interests of the country. Now, I want to ask the members of

this House and the people of this country ; could there have been a straighter chance of taking a vote of the House upon a great principle of policy? My hon. friend talks of great problems. Is not that a problem? On the showing of my hon. friends from Maissoneuve (Mr. Lemieux) and Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie), is not that a problem of enormous size, bigger than the question of six vacant seats? But again, I say that my hon. friend runs away from that problem and brings in a resolution which, after all, has no earthly connection in logic with the Estimates of the Marine Department, and certainly has no earthly connection with the waste of millions of the people's money upon the building of ships which are worse than useless, according to the showing of the hon. gentleman's own friends.
I quoted a figure myself this afternoon.
I am not going into the details of the shipping question as I should be out of order if I did. I merely quote the figure again to illustrate my point. I said it was freely stated in the newspapers of this country that up to the time of the armistice only sixteen and a half millions of dollars had been spent by the Government on a merchant marine. The figure now teaches to pretty nearly seventy millions. That is to say, according to the showing of my hon. friend's followers, fifty millions have gone wrong since the time that this policy should have been given up. Then why have we not a resolution of confidence or no confidence in the government on the very question which logically is before the House-that is the estimates of the Minister of Marine? These are two of the reasons why I shall vote against the amendement of my hon. friend. The third reason is this, that what my hon. friend has submitted, is in the first place, a proposal to reve.rse what has been the procedure of the Parliament of Canada from Confedration to this moment. What has been that procedure? The procedure has been that the laws of Canada,'made in the wisdom of our forefathers, have left the discretion as to the calling of an election in the hands of the government of the day. That is the principle and there is no getting away from it, that has been the principle of the procedure of the government of Canada until the Act of a couple of years ago. The proposal of my hon. friend is that we reverse that procedure which, I repeat, has substantially existed from Confederation to the present moment.
But what is the second element in the proposal? The second element in the proposal is that it asks us to reverse the law of the land by a resolution in Parliament on this particular question. My hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) has said very truly that they have a definite law in Britain on this question of by-elections, and he has told the House what that law is. The law has entirely removed the discretion from the government of the day in Britain and put it in the hands of the Speaker. Every byelection there takes place automatically within a certain time, but we do not have an hon. gentleman-whether he be leader of the Opposition or whatever position he occupies in the British House-rising in his place, after an hour or an hour and a half's notice to other members of the House, and proposing that the law of Britain shall be overridden, the law which settles the method of calling by-elections. Well, I respectfully submit to my hon. friend from Quebec East and to my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, that we have a law here and that as law-abiding subjects of the British Empire we are as much concerned in obedience to the law in Canada-whatever that law may be-as they are in Britain to the law over there; and my hon. friend's argument from the case of Britain, so far from helping him, is absolutely opposed to his point of view. Their law is different from ours- made by their Parliament, as our law was made by our Parliament. They carry out their byelections according to law. To be logical, -and not only to be logical but to be constitutional, and to show the proper regard which Parliament always should show for the laws of the land-we surely ought to live according to this law. And when was it carried? The law under which by-elections of the Canadian Parliament are now carried out was adopted two sessions ago by this very Parliament, con- -stituted of the very personnel that constitutes it now, and it was adopted on the initiative of an hon. gentleman who sits behind, and is a supporter of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: And carried unanimously.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Yes, carried unanimously; both sides agreed to it. But the strong point is that it was carried on the initiative of an hon. member for one of the divisions of Montreal who, I think, has

earned the gratitude ef the whole country by trying, at any rate, to limit the time during which the discretion of a government shall be allowed to operate in this particular direction. Now, Mr. Speaker, constituted as I am-with the desire to be logical, and with the desire to obey the dictates of the constitution and the law of the land-for the life of me I cannot understand how hon. gentlemen get over the argument that I have just presented to them. If the law is wrong-and that would be a frightful admission for my hon. friend from Montreal because he applied his acute legal brain to the drawing of it-if he says that he made a mistake in drawing that Act and the whole Parliament of Canada made a mistake in passing it-what is .our logical duty ? What is the logical duty of any Parliament to-day with a bad law? It is not to bring in a resolution to override that law; it is to alter it. That is the manifest duty of the citizens and legislators of Canada. It is true if the law happens to be a tariff one it is bad; it is true that it is our duty to express our opinions upon tariff laws and every other law here; but for the purposes of an Act like this surely our manifest duty, if the law is wrong, is to alter it. For my part I will simply close by saying that I cannot conceive of any greater indignity being placed on this Parliament-and I use the words with deliberation and forethought-I cannot conceive of any greater indignity being placed on this Parliament than to ask it-by means of a resolution dictated largely, I fear, by sheer party expediency-to override by its own act a solemn law which it placed on the statute book only two years ago.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I would like to make one or two
observations in regard to this matter, and I do not think it will be necessary in noting the salient points to occupy as much time as did the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) in his ponderous effort of a short time ago. The hon. member waxed very indignant over the fact that there were certain constituencies in Canada which are not at present represented in this House. He declared, as every person will admit, that it is the right of every constituency in Canada to be represented in Parliament; and he went on to talk about the people who had fought and the blood that had been shed, to gain the people the great boon of being represented in Parliament. The hon. gentleman, however, conveniently passed over a situation which exists in regard to a

certain constituency in Canada which it seems to me should have occurred to him, to say nothing of his associates. I agree with the hon. gentleman that it is the right of every Canadian constituency to be represented in this Parliament, but let me ask this question:	what about
the two constituencies represented at the present time by the hon. member who sits immediately to the right of the official leader of the Opposition? Why is it that that hon. gentleman has not resigned one of those seats and given its constituents an opportunity to elect a representative to this House? The hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) complains that certain constituencies have been deprived of representation for a period of two or three months, but it does not seem to affect him in the slightest degree that one ' at least of the two constituencies I have referred to has been deprived of direct representation for a period of four years. Why does not the leader of the Opposition prevail upon the hon. gentleman who sits to his right to vacate one of those seats and give opportunity for an election either in the constituency of Gaspe or in the constituency of Maisonneuve? I think the reason was suggested by the hon. member for Red Deer. The hon. leader of the official Opposition has taken part in certain byelections, it is true, and he has figured in one part of the country in one way and in another part of the country in another way. I believe if the truth were known and we got at his real reasons for not bringing on an election in either of those constituencies it would be that he is afraid to test the opinion of ihe electorate there.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Oh, Oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Let us have a
good laugh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
It is the privilege of hon. gentlemen opposite, Mr. Speaker, and especially of my hon. friend from Chambly and Vercheres, to laugh. He is so beautiful at all times that he cannot add to his beauty even when he cracks his face in a laugh. But when the hon. leader of the Opposition taunts the Government with being afraid to bring on elections in certain constituencies, it is obvious that if he has a right to draw that conclusion, I certainly have a corresponding right to draw my conclusion as to why de does not prevail upon the hon. gentleman who sits to his right to vacate one of his two seats and test the opinion of its constituents. I have stated my opinion that he is afraid to test the feeling in one of those

constituencies which is largely interested in manufacturing; and in the other, which, I believe, is largely rural, he is also afraid to test its opinion, just as he has shown himself afraid to test the opinion of his follow-[DOT] ers in this House by a straight tariff resolution, as evidenced by his naked amendment on the Address.
But, Mr. Speaker, let us consider for a moment as to why it would be unreasonable to expect any person in this chamber, excepting the hon. leader of the official Opposition himself, to vote for the resolution which he has moved. I think I am right in saying that he was not a member of the House in the session of 1919 when the Bill was passed fixing the time when elections must be held at six months. If he was not then present, we cannot hold him responsible for that piece of legislation. But the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's was a member at that time, and in seconding this resolution he is casting a reflection upon the wisdom of the vote which he gave when that Act was passed. Is it reasonable to ask me or any other member to vote for a resolution worded as this resolution is when two sessions ago a law was unanimously enacted placing the discretionary power in the hands of the Government at six months in regard to the holding of by-elections. If that law is wrong, and six months is too long a time to allow, the law should be amended; but so long as that statute remains in force, then the discretion of the Government is within that six months, just as its discretion was unlimited before that legislation was passed.
I contend that no hon. member who voted for that law two sessions ago can logically or reasonably vote for the amendment which has been moved by the hon. the leader of the Opposition this afternoon.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this resolution states that the House is of opinion that representation in Parliament being a fundamental right of the people, writs should be issued, and so on. There can be no doubt whatever that that fundamental right Should be given to the people as far as it is reasonably possible, and if we are to look upon this resolution as merely a pious declaration of opinion, there can be no question of what we ought to do in regard to the first part of it. But the question may arise as to what we should do in view of the fact that we believe that all persons should be represented in this House, and that some are
not so represented. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), we passed a law a short time ago providing for cases of this kind, and I think it was well that we did so. There may be some ground of complaint as to that legislation, and if it were proposed to amend it by limiting still further the power of the Government in regard to the time within which to hold by-elections, I think it would be disposed, as I feel at present, to support a motion of that kind. That, however, is not what we are asked to do here. As has been stated by the last two speakers, we are asked practically to ignore that law, and to act now in a way different from what we decided should be done when we passed that legislation. I do not think that is the proper way to go about it. In doing the right thing we should do it in the right way.
Something has been said about the resignation of a former member of this House, Sir Herbert Ames, and although I was not present during all the discussion, it seems to me, in the absence of some better explanations that I have heard, that there is an element of suspicion about that matter, and it should be cleared up.
Our law provides that a writ must be issued for a by-election within six months of the issuing of your warrant, Mr. Speaker. But so far as I can read the Election Act, there is no time fixed within which the polling must take place, and it seems to me that perhaps the law is rather weak in that particular. I think we depended on the government of the day to deal fairly in that respect. Whether this Government have dealt fairly or not in regard to it, I have been advised, whether rightly or wrongly, that the writ was issued for the East Elgin election some three months before the election was held. If the Government hold off by-elections through the power which they have of fixing the date on which the polling is to take place, then we might as well not have any date fixed for by-elections at all. I think we should deal with this weakness in our present legislation in the way I have suggested, that is, by amending that legislation rather than by bringing in resolutions to overcome the defect. From the reports I have received in regard to the East Elgin by-election, there appears to be an element of suspicion surrounding it, and I think we ought to have some explanation. But the

mere fact that there is some suspicion in connection with certain things the Government has done does not in my opinion, justify our passing a resolution by which, in effect, we are asked to ignore the law of the land and to condemn the Government for not doing things which the law of the land does not require them to do. For that reason I shall feel myself justified in voting against this resolution. Not only do I feel justified, but I feel it my duty to do so and I have made these remarks in order to explain my position.
I am fully in accord with the sentiment expressed in the beginning of the resolution, that every part of the country should be represented in this House, and if the law is such now that the Government can prevent any part of the country having proper representation we should amend the law accordingly. But I do not see how we would gain very much even if the resolution were accepted by the Government and they took the necessary steps to at once issue writs for elections to fill the existing vacancies, for I hope this session will not last so many months that we shall be kept here long enough for the successful candidates of those by-elections to take their seats. At any rate I do not think any good purpose is served by introducing new members during the last few days of the session when we are rushing business through and trying to get home. .

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's):
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr Speaker, the question has
been so fully discussed that I can hardly hope to add anything material at this late stage; yet there are two or three thoughts to which I should like to be permitted briefly to call attention.
In the discussion that occurred a few days ago I ventured, presuming, perhaps upon my long experience in this House, to say to my right hon. friend the leader of the Government (Mr. Meighen), that I thought he would have been wise if instead of cracking the party whip and treating the amendment then offered as a non-confidence motion he had accepted it, because it simply asserted one of the vital principles of parliamentary government. From what has occurred since, from the discussion in ' the press and from reports that have reached me as to the views of hon. gentlemen in this House, privately expressed in general conversation, I am going to hazard the opinion that my right hon. friend rather regrets to-day that he did not

adopt that view. I may be mistaken, but he probably thinks it would have been wiser had he accepted the motion. Well, at the risk of repeating myself I am going to express regret again that my right hon. friend does not see the wisdom of accepting the motion that is now before the House, because it is simply the assertion of one of the very first principles of our parliamentary government. When my right hon. friend says that this amendment also must be treated as a non-confidence motion, I again protest that he is not representing the matter fairly. I am speaking from memory, but I am quite sure I am safe in saying that there are precedents and good precedents under all governments in Canada for the acceptance by the Government of an amendment to supply when it contains within itself nothing obnoxious when it asserts something that is admittedly sound and right, which ought not to be voted down simply because it is an amendment to supply. I have not looked at authorities, but my recollection will, I think, justify my saying that. If it should turn out upon later inquiry that I am mistaken, I shall be the first to make correction, but I am pretty certain that I am right. It is not a conclusive argument, therefore, to say that this motion must be voted down because it is an amendment to suply; if it asserts something which is true and right and reasonable, then the House should accept it. I am afraid my right hon. friend is putting a strain upon the loyalty of his friends when he asks them to vote down propositions so simple, so vital to the administration of public affairs in accordance with the institutions of British parliamentary government.
Now, a word or two with regard to the question of notice. I would like to remind the House that under the rules of comparatively recent years, under a rule which, if it be not offensive, I might call a parliamentary strangulation, and for which my right hon. friend the Prime Minister is probably more responsible than anybody else, under the restrictions that are now placed upon discussion in this House, this is the only day in this week when we can challenge the action of the Government by a motion of this kind. There are three days for Government business this week, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday. On Thursday and Friday the Speaker leaves the Chair without any disucssion and we would have no opportunity on those days to submit such a motion. Therefore, unless we brought forward our motion this day, Tuesday, -we could not bring it forward for another week,

and that, I think, is sufficient reason. But let me say to my right hon. friend that beyond that there is a reason. We have been having a few holidays; members are scattered throughout the different provinces ; many of them have not yet returned. If we were to avail ourselves of this opportunity of bringing the motion before the House, then we had to have a hurried consultation this day after some of the members had returned. In these circumstances-circumstances	from which
my right hon. friend cannot entirely absolve himself, because he had a large part in making the rules-we were precluded from dealing with the matter unless we brought it forward as we did to-day on the motion to go into supply. My right hon. friend will see, therefore, that we were justified in proceeding as we did. I know that the intention of the leader of the Opposition was to give my right hon. friend all the notice that was possible. I quite agree that it is desirable that in these matters reasonable notice should be given. I would like to feel that he has all reasonable opportunity of meeting anything that we bring forward.
The right hon. gentleman had much to say about the practice of old times. If my hon. friend made a study of Hansard for the purpose of these references I am sure he must have found quite a number of occasions upon which he and his friends took a view very different from that which they take to-day. I have no doubt he will find on examining the old records that on many an occasion he and the former leader of the Government, the member for King's, N.S. (Sir Robert Borden) and others when they were in opposition were very vehement in demanding that there should be no delay in the issuance of the writs. However, I do not attach much importance to that. If the cases stated by my right hon. friend were as strong as he presents them-and I assume for the moment that he has presented them truthfully-if there was such delay in the holding of the by-elections as he describes, then I say I do not care under what government it was done, it was wrong and it is time we corrected it. But suppose I admit for the sake of argument that the hon. gentleman's contention is correct. Suppose he makes a point against my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition; suppose he makes a point against me as a member of the ministry of former years, what answer is that to the people of Canada? Is it any answer to them to say
that I did wrong many years ago, if wrong it was? Surely two wrongs, as the old adage goes, do not make a right, and instead of going back to what hon. gentlemen claim to be the errors of former days it would be far better for them to stand behind their own record of these days and demand that these faults, if they were faults, should no longer continue. What answer is it to the elector down in St. Antoine to be told: Oh well, we had this up in the House some years ago; Mr. King and Mr. Fielding discussed it on that occasion, and their attitude then was inconsistent with the attitude they take now. But, says the elector in St. Antoine, what have I do with the leader of the Opposition and the member for Shelburne and Queen's? I have my rights as an elector of Canada; I have a right to be represented. What answer is it to the electors of Yamaska? What answer to the electors of York-Sunbury? What answer to the electors in any part of Canada? When these electors say: I have the right to be represented in Parliament, the right hon. gentleman replies: Some years ago Mr. Fielding and Mr. King had different views, and we are going to stand on that. It is a poor argument; the world is moving today.
New occasions teach new duties,
Time makes ancient good uncouth;
He must upward still and onward Who would keep ahreast with truth.
Instead of relying on the practice of the olden days, how much better it would be to move forward with the times and stand for the right of the people to be represented in Parliament. That is the rule that my right hon. friend should follow; that is the procedure he should adopt, rather than talk of what we did many years ago. It is a fact that hundreds and thousands of the young men of this country who are prepared, whenever they have an opportunity, to vote, had no opportunity of so voting when these things occurred. I am not indifferent to the records of the past; we may learn much from them; but the world is moving, and if the principles set forth in this amendment are sound and reasonable, we should be prepared to accept them. They are sound and reasonable. What reasons can be given for not accepting them? None has been given today.
Yes, my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) said: We have the six months' rule. The nature of that rule has not been fairly stated; it has been quoted here in a manner

which would imply that the intention was that an election need not be held for six months. It is preposterous to say that that was the intention of the Act. It was not the intention of the Act. When you give the Government power to issue a writ within six months, it is absurd to say that they are entitled to take the full benefit of that law, because that would shut out a number of constituencies from representation for a whole session of Parliament. Put aside the question A, B and C; put aside the question of consistency or inconsistency; put it as a simple question of representation. What right have the people of Shelburne and Queen's to representation and the people of St. Antoine to be denied representation? What right have any of the members of this House to represent their constituencies here and at the same time to tell the people of Ya-maska and York-Sunbury that they have not a right to be represented? The point is that we ought to be ready to give these people early and prompt elections. I cannot see that my hon. friends opposite have given us a single argument other than the old story of what we did many years ago. I have not investigated that, but I have no doubt that in many of those cases, perhaps in all of them, good reasons could be shown. I am, however, going to assume, for the sake of argument, that we were wrong, and I say, unhesitatingly, that if the cases were as described by my right hon. friend, if we deprived any constituency of an election for years-I do not know who did so-that was wrong, and instead of defending the wrong, it is high time we came to a better understanding in regard to the situation. That is the whole question.
No reason in law or argument can be advanced against the motion of my hon. friend, and it ought not to be treated as a vote of want of confidence. Hon. members of this House who read that motion calmly, when they leave this House to-night and go home and have their constituents read it, will see that no good reasons have been given why the motion should not prevail. It is in the interest of prompt elections; it is in the interest of every section which has the right of parliamentary representation. There is no reason for this hocus-pocus on the part of the Government. Why should there be this monkey business over the resignation of the hon. member for St. Antoine? Why should the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middle-bro), for whom I have the highest esteem, be led astray by this hocus-pocus business

and get into trouble by being induced to sign documents which, on their face, as an hon. gentleman said, are somewhat suspicious? As regards my much respected friend, the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Whid-den), I have more than a kindly interest in his welfare; he is a son of an old political opponent, but an old friend, with whom I crossed swords many a time years ago in the legislature of Nova Scotia. I am sorry to find that estimable gentleman has been dragged into this miserable business by which suspicion, which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson) has spoken about, surrounds that resignation. All that shows the simple reason for accepting the motion of my hon. friend. Why not give the people of these respective constituencies an opportunity to have an election?
I forgot one reason my right hon. friend advanced. He said: "If you did have these by-elections, what would happen? We would have to go off to the constituencies and defend our cause; those gentlemen would not go, they would not grant pairs, and therefore, we would be at a disadvantage." My right hon. friend has paid us the compliment that if there were by-elections, he and his friends would have to go and fight them, while we could stay at home and win.
