speechtext: I do not think it is quite as bad as that. I did not say that at all. I did not say that hon. gentlemen opposite would not go; much less did I suggest that they could win, because they have won scarcely anything that I remember. I said that they could go; but that as the rules put it in their power to challenge the Government by a motion that was not debatable, they could bring on a motion at a time that suited them, but we could not do the same thing. I pointed out their advantage under the rules.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: The right hon gentleman's comment was in regard to pairs. He said that we would not grant pairs.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: If we did not pair, we would be in Parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Therefore, my right
hon. friend clearly implied that if there were by-elections, he and his friends would be obliged to go away and fight them; that we would not do so. We would have an advantage. I am.going to make a suggestion to my right hon. friend, if that was

a material point in his argument, and it was about as strong as any argument he used. If he is afraid of that, let him bring on the by-elections, and we will give him all the pairs he wants. I think the facts and the principles involved are so plain to every thinking man that I am amazed that any extensive argument should be deemed necessary. The whole question is this: Have the people of every part of Canada a right to be represented in Parliament? If they have, why not give it to them? No shadow of reason has been advanced why the constituencies of St. Antoine and Yamaska should not be given the privilege of representation at the earliest possible moment.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not quite sure whether there is adequate reason for me to intervene in this debate; but we have sat so long listening to arguments in support of a motion for which there was manifestly no adequate reason, that I am overcome by the evil example and led to add reasons where reasons are not required. We have been accustomed in this House to the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) making "much ado about nothing;" we have not as yet become accustomed to that line of action on the part of the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), nor, may I add, on the part of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding); but this evening they seem to have been overcome with the conviction that their leader had not had his usual success in making "much ado about nothing," or at all events, that he had not made as "much ado about nothing" as this particular "nothing" in their eyes required, and, therefore, they felt obliged to come to the rescue. The hon. gentleman who spoke last, (Mr. Fielding), to take him first in order, felt impelled to support this motion by representing it to be absolutely the most harmless thing in the world. Why, it did not mean anything at all; it was just the affirmation of a principle which nobody doubted and nobody disputed, and why on earth should we not affirm it? Why should it be suggested that this motion was a motion of want of confidence? The hon. gentleman's proposition amounts to this, that every time the Government comes to this House asking for Supply, this House may properly be stopped in order that we may affirm, for instance, that the sun stands 84
in the firmament, and we must not go into Supply; we must strike out all the words after "that," and substitute the indisputable declaration that the sun is in the firmament, and then hon. gentlemen will rise in indignation and will say: Why do you call this a vote of want of confidence? Why do you ask this House to refuse to affirm what is self-evident to all the world, namely, that the sun is in the firmament? Oh, ye unreasonable men!
Does the hon. gentleman ignore the fact that there are two portions to the motion? Before you come to affirm these perfectly innocent, harmless propositions, you ask this House to say to the Government's motion to go into Supply: No, you won't get your Supply. Why? Because it is essential that we should affirm so and so. Can there be any suggestion of utility in a performance of that kind if it is not implied that the conduct of the Government is in some way violating this principle which the House is called upon to affirm? And yet hon. gentlemen are amazed because we treat this as a want of confidence motion. I have no doubt of the sincerity of the last gentleman who spoke (Mr. Fielding), but I am puzzled to see how, in view of his sincerity, he conciliates his affirmation, on the one hand, that this motion is no motion of want of confidence, with the declaration in his next breath that if they had not made this motion to-day they would have had no opportunity this week to affirm this principle. Why, Mr. Speaker, if they wanted merely to affirm a principle, the Order Paper is open to them as it is to every hon. member of this House. They might have put this resolution on the Order Paper for tomorrow or the next day, and might have debated it to their hearts' content, but that would not have served their purpose; that would not have served the purpose of the people who are amazed that we think this is a motion of want of confidence. Why would it not have served their purpose? Because it would not have carried with it the censure that the refusal of this House on the Government's motion to go into Supply implies and carries with it, and because it would not have had in it the sting that if it were carried tonight they would point out tomorrow to be in it' -the sting of the imputation that this Government has not lived up, in the letter and in the spirit, to what is the real principle with regard to representation in this House. So much for the pretension of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's



that we are not face to face with a vote of want of confidence. So much for the pretension that all that is wanted is a declaration of this abstract principle of the right of everybody to representation. Now let us see the other nothings about which we have had so much ado to-day.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
You are getting quite
Shakespearian.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
A little Shakespeare
might not do hon. gentleman on the other side any harm at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
A little Moliere and
Corneille would do a lot of good to the Government side.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
It might, and therefore we have recourse to them. I steer clear of the Scriptures, however, since my experience the other day. I would not. for all the world resurrect once more the two scriptural familiars of my hon. friend from Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie),-his friends Pontius Pilate and Judas Iscariot. My hon. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) will have to pardon me if I should bring back to his memory by the allusion I have made to the title of a play, the memory of Shakespeare, which I hope he keeps alive in his heart, and by whose teaching I hope he will endeavour to profit.
To pass to some of the other nothings with regard to which we have had much ado, in the first place we have had a fierce denunciation of the tu quoque argument, and hon. gentlemen have seemed to take it that because the right hon. leader of this House ventured to refer to some past actions of their own he had no argument to make except that "we are bad, and you are worse." Now there is a purpose for which it is sometimes salutary to look back into the history of the past, even though it may not afford an argument to justify or condemn the particular action of to-day. If it were not for my dread of getting on scriptural ground and my respect for the preserves of the hon. member for Cape Breton'North and Victoria, I might remind hon. gentlemen opposite that it is written in a certain book that it is well for those who live in glass houses not to cast stones.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
That is not in the
Bible.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
says it is not in the Bible. We will not insist on its particular biblical situation, although I think I could satisfy my hon. friend on that point. However that may

be, perhaps it does not do hon. gentlemen any harm, when they wax warm in the heat of their indignation, to recall to them that perhaps a little of their heat is due to the fact that people living in glass houses are apt to find themselves in hothouses, and are therefore apt to get a little overheated about the shortcomings of other people; and perhaps a little dose of past history may do no harm in the way of calming them, even if their glass construction should escape destruction.
Of course, we all admit that two wrongs do not make a right. Of course they do not, but where is the wrong that has yet been established? Where is the wrong of to-day? Why, in most of these cases, it is a matter of a few weeks. Hon. gentlemen may say what they like but, as one of them did say, the legislation of 1919 fixed a reasonable delay. Parliament sat here and considered what was a reasonable delay, and Parliament fixed that reasonable delay at six months. Now I do not suggest that that means the Government must not hold an election until the end of six months; but it is the solemn judgment of Parliament that within a period of six months it is proper that the Government of the day should exercise its discretion as to when an election ought to be held. And what are we here asked to vote?-to pass an order by this House to issue the writ in all these cases tomorrow. Well, now, Mr. Speaker, the representation of the people of the country in this House is important, and the choice of their representative is important, and because those two things are important, it is important that elections should be conducted in such a manner as to give every opportunity to the electorate to exercise calmly their' judgment and pronounce, after fair discussion and calm consideration, upon the issues that are submitted to them. -That takes time, and it depends largely upon local conditions as to whether one particular moment or another is the time when you may get the proper judgment of the rural people- Take this very proposal that is urged upon us to-night. If we issued these writs to-morrow we should be holding elections in certain rural constituencies-in Medicine Hat and Yamaska-in view of the delays that must necessarily intervene, just at the time when these rural populations will be actually taking up the important work of their seeding and when they will be very loath and averse to being called away from it to engage in the determination of important political questions that are to be dealt with and to follow up

that by an election. I just point that out to show the wisdom of Parliament when it confided to the government of the country a reasonable period of time within which to select the proper moment when the people will have the best opportunity of providing themselves with the representation to which they are entitled. If the importance of that is realized, I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the common sense of the House, that a month more or less in the time that elapses, within the six months to which we are limited, is a matter of very little consequence indeed, and I am quite justified in describing all this fuss as "much ado about nothing."
As to the motives imputed to the Government in this connection, it is hardly necessary, I think, that I should point out that this is the first government in the Dominion of Canada that has submitted itself to a Parliamentary rule restricting the time to which it might suspend elections; and to impute gratuitously to a government whose action made that rule possible, any desire to abuse the discretion, so limited at its own instance, in order to defeat the rights of the electors, is a proposition which, I must say, with all respect to the hon. gentleman who moved this resolution, and the hon. gentleman who seconded it, they will, on reflection, realize was more than ungenerous-was absolutely unfair.
Now, I do not want to take up time with the smallest of the nothings about which there has been so much ado. But there is the matter of the resignation of my very good friend Sir Herbert Ames. I am sure Sir Herbert will be cut to the quick when he reads the report of the address of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), and finds that he has been charged with being a party to a hocus-pocus in regard to his resignation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Oh, no; I did not make any charge against him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Oh! Then the hon.
gentleman made no charge against the only person in the world who had control of that resignation! Who was it that approached the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Mid-dleboro), and the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Whidden), and asked them to sign this document? Sir Herbert Ames, the gentleman who, my hon. friend would not for one moment suggest, would have anything to do with hocus-pocus. But what was the hocus-pocus that took place? It
844	[DOT]
was the witnessing of the signature of Sir Herbert Ames, at the instance of Sir Herbert himself, by the hon. member for North Grey and the hon. member for Brandon; and my hon. friend almost weeps over the unfortunate condition in which those two gentlemen find themselves in having been mixed up in this disgraceful proceeding. But Sir Herbert Ames, at whose instance they signed the document as witnesses, stands immaculate, unconnected with the hocus-pocus. For him the hon. gentleman has no word of condemnation; and in that let me say that I join most heartily with him; I have no word of condemnation for Sir Herbert. But I cannot follow the hon. member in his commiseration, if not condemnation, of the two other gentlemen who did what Sir Herbert asked them to do. I cannot agree with my hon. friend in his views in regard to this awful offence, and the falsehood imputed to those who signed the document as witnesses because the date was not on it; nor can I admire the learning and the legal lore to which we have been treated this evening upon this question of the necessity of witnesses certifying to the dates of documents. Hon. genltemen are positive about it. Why, it is so clear to them that there are not in the English language words lucid enough to do justice to its clarity. For common mortals who read the statute, however, I submit that what they find there is that there must be but the signing and sealing before a witness. There is not a word in the statute to require the date in the document, and hon. gentlemen read into a prescription that does not require such a provision at all, a witnessing to the date of a document. I will not undertake to speak for other provinces, but some of the lawyers who spoke are distinguished members of the legal profession in my own province, and I think that they would be satisfied with the sufficiency of a witness to a signature who does not witness to the date at all, if they turned up the civil code of the province of Quebec, wherein they would find, in regard to probably the most solemn document to which only two witnesses are required-that is, one of the forms of will in that province derived from the laws of England-that it is in so many words declared to be sufficient that the individual should exhibit his signature,-not write it in anyone's presence but exhibit a signature written previously, possibly on some date the witnesses knew nothing of-and then they sign to attest the signature. What is important about this document is the signature of Sir Herbert

Ames, and that is what the witnesses attested.
Now, we have all this talk and this reading of the speech in the Empire Parliamentary Association's Report, in which it is stated that Sir Herbert said that his resignation was in the hands of the Speaker; and hon. gentlemen are exercised as to whether people do or do not believe that statement, while all the time they run away from the perfectly manifest fact that, unless the veracity of the speaker he put in question, the very most that can he said is that Sir Herbert made a mistake in speaking. Now, I do not know in whose hands he left the resignation. I do not know what reason he had at that time for being under the impression that it had already reached the hands of the Speaker. I do not know whether he did or did not change his mind, or whether he had been under the impression that he had taken steps to send it to the Speaker or not. I simply do not know anything of this; I have no explanation to offer, and I have no responsibility so far as all this is concerned; nor has the Government any responsibility or obligation, or explanation, for it. Sir Herbert is an honourable gentleman; hon. members profess their confidence in him. He has the key to all this, and if they are curious about the relations between Sir Herbert and his trusted friends, I can only suggest that they apply to him, in whose honour I have the same confidence as they have, and I have no doubt they will get ample satisfaction for their curiosity. But, after all, what is it but empty curiosity? If they will read their statute they will find that a resignation is an effective document only from the moment it reaches the Speaker's hands. Just as a promissory note, so long as the maker keeps it in his own hands or in the hands of his own agent, binds him to nobody and to nothing, so that resignation has no binding legal effect until it has passed into the hands of the Speaker. And if whoever was the custodian of it, had chosen to tear the document to pieces before it reached there, he would have been responsible to Sir Herbert Ames and to Sir Herbert Ames alone. Until that document reached the Speaker, Sir Herbert Ames was as fully a member of this House as any of us who sit here to-night.
I am not going, except for the purpose of correcting one or two statements, to refer to the past. I deem it to be only proper, however, that the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) should be corrected in his statement that never up to the time referred to had there been

a period when the session went by without a constituency being represented in Parliament. Let me just mention one case that my eye falls on, and it is a startling one-the case of West Durham where, in the general elections of 1900, by reason of some irregularity, no return was made of the election that took place in that year, and no by-election to fill the vacancy occurred until January 15,	1902 -[DOT]
that is to say from November, 1900, till January, 1902-and most assuredly it will not be suggested that there was not a session during that period.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Was there a proceeding before the courts in reference to that election in the meanwhile?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: There had been no election; the returning officer did not return any candidate as elected. There was nothing before the courts because no return had been made.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Then there was no proceeding of any kind before the courts?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I cannot see on what such a proceeding could have been based.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: What was the evidence of a vacancy?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: The best evidence of a vacancy was that in the general election- a writ was issued for an election in West Durham as well as everywhere else, but the return day went by and no return came.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: That might not' be technical evidence of a vacancy; there might be reasons for that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: There was no evidence of any body being the member. The vacancy occurred when a general election was called, and the vacancy continued to exist until somebody was returned to represent that constituency. Ordinarily somebody does get returned for a constituency and the vacancy in that riding results from his disappearance. Here the vacancy was not the result of the non-appearance of anybody; the vacancy had existed since the House had been dissolved and continued to exist. There is also the case to which my hon. friend from Frontenac referred. We have had, sitting in this House ever since the general elections of 1917, an hon. gentleman who occupies two seats and thereby excludes one of these ridings from representation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: They both have representatives; they both have the man of their choice. .

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I would say that one has a representative or else neither has. My hon. friend from Maisonneuve and likewise from Gaspe-the gentleman who comes from opposite directions at the same time-is a man of fairly goodly proportions, but I fancy that if you divided him between the two counties neither of them would have a complete member.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: He would be dismembered.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Yes, as the hon. gentleman suggests, in the operation the member becomes dismembered, and the constituency is deprived of a member.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Is the right hon. gentleman aware that one of these seats has been contested and that it is impossible for the hon. member in question to resign while the case is before the courts?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I have heard it so
stated. I am not of an overwhelmingly suspicious turn of mind, but when I am told that an hon. member has been for a period of four years the object of a fierce onslaught on the part of a determined opponent insisting on driving him from his seat and leaving him with a broken heart because that inconsiderate action deprives him of resigning one seat .or the other, may I confess that notwithstanding the high respect I entertain for my hon. friend the dual member for Gaspe and Maisonneuve I cannot keep out of my mind a certain suspicion-I wonder what the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) thinks about it-a certain suspicion that if the contestation was not more likely to keep the hon. gentleman in two seats than to drive him from one, it might probably disappear. While we are on the question may I say that the thought has very frequently occurred to me-how did that contestation come about? There was a great reproach made to the legislation with respect to elections which preceded the last general election, the reproach being that as the law operates the thirty or forty days within which it was essential to file a petition in contestation of an election, actually expired before we got the return. Consequently it was said- and apparently was recognized in every constituency in Canada except the one of the two in which the petition now referred
to was filed-that there was no opportunity to file a petition.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
May I suggest to the
right hon. gentleman that if there is any abuse in the administration of justice in the province of Quebec, or elsewhere, it is the duty of the Minister of Justice to see that it is corrected.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I have not suggested that there is any abuse.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Or suspicion of any?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: May I gently intimate to the hon. member for Quebec South that if the Minister of Justice should take upon himself to attempt to direct or control the administration of justice in the province of Quebec he would be very promptly and very politely asked by the Attorney General of that province to mind his own business. The hon. gentleman shares a misapprehension that is very common in this country, a misapprehension that the Minister of Justice has some control or direction of the administration of justice, a matter which our constitution confides, and confides exclusively, to the provinces. That being the case, I can only recommend the hon. gentleman to carry his suggestion to his very good friend the Attorney General for the province of Quebec, who, no doubt, will give it every attention.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
And then have it referred back to the Minister of Justice in order that he should amend the law about which he complains.
i Mr. DOHERTY: But you have not complained about the law. I am sorry the hon. member for Maisonneuve and for Gasp6 (Mr. Lemieux) is not here this eveping. I would suggest to him in the most friendly way that it would be wise on his part to let
the world know who the petitioner is in that contestation, and in what court that petition is lodged, so that it may be open to inspection by the general public, who may be less confiding than I am, to satisfy themselves of its actual existence.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Why not appoint a royal commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen who are so resourceful might perhaps themselves find out for the benefit of the general public. However, it cannot leave one unmoved to observe the absolutely unperturbed condition of the hon. leader of the Opposition and the hon. gentleman who seconds this motion in face of the depriva-

tion of the people of one or other of those constituencies of Gaspe and Maisonneuve of representation in this House; and the contrast is somewhat remarkable.
Now, Mr. Speaker, with apologies for having myself contributed anything to this "much ado about nothing," I think I may safely resume my seat, feeling that I have no anxiety that I have not said all that could be usefully said, my only regret being that I should have wasted so much time over matter calling after all for so very little serious consideration.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the closing sentences of the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) were, it seems to me, hardly consistent. He apologised to the House for taking up so much time on a matter that he thinks of so little importance; but if he thinks it of so little importance why did he waste the time of the House? It did appear to me in listening to his opening and closing remarks that the government benches having debated this matter in solemn form during the afternoon and the first part of the evening, apparently decided to put up a joker at the end in the hope of overwhelming the resolution with ridicule. That would appear to be the only conclusion to be drawn from the speech delivered by the Minister of Justice.
But, taking up the last part of his address first, he referred to the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) and made some jocular remarks to the effect that if the hon. gentleman could be divided into two he might represent both Gaspe and Maisonneuve. Let me say to the minister in all seriousness that the fact remains that my hon. friend was elected by both of those constituencies. He stood for the verdict of the people, and that verdict said that he was their choice to represent them in this House. Now let the Government go and do the same thing in these constituencies which have been without representation for many months. That is what we are complaining about, and it is what the Government shrink from doing. The Minister of Justice says, to quote his own words, "It appears to me there is very much ado about nothing. Why should this House stop and debate the question, if it so seems fit to hon. members of the Opposition, whether or not the sun stands in the firmament? "Now, Sir, as to there being, much ado about nothing, let me bring this phase of the matter to the attention of the House. Does the Prime Minister or does the MinisfMr. Doherty.]
ter of Justice think that to complain, as we do, of the disenfranchisement of 200,000 people for several months is much ado about nothing? If there is one thing we ought to have in Canada it is responsibility of government, and responsibility of government rests with the people. If the government of the day has decided that the people shall not be trusted-and apparently they have so decided-well and good, let the Government say so. But why does a minister holding one of the most important positions in the Government stand up and say to the House and the country that this motion is only being brought forward at the whim of the leader of the Opposition? Let me say to him and to the other members of the Government and their supporters that if they will only put their ear to the ground for a few moments they will find that this motion is not brought forward to satisfy the whim of the leader of the Opposition, but rather to satisfy the whim of the people of this Dominion.
The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) said this afternoon, if I understood him aright, that the question of the right of the hon. member for Leeds to hold a seat in this House he would have to refer to the Department of Justice. Has anybody the temerity, Mr. Speaker, to stand up in this House and say that when a man is being paid a fee of $100,000, as has been reported, for conducting the Government's case in an arbitration as appears to be the case from the Act passed for that purpose, and whicfh was cited by the hon. leader of the Opposition this afternoon, that he is not within the pay of the Government and does not infringe the provisions of the Independence of Parliament Act? Do you need any opinion of the Minister of Justice, Sir, on that point? You need the opinion of no one. The right hon. Prime Minister knows, every member on the Government side knows, and the people of this country know, that Sir Thomas White, the hon. member for Leeds to-day, has no more right to sit in this House than the man in the street.
How many people have been disfranchised for months? In the constituency of Leeds there are 36,753; in Medicine Hat, 24,481; in Yamaska, 20,387; in York, Sun-bury, 30,780-and in passing let me ask this question: Do I understand that your warrant, Sir, has been issued in the case of York-Sunbury? If it has' it is a most significant circumstance, and it has, I be-

lieve, been issued for one reason only, while writs for elections in the other constituencies that were vacant long before York-Sunbury have not yet been issued. The only reason is that York-Sunbury, the Government believe, is the one constituency in which they have the slightest hope of carrying a by-election. The constituency of West York has an electorate of 33,306; St. Antoine 34,794; making a total of 187,501, or in round numbers 200,000 people that today are disfranchised by the action of this Government.
When, Sir, the Act was passed that byelections should be brought on within six months of the vacancies occurring, did any one who discussed or voted for that measure believe for one moment that the whole period of six months was to run? No, the intention was that just as soon as possible writs were to be issued. That was the spirit of the law, and it is in that spirit that I ask the Government to live up to to-day.
This, Sir, is not an ordinary session, this is not an ordinary Parliament. It is, perhaps, one of the most extraordinary Parliaments that ever sat in this Dominion. This feature has been brought up before during this session, and I do not propose to rehash it now, but I have said before, and I repeat it now, that irrespective of all precedent or anything else, there was a distinct promise that at the conclusion of the war this Government would appeal to the country. But, Sir, leaving all that aside, what do we find? We find after reading the statement of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) that we have the most appalling railway deficit in the history of our country-a defiicit of ten dollars for each man, woman and child in Canada. We have before us that most contentious question of the expenditure of millions upon the mercantile marine, a statement in connection with which was made to-day by the Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne). In view of these facts, and of the fact that all constituencies are not represented, can it be said either in this House or out of it that this Parliament has the right to go on with a willy-nilly policy? I say that the only fair thing to do is to let every constituency be represented before these important questions are taken into consideration with a view to making radical changes. Every constituency has the right to be represented, and I ask the Government to see that that right is acceded to.
There is one question I would like to ask of my friends in the far end of the chamber, especially the member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark). I ask it in no spirit of controversy, but the matter is of some interest. The question came up in the House the other day of practically an investigation of the railway systems of Canada. In other words, it was simply this: that the people of Canada, the shareholders in the publicly-owned railroads, should have the right to know whence their money was coming and whither it was going; the right to know how that money was spent and where the vouchers were; the right to speak absolutely as shareholders of a Company. The people who are being taxed for these roads have been denied the right to know whence these moneys came and whither they went. When this question is discussed the hon. member for Red Deer and a number of the other members of his party absolutely vote against any such investigation. Why I know not, but I should like to know. I am asking these hon. gentlemen-for whom the old parties were hardly good enough-
I am asking them in all seriousness-why they take that attitude. The hon. member for Red Deer says that the by-elections should not be brought on except at the will of the Government. In other words he says: We do not want investigation; we do not want representation. It is a nice point; I ask the question out of curiosity. There are many farmers in my constituency and I want to tell them; they are looking for enlightenmen. When the hon. member for Red Deer stands up and in, that vehement manner which is characteristic of him, says in trumpet-like tones to the farmers all over this broad Dominion, says to the members of this House, says, indeed, to every man, woman and child in Canada: We want neither representation nor investigation-I ask the hon. member for Red Deer where he and his party get off?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I as a matter of order tell my hon. friend that I get off by saying that I did not say what he says I said?

speakeroldname: Mr. S. W. JACOBS (George Etienne Cartier):
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been waiting all evening to hear some explanation from the two witnesses to this famous document. As the House is about to have the question put, and nothing has been heard from these two witnesses I merely rise to express my surprise that these gentlemen, whose names have been bandied

about so freely both inside the House and out of it during the last two or three weeks, have not considered it necessary to offer to the House and to the country some explanation as to what became of this document between July 21 and March 18. Sir Herbert Ames on July 21 stated that his resignation was in the Speaker's hands. Some time during this month you, Mr. Speaker, formally stated to the House that the document was not in your hands and that you had not received it, and following that statement the famous resignation was forthwith placed in your hands. Now, where was it during that time? The Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen), who is supposed to know something about the doings of his party, said that he knew nothing whatever concerning it. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) knew nothing about it. No one knew anything about the document. May I suggest that it was perhaps in the dead letter office? It would have been wise if the Postmaster General had been a member of this House in order that he might have said something about that part of his department which is dead.
Another suggestion, Mr. Speaker, I might offer is that when Sir Herbert Ames said his resignation was in the Speaker's hands, possibly he meant that, as he was the speaker, the resignation was in his own hands at the time. The whole matter is enveloped in so much mystery that the chief whip on the Government side, the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middle-bro) and the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Whidden) might give us some explanation as to when that document came into their hands and why it was not received by you, Mr. Speaker, until a few days ago. There must have been some reason for it. Were they acting on the instructions of Sir Herbert Ames? They certainly were not acting on the instructions of the right hon. Prime Minister. They were not acting on the instructions of the Minister of Justice, because we have the statements of these two gentlemen that they knew nothing whatever about the document. Were the two gentlemen who witnessed it acting on their own initiative? If so, we would like to know why. Was it in the interests of the country that they were so acting? Was it in the interests of Sir Herbert Ames, or was it in the interests of the Tory party? The country should know something about this. The whole transaction has all the characteristics of a slight-of-hand trick. Sir Herbert Ames states that he placed the document in your hands, Mr. Speaker, but you do not re-.
ceive it; then six or seven months afterwards it is found in the hands of the chief whip of the party.
A word or two has been said to-night with regard to the Bill which I had the honour of introducing into the House a couple of sessions ago and which declared that elections should be held within six months from the vacating of the seat. The Prime Minister seems to think that that law gave the Government discretion; he says: "It is for us to say when we shall have these by-elections; it is for the Government to exercise its discretion." Well, I thought at the time I introduced the Bill that it was for the benefit of the people, not to suit the discretion of the Government, but I must have made a mistake. I was a new member at the time and naturally was deceived by the arts and wiles of the Government. They ought not to have taken advantage of a poor member in that way.
When this measure was originally drafted it provided that the by-election should be held sixty days after the seat was declared vacant. The Bill was sent to the Committee on Privileges and Elections, of which that astute gentleman the Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie) was chairman. Hon. gentlemen on the other side, with tears in their eyes, represented to those who were supporting the Bill, that it would be manifestly unfair to force the holding of a by-election within sixty days. I remember that the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer), whom I see before me, made use of that argument. He said: "Take my own district, which runs from somewhere around Lake Superior to Hudson Bay and is as extensive as a large part of Europe; it would be impossible to canvass the electors of that district; it would be almost impossible within sixty days to enable the people to hear the dulcet tones of my voice." The hon. member pointed out that a period of six months was a reasonable time in which everyone could hear him expound his views to the people. He said that it would take at least six months to prepare lists in that wild and unorganized district, the district which sends him to this House. We were soft-hearted people and we fell. We agreed with the hon. member and we thought that after all, half a loaf was better than no bread, and we accepted the six months. It never was contemplated at the time that this period of six months was to be given in order that, as the Prime Minister said, the Government in that time

could exercise its discretion as to when an election should be brought on. If that is the view which he takes, he certainly has distorted what we considered should be the law and were willing to agree to, when the matter came before the House after the committee had reported.
I heartily concur in the views expressed by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) as to the necessity for bringing on these elections now. It may not suit the convenience of the Government to have these elections brought on; but, as has been said by every hon. member on this side who has spoken in this debate, it is in the interest of the country that the people of these disfranchised constituencies should have a right to have their views expressed on the floor of the House on the highly important matters which are to be brought before us within a very short time. Only a few evenings ago we heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) declare, in the most solemn way, that, with regard to the railway situation, we are facing one of the most important crises in the history of the country since Confederation. Surely, every element of this population, of this community, has a right to be represented in this House when those important matters are to be discussed. I consider that the Government are making a serious tactical blunder when they refuse to allow this resolution to go through. The temper of the people is such that they cannot stand, as the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) said, very much further hocus-pocus business in this House. Their temper is such that they want to have matters fully discussed; they want to know the financial condition of the country, and every constituency be represented in this House at this crucial moment. I for one am very glad to cast my vote in favour of the amendment which has been moved to-night by the leader of the Opposition.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I was paired with the hon. member for East Algoma, (Mr. Nicholson). Had I not been so paired, I would have voted for the amendment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I was paired with the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn). Had I not been so paired, I would have voted for the amendment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I would ask my right hon. friend if he does not think it is a little early in the morning to begin taking up Estimates.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I do not know how the business of the House is to be done if we are always to have an amendment to the motion for Supply, and then land up too late at night to do any work. It is pretty late to be commencing Estimates, but it is important that the Estimates be considered, and we are getting on very, very slowly.

Although the Government has brought the Estimates on every day for quite a length of time now, we have scarcely anything through.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
May I ask who is the
Minister of the Interior at the present time?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman
does not know, it is the Hon. Sir James Lougheed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I should like again to speak to the Prime Minister. I think it is perfectly proper that matters of general and great public interest should be discussed. We need not necessarily end this session at a particular date as my' right hon. friend has intimated this evening and if there is public business to be carried on we are prepared to stay here in Ottawa for a considerable period of time until it is done satisfactorily, but we do not wish to discuss the business of this country after midnight. We propose to do it at a time when we can give to it all the attention that it demands.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Some of us are quite a long way from home and want something to do. I have wandered about Ottawa for five days now with little to do. I am an older man than the leader of the Opposition, but I am quite prepared to go on with the business of the House now. I have been in this House when we carried on business continuously day and night. I helped to do it, with the co-operation of my hon. friends. I am sure my hon. friends are not so old that they cannot stay and work for a little while yet.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I do not want to stay
here all night, and I do not propose to stay here all night. If the hon. member for Red Deer does not go home that is his misfortune, not my fault. Apparently he has had a better rest than those who went home. Some go for pleasure and others go for work. I have not the advantage of being a gentleman farmer, and when I go home I have to do something. Let us begin by getting a little information. I notice an increase in this item of $42,250. How is that accounted for?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: That is accounted for entirely by statutory increases.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I find by the details on
page 81 that we are providing salaries for assistant deputy, publicity assistant, and custodian of survey equipment. I do not know that there is anything in the statutes

providing for increases for these men. Then there is a senior statistical clerk; statistical clerk, forestry; statistical clerk, natural resources and intelligence. I thought all this work of collecting statistics was transferred to the Department of Trade and Commerce to co-ordinate the work and save money to the country. I should like some explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
These men are engaged
in the compilation of statistics with regard to our natural resources, and they come under the Interior Department.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: The $42,250 is made up of increases to those men for the coming year?	*

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Yes, the statutory increases for all these positions.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: They are entitled to these increases by statute?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Does that include the
bonus ?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
The
item calls for salaries for four editors. What do these four editors edit?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: These editors are connected with the various branches of the department, such as the Astronomical Branch. They edit the publications that are issued by the various branches of the Department of the Interior.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: What publications does the department issue?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: It issues monthly bulletins regarding astronomical questions and other matters that are dealt with. -

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Where are they printed?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: At the Bureau.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: -Is it the intention of the Government again to amalgamate the Department of the Interior and the Department of Immigration and Colonization? It seems that at the time the departments were separated it was a more matter of convenience for the Government to make an appointment, and I should like to know whether it is the intention to amalgamate them again?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
The amalgamation has not been considered by the Government. The importance of the Immigration Department is such that it takes considerable time
itself. I would not say that amalgamation may not he possible later on, but it must he remembered that the Mines Department has also been placed under the Minister of the Interior.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Is there any talk
about amalgamating the Department of the Interior and the Customs Department?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Oh no; there is no talk of that. I think the hon. gentleman means the Inland Revenue Department and the Customs. They are being amalgamated.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I am
not entirely satisfied with the explanation in regard to the editors. My hon. friend told me that these four editors of monthly bulletins were being paid over $9,000 in salaries. Now, in the town in which I live I know an old gentleman of over 70 who issues a paper twice a week all alone. He does the whole work and his paper is a bigger thing than these monthly bulletins. I hope the minister does not mean to say that these gentlemen are working a whole month on these little bulletins.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Perhaps I may be
excused if I say something on this subject, because I have some familiarity with it. The hon. member must not labour under the impression that these are new appointments. These editors have been in the service for many years, I think prior to 1911. The Astronomical Branch, which has charge of the observatories in Ottawa and Victoria, would not be performing its functions as such at all if it did not issue publications recording its achievements and observations, and these publications must necessarily be edited by a man who knows the work of the observatories. I am sure that Dr. Klotz could give the hon. member a more detailed explanation than I can. His staff has been so very much reduced that if the hon. gentleman met him he would listen to a wail of complaints at the parsimony of the Government in not granting more money for his observatories. I do not think there has been any increase; in fact, there has been a reduction. It is, of course, essential to have someone to edit the publication of this branch, and the same is true in regard to the natural resources branch. Its business is to com-; pile into systematic and readable form information as to the natural resources of this country, and well has it performed its task. The head of the branch is Mr. Lynch, one of the ablest of public servants, ap-

pointed long before the Government of Sir Wilfrid went out of office; and without an editor that branch could not do its work. The same can be said of the Geodetic Survey. That is one great survey that is being conducted in the Dominion, and in relation to it all other surveys take their place. It is the primary one, to which other surveys are related and to which they are more or less subsidiary. Necessarily, its work takes the form of publications which must also be edited, and these editors are retained for this purpose.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I notice on page 82 a
junior law clerk at $1,680, and a senior law clerk-stenographer at $1,500. Now, I have always been aware that I belong to a very poorly paid profession, but I did not think that a kind and benevolent Government such as this could imagine that after having gone through three or four years of study in a law school, any one who qualified for the position of law clerk in the employ of the Government would be worth only something like $100 more than an ordinary stenographer. I do not desire to ask the 'Government to spend more money; they have spent enough, the Lord only knows; but I think it is most unfair to the members of the profession to which I belong, to give them what I might call starvation wages.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
What is the
name of the junior clerk?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Am I to receive an explanation from the minister as to how it is that a barrister receives only $100 or so more than a stenographer? I presume this is a barrister, and it does not seem reasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
These are both stenographers who are familiar with law terms, and this classification is made by the Civil Service Commission.
Mr. POWER. I see that there are really three law clerks, two at $2,040 and one at $1,800. Will the minister explain what their duties and qualifications are, who are the present incumbents, when they were appointed, and from what universities they graduated? I forgot to add that there was a departmental solicitor, and I should like to know something about his qualifications too.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Is he still alive?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
The duty of these men
is to draw up grazing and mining conveyances and leases in connection with the Department of the Interior, and to do the usual law work appertaining thereto.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: What are their names?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: One of them is Mr. W. McQuarrie; I am sorry I cannot give the other names.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I know one of these
law clerks, who happened to be one of my classmates at the law school. He has been a lawyer for a number of years and is receiving only $2,040, while I see on page 8 a young lady clerk is receiving $2,400 a year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
She has other
duties to perform.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Was her salary fixed by the Civil Service Commission?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
What is her
name?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: S. Clapp.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: This young lady has been designated as "Assistant Private Secretary." She had five years experience in Toronto law offices before coming to Ottawa, on February 9, 1917, as secretary to Mr. S. A. Armstrong, formerly assistant Provincial Secretary, Ontario, then Director of the Military Hospitals' Commission, and afterwards Deputy Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. Miss Clapp was employed in this capacity until Mr. Armstrong left the department in July, 1918, when she was transferred to the minister's office as assistant private secretary. She was thus employed until October, 1920, when upon Sir James Lougheed being appointed Minister of the Interior, she was transferred to the Interior Department. Sir James Lougheed is now minister in charge of the following: Department of the Interior, Department of Indian Affairs, Department of Mines, Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, Board of Pension Commissioners, Soldiers' Settlement Board and is Government leader in the Senate. The ministers' secretarial work in connection with the foregoing is carried on by two private secretaries and Miss Clapp as assistant private secretary. Miss Clapp's salary as indicated in the Estimates will not carry with it the usual secretarial allowance of $600 or any other allowances. Miss Clapp's transfer does not make any increase in the secretarial staff of the office of the Minister of Interior.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Dispense.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
One of these clerks, who has had eighteen years' experience, is only

getting $2,040 while acording to the statement of the minister this young lady, with five years' experience only, is in receipt of $2,400. I do not think that the discrimination is at all fair.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: This young lady is assistant private secretary.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: How many secretaries are there to the Minuter of Interior?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Two private secretaries and one assistant private secretary. But he administers, as I have already pointed out, the Department of the Interior, the Department of Indian Affairs, the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, the Board of Pension Commissioners, the Soldiers' Settlement Board, and is leader in the Senate.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: A short time ago the minister mentioned that a bulletin was published by the Department of the Interior, which bulletin, if I am not mistaken relates to astronomy. I would like to know from the minister if it is the custom of the department to print that bulletin in both languages? If my information is correct it is not published in French, although the subjects treated of in the bulletin are most interesting and should be published in French and distributed throughout our provinces, a proceeding which would be productive of good results. In making this request I am not asking favour, hut simply asserting a right. The publications by the Department of the Interior are official documents issued under the authority of the Federal Government. Now, as is well known, English and French are official languages and therefore if the Department of the Interior, or any other department, wishes to publish bulletins, or monthly statements of any kind, these publications should be issued in both languages. There is this further reason for pursuing such a course: There are already translators in the department and it would be very easy for the minister to see that in future all publications by the department are printed in both languages. Then the population of my own province, as well as the population of the English provinces, would he able to take advantage of these publications. I think it will be sufficient to draw the attention of the minister to the matter to cause him to see that the present condition of things is immediately remedied.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Some of the publications issued by the department are now published in French, but I will be very glad to bring what my hon. friend has said to the attention of the Minister of the Interior.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: There seems to be some discrimination shown in the matter of increases. Some officials are drawing salaries of $4,000, others $3,000, and others again $2,500, or $2,000. These se(em to be the officials who are getting increases whereas the poor fellow who is only paid $1,000 does not appear to be receiving any consideration. It appears to me that the men in humble positions-who have families to raise and clothe and educate just as the higher salaried men have-are entitled to some attention. If increases in stipend are being given, surely those men who receive only $1,000 a year are as much entitled to an increase as are the higher officials who are paid three or four thousand dollars a year?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: The remuneration is not now arranged by the department but by the Civil Service Commission who fix these increases from time to time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: There is a very strange item at page 32 of the Estimates where I notice that salaries are being voted for two senior messengers and also for eight messenger clerks. What work is performed by the clerks of these messengers may I ask?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
There are two senior
messengers, one in the Natural Resources Branch, and the other in the deputy's office. "Messenger clerks" is the new designation given by the Civil Service Commission to ordinary messengers.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I think that designation ought to disappear from the Estimates. It may be all right to have senior messengers but why do you want to have messenger clerks for them? With all due respect to the Civil Service (jommission they do not, so far, seem to know very much about the duties entrusted to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: These men have to perform the duties of an ordinary messenger, but occasionally they are employed in doing some little office work that does not strictly belong to their duties.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
In that case call them messengers, why term them "messenger

clerks"? I move that the word "clerk" be stricken out of the designation.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I notice there is still another grade of messengers and that is "confidential messengers". I would like to know what duties these confidential messengers perform, and why they are so designated?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: The confidential messenger carries cash from one department to another and handles cheques. He has a good deal of responsibility as compared with the ordinary messenger.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: The other day when we were considering the Estimates of the Minister of Justice he gave an entirely different definition of a confidential messenger.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: But there is no money handled in his department.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I have explained the
duties of these men in the Department of the Interior. I do not know anything about how they do their work in the Department of Justice.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: It appears that salaries are voted for officials who look after the Government lands. I suppose these must be the lands held by the Federal Government in the western provinces. Is it the intention of the Government to come to any decision as to those western lands? I saw in the papers a few months ago that a conference of Western premiers had been held in Ottawa, and I would like to hear from the minister if the matters then discussed have been considered by the Cabinet and any conclusion reached in regard to the natural resources which have been claimed by the western provinces since their creation by the Laurier government fifteen years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
This has been a live
question in the West for many years, and the various provinces have made efforts to secure these Dominion lands. A meeting was held here within the last twelve or eighteen months and the matter was discussed, but up to the present time the Government has reached no definite conclusion in regard to the matter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
On page 81 I notice 3 Chief Map Draftsmen, 12 Principal Map Draftsmen, 30 Senior Map Draftsmen, 26 Map Draftsmen, 1 Junior Map Draftsman,

2 Principal Draftsmen, 4 Senior Draftsmen, 6 Draftsmen-86 in all. What are these Chief, Principal and Senior Map Draftsmen?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: These are all classifications made by the Civil Service Commission and cover the making of maps for the Lands Department, the Natural Resources Department, the Mines Department, the Observatories, and the Water Powers branch. The definition of Chief Map Draftsman is: supervising the preparation of sectional, topographical, geological, geographical, and other maps, corresponding with surveyors and others in connection with map preparation. The definition of Principal Draftsman: is supervising the compilation and plotting 6f survey maps and plans from notes, and assisting in the examination and checking of plans submitted by various district engineers and contractors.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Although there is a very considerable increase in these Estimates, the minister in charge of the department has made no suggestion whatever as to the possibility of cutting down expenses. I think the minister who is now endeavouring to pass these Estimates must realize the position in which the country finds itself. It is very hard in a committee such as this to make adequate criticisms of various items; we can only do our best from the information which the mere Estimate places before us. But in view of the present financial situation and of the fact that immigration is proceeding at a very slow rate, surely there should be an opportunity of cutting down expenses in this department. It is quite impossible for any private member to say just what officer should be let out, or just what expense could be curtailed; but we have got to cut our coat according to our cloth, and the only way to reduce the expense of government is by cutting down a little here and a little there. I do not suggest for a moment, Mr. Chairman, that salaries should be cut down, but I want to see better service given. It seems to me that in many offices a smaller personnel could do the work as efficiently, and perhaps more efficiently, than those who are presently engaged there. And that is what we would like to have from the minister,-some plan for cutting down expenses. Of course, it is not quite fair to ask this minister to talk about a department with which, after all, his connection is merely to get the Estimates through this House. His ability and courtesy always impress us, but look at the striking difference between to-night,

when he seeks information from the deputy on every point and has to keep us waiting in answering questions, and the facility with which he answered questions when he was passing his own Estimates. At that time it was a pleasure to ask him questions, for the information, accurate and interesting, simply flowed from him. Now, why have we not a right to have the Minister of the Interior, of this great spending department, in this House to answer for his own Estimates? Could anything be more striking as to the fitness of the stand taken the other day by the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) and other members on this side that these great spending departments should have their ministers sitting in this chamber? That is something which I wish to strongly impress upon the Government. We realize that the minister in his courteous and able manner is doing the best he can with these Estimates, but how can he do justice to the situation when he has to have recourse to 'his deputy and practically read all the information he gives us. And I believe in an eight-hour day. I do not think you will advance the business of the country by insisting on proceeding in the small hours of the morning. However, if it is thought wise to go on, of course we will endeavour to do our duty in this connection. But let me make this suggestion. I have in my hand a pamphlet dealing with adjustment of geodetic triangulation in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, publication No. 2. I presume this pamphlet has been distributed to every member of the House; at any rate, I made no special application for it yet I find it in my box. Now, I defy the minister, who belongs to a learned profession, to make head or tail out of this geodetic triangulation. It is all higher mathematics. The member for North Cape Breton asks me to explain some of the diagrams. I can no more do that than I can talk Gaelic; it is beyond me. My learned and hon. friend from Dorchester suggests that this pamphlet is published with the intention of bringing the two provinces together along geometrical lines. But the point I want to make in all seriousness is that although these pamphlets may be of interest to highly trained technical men, such as surveyors and engineers, to send them broadcast throughout even the House of Commons is a pure waste of public money. These are suggestions which I throw out for the time being, [DOT] and if the minister who is in charge of the department can help us by suggesting how public money can be saved in the conduct of it, we will all gratefully listen to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: The pamphlet which the hon. gentleman has just referred to is for the use of surveyors and other professional men. These pamphlets are distributed in the various provinces and exchanged with other countries for similar publications. With regard to running this department in an economical way, I may say, the minister is at present engaged in a general reorganization with a view to effecting a substantial saving. There are no increases other than the statutory increases. He is retiring a number of employees who are getting up in years and he is combining a number of branches with a view to making a saving. I shall be glad to bring to his attention when he returns the fact that this matter was mentioned by the hon. member for Brome.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Can the minister make
such a reorganization- of his personnel without the consent of the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
By the combination of
branches, I think he can move a considerable distance in that direction.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: But how far?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Sufficiently to obtain
very much better results through the combination of staffs in different branches.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I would direct the
attention of the committee to a most extraordinary condition of things. When hon. members ask for information in connection with railways they are told that the information cannot be furnished because the railways are managed by a body independent of the Government. If we turn to the Mercantile Marine we are told that it also is run by a separate corporation and that details and information will be supplied by that corporation and not by the Government. Then, when we put questions in connection with civil employees in other departments we are told that the Civil Service Commission, another body independent of the Government, is responsible, not the Government itself. This is a very serious condition and every hon. member should try to bring about a change. If we are to have responsible government in Canada, members are not to be referred to outside bodies when they ask for information; if so we might just as well abolish the House of Commons. Under our constitution the House of Commons is supposed to have the power of the purse, but I doubt very much whether we have that power. Hundreds of millions are spent every year on our railways and'

hon. members cannot obtain any information in connection with them; the managing body can spend what it likes and the House of Commons has to pay. The same is true of the Mercantile Marine. Now, when we come to the civil service, if there is any body of persons who should be responsible to the representatives of the people it is certainly the civil employees. Even when the Minister of Agriculture was explaining his Estimates he stated on a number of occasions in answer to inquiries from this side:	I cannot give the information; that
matter is settled by the Civil Service Commission. I say that if this system continues, both the power of the purse and responsible government will disappear. The minister ought to be master of his department; if he is not, who is? If the ministers who compose the Cabinet are not masters of their various departments, it is about time we should know who runs this country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: The Civil Service Commission.
