maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Apparently the Civil
Service Commission runs it so far as the Civil Service employees are concerned. The Toronto financiers run it so far as the railways are concerned, and as to who runs the boats we shall know that when the marine Estimates come before the House. The condition which prevails in Ottawa is unbearable, and unless there is protest from both sides of the House-because every member is interested-unless there is a strong and earnest movement to bring about the re-establishment of constitutional institutions in Canada as they existed before the war, we shall wake up and find that we have in this country not responsible government, but autocratic government. It is to be regretted that the head of this department we are now considering, in connection with which such a large amount of public money is spent, is not in the House to furnish the necessary explanations. He is replaced, it is true, by a very sympathetic minister; in fact I think the Minister of Agriculture was chosen purposely because his colleagues know how sympathetic he is to this side. We have confidence in the Minister of Africulture so far as his own department is concerned; we know that every cent we have voted for his department will be well spent. But the moneys which we give to-night, if we give any, will be spent, not by my hon. friend, but by another minister whom we do not know even by sight, for he sits in the Senate. My hon. friend is not in a position .	,
to give to the committee the information which it desires. The member for Brome asked whether it is possible to reduce the expenses of the department. That is a fair question, but the minister cannot answer it because he has not the information. Indeed, he could not do it even if he were the head of the department, because judging from the answer which he has just given he would have to apply to the Civil Service Commission before he could reduce the personnel of the staff.
The minister, in answer to a question which I put in connection with the Dominion lands in the West, told me that the matter was under advisement. That was a very diplomatic answer, but without discussing this question on its merits I would point' out that the financial situation in Canada is very bad. Every hon. gentleman realizes the necessity for a reduction in expenditure with a view to the stabilizing of our financial condition and status. Why should not the Government cease giving vast sums of money to the different provinces for roads, technical schools, .housing schemes, and other different things? Those grants are given, not because the older provinces need them. The older provinces are in a better financial condition than the federal government is. The credit of the province of Quebec is by far higher than that of the Dominion of Canada. Quebec does not need any of these federal credits; we do not want them; let the Government keep the little money they have. Some hon. gentlemen opposite might say: "If the eastern provinces do
1 a.m. not need that money, maybe the western provinces need it." Instead of taking money that we do not possess in the Federal treasury and giving it to the western provinces, why not stop those grants and give to the western provinces their natural resources? They would then have large revenues that would meet their expenditures, and Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta could carry on the government of these provinces without calling on the Federal Government for assistance. This is a very important question. I see some of my western friends in their seats, and we should, to-night, endeavour to secure from the Government a more definite answer on this all-important question of Dominion lands in the western provinces. These remarks are addressed to the minister in entirely good faith. I know he is not in a position to speak with full authority as regards the Department of the Interior; but next to him I see the Minister of Justice

(Mr. Doherty), and I am quite sure that nothing of any great importance would be decided without that right hon. gentleman being consulted, so that if the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) cannot furnish the information, I am quite sure the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister will do so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I do not know that
the subject of natural resources is connected with the Civil Government Estimates, but I shall be glad to make a short answer to the hon. gentleman. The question of natural resources has occupied the attention of government and of political parties for some time. I have no doubt the hon. member will recall a somewhat celebrated, but, I think, very often lamented convention that was held in the city of Ottawa in August, 1919, at which convention, amongst other resolutions-almost innumerable others-a resolution was passed referring to this very question. That resolution called for the transfer to the western provinces of their natural resources on terms that would be fair to the other provinces of Confederation. With the principle of that resolution, coupled with the condition-I have no fault to find. I might remark though, in passing, that the natural resources were reserved from the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, initially by hon. gentlemen opposite, and the complications that are now involved in any question of the retransfer all arise from the fact that those resources were initially withheld.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Were they not withheld from Manitoba in the same way?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
They were withheld
from Manitoba, I forget the year, but shortly after Confederation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: But on the same principle when the province was created.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
The same principle, I
know.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: What about the extension of Manitoba?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: When the natural resources were withheld from Manitoba and Manitoba requested to be put in the same position as Alberta and Saskatchewan, the same had to apply to the extension of Manitoba; there was nothing else to do. That is what Manitoba asked for; that is what Manitoba received.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
The
reservation was made first for Manitoba,
and my right hon. friend says that we are responsible for Saskatchewan and Alberta. Who was responsible for Manitoba?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: The government of the day that made the reservation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Who were they?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I am not sure. My statement anyway is correct that hon. gentlemen are responsible in respect of Saskatchewan and Alberta.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Following your
precedent.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: It is the same old tu quoque argument.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman himself was jumping at it a moment ago; he should not despise it now. I am not making anything in the way of a tu quoque argument; I am simply stating the facts and the difficulties in the way of this question. They arise from the fact that the resources were reserved; that they did not pass to the provinces. Whatever the reasons were that moved governments of the day to reserve those resources, the fact is that they were reserved, and that public policy since then has adjusted itself to that situation, public policy in respect of not only subsidies but every policy that appertains to western Canada and, much more, appertains to eastern Canada. Scarcely a step has been taken in regard to administration and the laying out of lines of policy as to the west, that has not been dictated in part by the fact that those resources were reserved. For example, as regards railway policies, under the responsibility of the Federal Government lines of railway were projected, were entered into that probably would not have been entred into, but the fact that the resources were reserved. In respect of water-power, in respect of irrigation, obligations were undertaken that undoubtedly would not have been undertaken but for the fact that such resources were reserved. I could go from one thing to another; all these things have been incurred, and the prooortion of outlay of the federal Government that is attributable to the fact that the resources were reserved is something that it is virtually impossible to ascertain. It is just like attempting, after a long series of years, to go back and under a process that is long and involved. An accounting will not do it; indeed, it is impossible to get at anything that can be said to be an exact return of justice to those provinces and, at the same time, fair



to the others. At every point of the process some difficulty arises that virtually involve the whole question and makes us determine what would have been done if such and such had not been the case, something that no one can, with any certainty, determined at all. Consequently, when a Government, however anxious it may be to solve this problem, to return the resources to the western provinces, sets about to get a solution based upon any principle at all, it is met with difficulties that are almost insurmountable when you take into account the fact that the other provinces must consider the solution fair. Hon. gentlemen opposite have acceded to the principle that a solution cannot be found which does not take into account the fairness that applies to the other provinces that have been parties to the subsidies the West has obtained arising from that reservation. We have attempted time after time to get a solution; we have not succeeded. We are still engaged in the effort, and we are sincerely anxious to obtain a solution. If hon. gentlemen were in power, I think they would be anxious to obtain a solution, but they would meet precisely the same difficulties which we have encountered. I do not think, however, we would find the hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) ready to accede to anything that western Canada would agree to. None of the western provinces has as yet agreed to accept any deduction from its subsidies, got in lieu of lands if the resources are transferred. They take the ground that the resources should be transferred and the subsidies retained, because they maintain that already sufficient resources have been alienated, as they express it, to make up for the subsidies. That is the position of the matter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I happened to be a member of the House at the time the western provinces were organized, and I recollect distinctly the discussions that took place on that occasion. The decision that was arrived at was this, that it would not be wise at that stage of the progress of the Dominion to hand over to the western provinces the lands, because the immigration policy was in the hands of the Dominion Government and it was thought that the two should go together, so that when the Dominion Immigration Department found a good settler in Europe and brought him to Canada they should be able to place him on the land without any interference by the local legislatures of these new provinces. The Parliament

of that day arrived at a solution by contributing a larger sum of money to the western provinces. That was regarded as fair by the representatives of the western provinces at that time, so the matter was settled in that way, and that large subsidy has been paid to the western provinces ever since that date. If they claim their lands now, it will be necessary, of course, for them to account for the money that has been paid to them during all these years since the western provinces were organized. That is only fair to the other provinces. I have no desire to inflict any injury on the western provinces; my only desire is to arrive at a fair solution. I should like to know whether my right hon. friend agrees with the decision that was arrived at by the premiers of all the provinces when this matter was dealt with, to the effect that the rights of the other provinces had to be recognized, and that the eastern provinces, as well as the western, have certain rights in this matter. Does my right hon. friend agree with the decision that was arrived at by the premiers of the various provinces? The position that has been taken by my right hon. friend and by some other gentlemen from the West for some years past, as I understand it, has been that the natural resources of the western provinces should be handed over to them now, the western provinces retaining the large subsidies that were given to them in lieu of their resources. Is that his position at the present time?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I do not know to what agreement between the premiers my hon. friend refers. I would be very much surprised if he can find what was agreed on by the premiers of the provinces of Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
My
right hon. friend quoted it a moment ago. He said that it was to be done with regard to the rights of the other provinces.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I will refer to that in a moment. I understood the hon. gentleman to say that the premiers of the different provinces had come to some agreement in respect to this matter. If they have, I would be delighted to be informed of what it was. I do not think they ever agreed on anything, and I may possibly be permitted to express despair that they ever will. The hon. member says that if the western provinces get their resources, they must account for the moneys they have received ever since these subsidies were granted in lieu of resources. I under-

stand him to mean that they should pay that money back. I want to tell him right now there is not one Government of the three Prairie Provinces that would consider that for one moment. They have never agreed as yet, even to a deduction in any degree whatsoever from the subsidies payable in future in lieu of lands. I communicated with the premiers of all the provinces by letter, prior to our last conference, and told them that if any substantial progress was to be made they should let us know what they were ready to do. Were they ready to accept a deduction in subsidy in lieu of lands, or were they ready to wipe it out? I got no affirmative answer. They take this ground now. They say: You were trustees for us for these lands. Now we ask you to account for everything you have got, and not only everything you have got, but for everything you should have got; if you had a piece of land homesteaded, for instance, instead of selling it, you should pay us the amount you could have sold it for. You account to us as trustees, and we will account to you for the subsidies received. I pointed out that at every stage of the accounting the whole question would come into view at once as to what appropriations of this Parliament were made because the lands were reserved to us, and what were not. I do not think the wit of man could ever tell that. In respect to immigration, for instance, could it be told? Are you going to ascribe all the expenditure this Government has been put to for immigration in all these years to the fact that these lands were reserved, and reserved for immigration purposes? I do not think you should. It is true some of it was, but can any human being tell how much was? I do not think so. Nor could any human being tell what money was spent by this Government in respect of railways, in respect of water-powers, in respect of irrigation, in respect of many of these subjects arising from that fact. It could not be done by any process of accounting. You might make some rough attempt at a conclusion, but that is all it would be. I have urged upon the premiers of the different provinces that they should be ready to say just what they would be ready to do in respect to a deduction of the subsidy. If they are not prepared to accept any deduction at all, let them say so, and then we will say whether we consider it fair or not; but they have made no 851
statement in that regard. That is the position at the present time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I should like to say a word or two on the question of natural resources, since it has come up. I recollect quite distinctly in the year 1905, members of the then Federal Government coming into our province to endeavour to persuade the electors that the subsidies to be granted to the provinces in lieu of our natural resources was the best thing that could happen to the provinces. Now, I am not yet prepared to admit that the electorate of the Province of Saskatchewan really believed the statements that were made to them at that time, although perhaps the vote in the elections might show that they did. I myself took the view at that time, as I do to-day, that the natural resources of the province of Saskatchewan rightly belonged to the province. While under that influence we accepted the subsidy, the question has always been a very live one in the West and we have made repeated requests to different Governments and Oppositions that our natural resources be given back to us. I was one of a committee of three that waited upon the leader of the Opposition in the year 1911 in the city of Weyburn, and when we made the request that the natural resources should be handed over to the province we received the very positive statement that immediately upon the accession to office of the Conservative party of that time our natural resources would be handed to us. We accepted that statement in good faith, but as soon as the party got into power other considerations entered in, and obstacles were raised. Up to the present time I do not know that there has been as much earnestness shown by the Federal Government as has been shown by the provincial governments in an effort to get what we claim is simple justice.
I do not wish at this time to discuss the natural resources, as the subject is somewhat foreign to the question before us, but I think a resolution on the subject should be brought into the House later on. Representatives of our group will have something to say on that question.
I wish to endorse what has been said by the hon. member for Dorchester as to the minister who is in charge of these Estimates not being in a position to make the positive statements that I believe the House should have. It is deplorable, from my

point of view at least, that we should ask for information and be unable to receive a positive declaration from the minister giving us the precise facts asked for. When his own Estimates were before the House he could give us positive and reassuring statements, but to-night, in answer to questions by hon. gentlemen, all he can say is "I think this" and "I think that," which I submit must be absolutely unsatisfactory to all hon. members Who listen to the minister. I am sure that the minister himself must feel that in those circumstances he is handicapped in his efforts to give to the House such information as it has a right to expect. I do not know what to suggest in order to improve things, but I do think that almost any condition would be as good as the present. A large amount of money is being expended in this department, and I am sure the tax payers will demand some positive answers to the questions that are asked by hon. members. The older members of the House can perhaps suggest ways and means whereby we may be able to obtain the information we require. Personally, I think that it is certainly due to hon. members that definite answers should be made in reply to such queries as they put to the Government, and I do seriously submit that the present state of affairs is not satisfactory.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
This is a large item
and, as has been said, the Government has chosen for the purpose of putting it through an hon. gentleman who enjoys the greatest degree of sympathy on our side. Now, we are willing to show our sympathy by meeting him half way, and if it is agreed that we shall adjourn after the passage of this item, we will let it pass.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
We can let this item
pass if the Government agrees to adjourn.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I should really like to
have another department, that of Labour, entered upon, but I am prepared to accept the terms of the hon. member. We should surely get some more business done another night, however, and I sincerely trust that if another amendment comes on we shall be able to confine the debate thereon within reasonable limits.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I desire some information regarding the regulations appertaining to oil leases, which, I understand, are under the department. As these items are going through we find, from time to time, that it is impossible to go back in 
order to obtain information on subjects that have already been disposed of. The leader of the Government sometimes evinces a denseness in comprehending some remarks of hon. members on this side, and it is possible that when we come to some other item that may be in this department, we will find it convenient to press the Chairman to restrict the members on this side to the subject immediately under consideration. Now, there has been a great change in the regulations concerning oil leases in western Canada. The minister in charge of these Estimates may not be as familiar with the regulations as is the Prime Minister, who was previously in charge of this department. Will the right hon. gentleman inform me what led to the conclusion that the leases should not be allowed in future', as in the past, for prospectors to locate on Dominion lands with a view to prospecting for oil in Northern Alberta, oi British Columbia, or elsewhere? I do not know whether there is any other item in these Estimates that might afford an opportunity for putting this question, and I am anxious to have this information, because the matter is of considerable importance to the people of western Canada at the present time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
There is no doubt as
to the importance of the subject. The hon. member could undoubtedly bring up the discussion in several ways. He could introduce it under the item for Dominion Lands and Parks. That would be the proper item under which to discuss it, but of course it could not be taken up to-night; or he could have brought it up on a motion made some little time ago by the member for East Edmonton (Mr. Mackie), which was debated at some length; or on two or three other motions which are still on the Order Paper, if they are not disposed of, by the same hon. member. In the debate on the motion of the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Griesbach), I went into the subject in some detail. I have no doubt the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) was not here-

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Yes, I was, but no specific answer was given.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Oh my, yes; I gave a
rather complete answer as to why the leases were changed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: What was it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot give as complete a statement to-night as I gave on that occasion. At that time I had a memorandum on the subject. However,

I can give a little information regarding the matter. In the first place, I do not think there has been any material change in respect to the provinces my hon. friend refers to, that is, in respect to Dominion lands in Alberta, the Peace River belt, and the railway belt-the only parts we control -and Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Prom the best of my recollection, the only changes there, are in regard to the imposition of royalty, which it was thought was justified in the public interest, in order that the people as a whole might get some share of these resources, which are the property of the people of Canada. But there was a pretty substantial change in regard to the North West Territories lands, for the reason that it was felt that after the Fort Norman discovery, that field could be legitimately regarded, not as one for prospectors only, but as a proven field, where the existence of oil in quantity had been established, and consequently it was considered that the regulations should be altered so as to give that protection to the public interest that was justified, after the time of experiment had passed and the time of actually proven field had come. That is the reason for the change. It was felt that as oil in quantity had actually been discovered, it was not unjust that we should change the regulations so as to bring a larger share of the ultimate result, to the treasury. Consequently, it was provided that only one section in four should be finally taken by the locator, the other three reverting to the Crown, and also that the royalties therein provided for, should be reserved to the Crown. Now, I have given the hon. gentleman the reasons. The matter is under consideration to-day. You may go so far in restrictions as to discourage exploitation, and it is under consideration whether or not some fair priority right to the other three sections, 640 acres, might not in fairness be reserved to the man whose courage and venture are responsible for the location of the first section. That is under consideration; I cannot intimate whether it shall be done or not. Now, I have stated concisely the reason why the change was made in these regulations; it was because of a change in circumstances. The field passes from one fit only for a prospector in the hope "that oil might be found, to a field where oil has been found, or what is known as a proven field.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Have the regulations,
since the passing of that Order in Council,
been strictly lived up to, or have any filings been allowed since then?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: So far as I know, they have been strictly lived up to. The Order as first passed had, I think, a certain retroactive effect which was afterwards removed. I am not sure that I can give the exact date or the circumstances. There were certain applications for leases which would have to be denied under the regulations as first passed, and on representations made by very many it was felt that that was unjust, and the retroactive effect was removed. Every regulation has been lived up to, so far as I am aware, and I would be very much surprised if the Minister of the Interior did not insist that they be lived up to.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I understood the Prime
Minister to say that a man was now permitted to take in one whole section, whereas previously he could take in a tract not exceeding in all nineteen hundred and forty acres.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Nineteen hundred and twenty acres.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Was that the regulation
and is it still in force?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I cannot say just how he was allowed to take it. Previously he was allowed to have 1920 acres, but now he can only have 640 under the regulations as they stand in the Territories. I explained in detail the other day how the area might be taken out. I think I can recall the explanation and it is this:	He
can take out as much as four sections, or 2,560 acres, in four rectangular blocks. That is, he can file upon four restangular blocks aggregating not more than 2,560 acres, but within a certain period after he has had time to determine what he wants, if he has paid rent on the whole thing for one year, he then must select a square block containing not more than 640 acres, and in respect of that alone he gets a lease, that is all he is entitled to. At present it is under consideration whether he should not have the same right to the remaining three-quarters, in priority to others who may come after him and share the advantage of the risk that he ran.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Could the Prime Minister tell us what extent of land was leased on the retroactive policy as enunciated by him? He says that there were some people who had made claims to leases, and that they were allowed a retroactive right.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I could not give the
number of applications or the extent of lands to which they referred. I did hear the figures hut could not now recall them. I think there were quite a number.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Could the Prime Minister give the names of the people who made these applications?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I do not think I could
give the name of a single applicant.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Could the Prime Minister tell me whether a General Lindsay secured any lands under that arrangement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I could not tell my
hon. friend definitely, but I do not think so. The hon. gentleman's reference to General Lindsay must be in regard to another incident altogether.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: That may or may not be the case.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
If it is not then I
do not know anything about it. I do not think General Lindsay had any oil lands at all. So far as I know he had none except to this extent: he had a lease, made while I was Minister of the Interior, in respect of a certain area of land upon which he had the right to perform certain experiments in order to discover whether or not oil could be commercially produced from th oil sands. That is what General Lindsay got. I remember revising that lease over and over again after it was submitted to me by the officers of the department, and it finally went through. Whether General Lindsay has made much progress or not in his experiments I do not know, but I sincerely hope he has. So far as I know, or have ever heard, General Lindsay took out no leases of oil lands beyond what this particular contract made with the department gave him a right to have.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: When was that arrangement of which the Prime Minister speaks made with General Lindsay?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I will have to speak from recollection purely. I think it was about the spring of last year. I left the department in July and the arrangement was made, I would think, within six months of the time I left and at least three months before.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
On page 81 I notice that mention is made of a gentleman who holds a very lowly position, having regard to the salary paid him. He gets a salary of

$1,000 and occupies the position of cabinet maker. I would have suggested to the Prime Minister that when he left the Department of the Interior he should have brought his cabinet maker with him, or rather have brought a Cabinet reconstructor. Had he done that it would have saved him a great deal of the difficulty which, I understand, he has experienced since he became Prime Minister. Had he brought with him a gentleman learned in the art of cabinet making when he succeeded to the position of Prime Minister I have no doubt he would have succeeded better and would not have to encounter the serious difficulties which confront him at present. All that by way of coming to the question as to what the cabinet maker does in the department. What are the duties of this cabinet maker, and what has he got to do with Dominion lands?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: The cabinet maker in the Department of the Interior repairs furniture. He also makes boxes for shipping or moving specimens about from one place to another, and is a general handy man in any work around the department that requires the use of tools.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: May I ask the Minister whether the department has at its disposal the miniature natural resources cabinets "which formerly were distributed to schools of a certain grade-cabinets filled, I think with specimens of the different minerals of the country? If so, I would like to know if these cabinets can now be obtained from the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
There are none in the
Department of the Interior, but they may still be issuing them in connection with the Mines Branch. I will get that information for my hon. friend when we take up the Estimates of that branch.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I am sorry that at this late hour we are obliged to let the item pass without having full information in regard to a good many details. For instance, I notice that on page 80 of the Estimates reference is made to an International Boundary Commissioner and a Surveyor General. I would like to find out whether the duties of the two gentleman are identical or not? I would also like to ascertain whether the Surveyor General has drawn a line showing the boundary between Labrador and the Province of Quebec, and what lands are possessed by Newfound-

land and the Province of Quebec, repesct-ively, in the Ungava district?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: The Surveyor General and the International Boundary Commissioner are by no means the same man. The Surveyor General is Doctor Deville and the Boundary Commissioner is Mr. J. J. McCarthy. That is the answer to the hon. gentleman's first question. In reply to his next question as to the work of the International Boundary Commission, I understand all that the commission has to do is simply complete the preparation of the reports. The work has been tapering off for some time and, I believe, is now complete. As to whether the Surveyor General has delimited the boundary between Newfoundland and Canada on the Labrador cCast, I have no doubt that that boundary is laid out in the main and can be located all right as it is placed by Canada. It should be located by Canada and the province of Quebec. The location, I believe, is now under way, though it has never been actually brought, to a head. I have always felt that the province of Quebec is chiefly concerned in this matter, and that when it is brought to a head the province of Quebec and the Dominion should be specially represented by counsel. I do not know just what is delaying the matter now, but I am quite certain that if at any time the province of Quebec wishes to go ahead their wishes will be very carefully, and probably sympathetically, considered.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I find that out of 822
employees in this department there are 524 clerks and clerk stenographers. I see there are 339 clerks and 185 stenographers, or 524 out of a total of 822 employees in this department.'' What class of work are these clerks and stenographers doing, and are they fully employed all the time? If they are not fully employed, is it the intention to reduce the staff and cut down expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
These clerks are all fully engaged in the various departments, such as the mines department, the lands department, the natural resources branch, the mines branch, the observatories and the waterways. It is the intention of the minister to reorganize the various branches and to economize. He is already combining certain branches to lessen the staff; and while the Civil Service Commission makes the appointments and fixes the salaries, he has the right to dismiss any of his staff for whom he has no woi'k. With the exception of the
statutory increases this year, there has been no increase in this department.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I see there is a small
vote for the Commissioner of Dominion Parks. If my memory serves me right the Prime Minister last year introduced legislation concerning our Dominion parks. Have any new parks been formed under this law; if so, where?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I am informed that no new parks have been constituted. The Commissioner of Dominion Parks is Mr. Harkin, a very old public servant. I do not know that I have quite in mind the legislation the hon member refers to. Was it an Act providing for the creation of new parks?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: It was passed two years ago if I am not mistaken.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I remember something was done as to Point Pelee shortly afterwards. I have before me a list of all the parks: Rocky Mountains park, Yoho park, Glacier park, Revelstoke park, Kootenay park, Jasper park, Waterton lakes, St. Lawrence islands, Broder park-this park was created in 1919-Buffalo park, Elk island, Foremost Antelope reserve, Fort Howe, Fort Anne, Port Pelly park reserve, Point Pelee. Two of those parks have been created since the passing of the Act referred to by the hon. member.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
What are the duties of
the superintendent of the Natural Resources Intelligence department?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: That gentleman is Mr. Lynch, to whom I referred some time ago. The Natural Resources Intelligence department collects and distributes intelligence respecting the natural resources of Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I noticed in the press a
few days ago that two townships were to be taken out of the Riding Mountain park in the Dauphin district. My recollection is that that is a rolling country of a more or less sandy nature, and a few years ago it would not have been considered as at all fit for settlement. Are these lands of first class quality? What was the report of the surveyor general when he originally surveyed these lands?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
quite right as to the Riding Mountain park being rolling country and generally light as to soil. The Government was urged, according to my recollection solely by returned men, to open certain parts of that park that were suitable for farming. The Parks

branch usually resists anything being taken out of the parks, and the Forestry branch almost invariably resists. Consequently a survey, was made by officers jointly, and as a result of that survey very small areas were authorized by Parliament to be taken out. I think that only part of what was authorized was taken out. The amount found fit for cultivation was relatively very small indeed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
The newspaper report
mentioned two townships. I would think it would be impossible to get that area of good land in the Riding Mountain park. What was the area taken out, and was it taken in consecutive sections?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: The exact area taken out can be obtained, and I will secure the information. I know, speaking from memory, there was nothing like two townships taken out, and I think the newspaper report must be in error in that regard. I think there were isolated pieces taken at three or four different points.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
The newspaper report
may have been in error.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: It may have been right, but I do not think so.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I am quite willing to accept the Prime Minister's word as to that. I always accept his statements here when I have to. But I am not asking now for what may be nearly accurate, but for accurate information from the department, and I do not think the Prime Minister will attempt to argue that such a request is unfair. I presume that these sections or quarter sections of land were at least on the fringe of the reserve. I hope it has not been the custom of the department to go in and select portions of land in the interior of the reserve for settlers to take up. I do not think the minister could expect members of the Opposition to quietly sit down and allow the Government to dispose of all the parks without asking some questions, nor do I think that he should resent the asking of questions about any of our parks. Certainly the minister in charge of the Estimates should have information about this transaction. I think that he should be in a position to state what portions have been taken and under what conditions they have been taken-whether or not the land has been passed as good agricultural land. I can understand that there are Indian reserves and park reserves adjacent to settlement, in some cases close to railways, that a settler would take in preference to better land in a district furf -Ur. MeighenJ
ther away from settlement or from railways, but whether it would be good business to allow such lands to be taken up simply because of their more desirable location is another question and a question for the Government to answer. If those lands are not first-class farm lands it is a question open to debate whether the Government should allow them to be settled on. The Minister of Agriculture had the experience in Kapuskasing in Northern Ontario of settling people on land where they could make no headway, and the Ontario Government has since taken them out of there. A similar condition might arise with respect to settlements on the western lands controlled by the Government. Unless the land will provide a living for the returned soldier, he should not be allowed to settle on it. I would like from the minister in charge of the Estimates a report of the surveyors-not only the recent report but the original report, because these lands were originally surveyed some forty years ago and in each case the Surveyor-General made an accurate report of the condition of the land. Is the minister prepared to take the responsibility of placing returned soldiers on this land whether they are experienced men or not?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: The Act stipulated the land that was authorized to be taken out. When the Act was passed full information was given to the House as to why it was passed and as to the reports upon which it was based. I do not know whether or not all that was authorized to be taken out was taken out or what the area was; no minister and no officer would carry that in his head. I have said to the hon. member that the exact area will be given to him while these Estimates are before the committee.	-

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
The Prime Minister seems to imply that every member on this side should know of all legislation and every Order in Council that is passed and of everything that takes place in this House. It has been the custom for the Government to state each evening what business will be taken up in the House the next day. At the last sitting the Prime Minister said that certain Estimates would be brought up, and members who were not interested in those two items-perhaps I should say "departments", because the right hon. gentleman called me to order the other day for using the word "item" instead of "department"-members of the Opposition who were not particularly interested in the

departments which were to be taken up might not think it necessary to be in their places in the House. After giving us his assurance that two specific departments would be taken up, the Prime Minister came down to-day and moved to go into supply on an entirely different department. I thought I heard the Minister of Marine make a statement to the House today, and I thought I heard a letter read from the Prime Minister to the leader of the Opposition stating that the Minister of Marine wished to make a statement. During the discussion on that statement it was impossible for members of the Opposition to know whether it was the intention to go into the Marine Estimates or not; of course, if you went into the matter when the Estimates were up, the chairman would very properly tell you that you should not object to the principle of the Merchant Marine while any single item was being dealt with. If the Prime Minister will continue the practice which, I understand, has been in vogue for many years, of giving information in a straightforward way so that members of the Opposition shall have an intimation of what to expect on the following day, he will, perhaps, find not quite so much opposition to some of the things which he wishes to do. All hon. members on this side, I am sure, are quite anxious to oppose most of the measures of the Government because their measures as a rule are opposed to the principles of Liberalism. But there are some members on this side-I am not speaking for myself now-who have no desire to obstruct legislation or to obstruct Estimates, and if the minister in charge wishes to make such fine distinctions between words and terms and thinks that he is going to make any headway by criticising and lecturing members of the Opposition every time they ask for information, I think he will find that he is heading toward the bottom of the well, not toward the top.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: What I stated to the House in answer to the leader of the Opposition was that we would take up the departments of Labour and Interior, and that immediately on getting into supply we would take up the Department of the Interior. That constitutes an answer to the hon. member. He refers to some lecturing that has been done from this side; I do not know who did it. I plead not guilty on behalf of all concerned.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I accept the Prime Minister's explanation, of course. He stated that the Department of the Interior would be taken up, but what better intimation could we hiave of what department is to be taken up than in the fact that a certain minister makes the motion to go into Supply or speaks to the motion when it is made? It has been the custom, at least since I have been here, for the minister to make a general statement regarding his department on a motion to go into Supply. If the .Minister of Marine wished to make that statement-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I regret that I must call the hon. member to order. His remarks are certainly not relevant to the item before the committee. We cannot, without having a point of order before the Chair, enter into a discussion of customs and procedure and continue that discussion during the entire evening.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: How long has the present minister been in charge of the department; since he has been in charge how many employees have been dismissed from the department, and what are the names of those who have dismissed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: The minister has been in charge since July 10, 1920. There have been two or three dismissals. Several have been retired under the statute passed by the House and given the gratuity or allowance provided by the statute. That has been done in the interest of economy. If the hon. member wishes to have the names, I will secure them and give them to him while the estimates of this department are under consideration.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: I would imagine that the official in front of the Prime Minister would be able to furnish the information now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: He informs me that he has not the information here.'

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: What are the duties of the director of water-powers, and in what part or parts of Canada 'does he carry out those duties?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
His name is Mr. J. B.
Challies. He performs services in all parts of Canada, directly in the provinces where the resources are the property of the Dominion, through the Governments of the other provinces where the resources are not the the property of the Dominion. Arrangements have been made, I know, with New

Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Ontario, and, I am informed, with Quebec. The services of that branch, which is under the charge of Mr. Challies, are in that way for the purposes of getting information for the use of the water-powers of all the provinces. If the hon. member will consult the Government of his province, he will find they are highly appreciative of the assistance given by that branch.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: According to the statement of the Prime Minister, the director of waterpowers has something to do with the province of Quebec, and he led us to understand that the Dominion Government and the Provincial Government had come to some understanding as to the duties of that man in Quebec. The statement of the right hon. gentleman may be correct; I would like to take it as such; if it is, we are entitled to more details so as to find out what has taken place between the Federal Government and the Government of Quebec as regards the director of waterpowers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I am informed by the
official who is in front of me that they have been doing work in Quebec, although I cannot recollect it myself. I recollect agreements with Ontario, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. I have letters from at least one or two of the members of those Governments appreciative of the work done. I do not know that any difficulty has arisen with respect to the Quebec Government. It may be that the information given to me is not correct. I have a recollection myself of negotiations with the Government of Quebec; but I will get the full details for the hon'. gentleman, and when this matter comes up under the appropriation for Dominion lands and parks, which we are not taking up now, Mr. Challies will be present himself.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: It comes under the director of waterpowers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: That is just the salary of the director, but all information as to what he does and his branch does in the various provinces properly comes under the appropriation for Dominion lands and parks. Mr. Challies will be available and the very fullest information can be given.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I should like to obtain
a great deal of information with regard to the director of forestry and details of what has been done by this department for forestry. I should like, if, at some future time when these Estimates are before the House, I might be allowed to discuss the

question of forestry, to call the Government's attention to the fact that in the eastern provinces a large number of big trees are being destroyed by bud-worms and other worms and to point out that it is the duty of the federal Government to help the provincial governments to overcome these pests. It is true the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Can-2 a.m. non) says that the provinces do not need the federal Government money; but in this respect at any rate, I contend that the forests of our country are of such paramount importance that the federal Government should assist in every possible way to look after their conservation and preservation. I should like also, at the time that these other Estimates are brought up, to go into the question with the minister of what body is taking the place of the Commission of Conservation with regard, for instance, to losses that might be occasioned in our forests by fire. All this, I am led to understand, subject, of course, to correction, could be gone into when other items under this department are before the House.
I should like, on my own behalf, to make this statement to the Prime Minister, that I think really we should begin our sittings about eight o'clock every evening. I notice that, as time goes on, as the hour grows later, the Prime Minister becomes more sweet tempered. This evening, and particularly in the last two hours, he has given us a remarkable example of how courteous and well disposed he can be. I would hope that the Prime Minister would be always so well disposed to give us information.
I am sure, if such were the case, we on this side of the House would be able to assist him, as we have assisted him tonight, in laying the details of the various departments before the House and the country. Really, in the future, if the Prime Minister would show the same disposition and magnanimity which he has shown to-night, we would have reciprocal arrangements of some kind whereby the business of the House would be greatly facilitated.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
Will it be possible for
the minister at some other date to take up the question of the policy of the Government with regard to homesteads? I mentioned this matter to the minister before, and at that time he seemed to intimate that the Government might institute a different policy with regard to homesteads; that is, they might adopt a policy of restricting homesteading to what might be

regarded as the railway area of the country and not allow settlers to take up homesteads in the more remote parts of Canada where they would have no chance of railway facilities and where, in a great many cases, they would be only taking hardships on themselves without being of any productive value to the country generally. Has any new policy been adopted by the Government, or has the Government considered the advisability of restricting homestead settlement to what might be regarded as the railway area of the country?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
No new policy has
been adopted, nor has a change been under the general consideration of the Government. The subject has been pretty fully discussed in the House on other occasions. 'There is a great deal to be said both ways; there is a great deal to be said in favour of doing away with homesteads altogether, but the Government has not come to that conclusion as yet. An opportunity for a discussion of the question, of course, will come on any of the remaining items, at least when those involving grants for Dominion lands are under review.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Item agreed to.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: Report progress.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext: An hour has gone by since the suggestion was made by the hon. member for Three Rivers that if the item passed we would take up no other item and go into no other department. However, on this occasion I shall not press the point, but on another occasion when the hon. member for Three Rivers or any other member comes to an understanding I think it would be well that it be lived up to or that the Government feel themselves free to take such procedure as they may deem advisable.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE GENERAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER
speechtext:
I think we would make greater progress if the Committee rose now.
Progress reported.
On the motion of Right Hon. Mr. Meighen,. the House adjourned at 2.12 a.m.
Wednesday.
Wednesday, March 30, 1921.
